items.title: South Korea commits $1 trillion to expand memory chip production, build AI data centers, and commercialize humanoid robots by 2028 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: South Korea to spend $1T on more memory chip production and humanoid robots
items.summary:
South Korea plans to invest $1 trillion by 2028 to expand its memory chip production, develop AI data centers, and commercialize humanoid robots. This initiative aims to strengthen the country's position in the global semiconductor market, support AI infrastructure, and advance physical AI technologies, including robotics for industrial use. The government and major tech companies like Samsung, SK Hynix, and Hyundai are leading these efforts to meet rising demand driven by the AI industry.

The investment includes $585 billion for new chip fabrication plants to double DRAM production, $357 billion for AI data centers across various provinces, and significant funding to develop humanoid robots through Hyundai's partnership with Boston Dynamics. These projects require substantial energy and water resources, prompting plans to secure power from renewable and nuclear sources. However, the push for automation has sparked concerns among labor unions about job security, leading to potential strikes and public debate over the distribution of profits from the AI boom.

items.title: Moondream details GPU bubble in AI model inference and introduces pipelined decoding to improve GPU utilization and reduce idle time [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Popping the GPU Bubble
items.summary:
Moondream's blog post explores the inefficiencies in GPU utilization during AI model inference, specifically addressing the issue known as the "GPU bubble," where GPUs remain idle while waiting for CPU instructions. The company introduces its inference engine, Photon, which uses a technique called pipelined decoding to overlap CPU and GPU tasks, significantly improving throughput and reducing idle time during token generation in language models.

The article details how traditional sequential processing causes the GPU to wait for the CPU to complete housekeeping tasks between generating tokens, leading to underutilization. Photon overcomes this by launching GPU computations for the next token before the CPU finishes processing the previous one, using mechanisms like ping-pong buffer slots to manage memory safely and maintain continuous GPU operation.

This approach allows Moondream to achieve near real-time inference speeds and up to 35% higher decoding throughput on NVIDIA hardware. The innovation highlights potential improvements in AI model efficiency by optimizing hardware coordination, which could influence future developments in AI inference engines and GPU utilization strategies.

items.originalTitle: LongCat-2.0, a large-scale MoE model with 1.6T total and 48B Active
items.summary:
LongCat has announced the release of LongCat-2.0, a large-scale mixture of experts (MoE) model featuring 1.6 trillion parameters, with 48 billion active parameters during operation. This development represents a significant advancement in scalable AI model architecture, aiming to enhance performance and efficiency in handling complex tasks.

The model leverages a mixture of experts approach to activate only a subset of its parameters for each input, allowing it to maintain a massive overall size while managing computational resources effectively. This design enables LongCat-2.0 to deliver powerful capabilities without the proportional increase in processing demands typically associated with such large models.

items.title: Ornith-1.0 launches self-improving open-source coding models with 9B to 397B parameters, featuring reinforcement learning and 256K token context windows [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Ornith-1.0: self-improving open-source models for agentic coding
items.summary:
Ornith-1.0 is a new open-source suite of self-improving coding models ranging from 9 billion to 397 billion parameters, designed to enhance agentic coding through reinforcement learning. These models, which include dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, achieve state-of-the-art performance on several coding benchmarks such as Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench. They feature a large 256K token context window and are licensed under MIT, making them freely accessible worldwide.

The models are built on top of Gemma 4 and Qwen 3.5 and utilize a novel training framework that jointly optimizes solution generation and the scaffolding guiding those solutions, improving search trajectories and output quality. Ornith-1.0 supports multiple serving environments, including vLLM and SGLang, and offers compatibility with OpenAI-style tool calls and reasoning parsers, facilitating advanced reasoning and tool integration in coding tasks.

Ornith-1.0's availability in various precision and format variants allows deployment on single or multi-GPU setups, with the smaller 9B model fitting on a single 80GB GPU and larger MoE models requiring distributed tensor parallelism. This release represents a significant advancement in open-source coding AI, providing powerful, scalable tools for developers and researchers.

items.title: Developer uses AI assistance to diagnose and address parsing regression in hyperscript language, illustrating AI's strengths and limitations in debugging [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Working With AI: A concrete example
items.summary:
A developer detailed their experience using AI assistance to diagnose and address a parsing regression in the hyperscript language, highlighting both the strengths and limitations of AI in debugging complex code. The issue arose from a recent update that caused the parser to misinterpret certain expressions, and AI helped quickly identify the root cause related to grammar changes during refactoring.

While AI was effective in pinpointing the problem, it was less successful in proposing a robust fix, offering solutions that were either too specific or introduced unnecessary complexity. This case illustrates the potential of AI as a valuable tool in software development, but also underscores the importance of human judgment to avoid overreliance and to implement appropriate solutions.

items.title: Researchers present TraceRetain, a framework for selective memory retention in frozen LLM agents that improves task success and robustness under noisy conditions in ALFWorld benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Selective Memory Retention for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced TraceRetain, a framework designed to enhance memory retention in frozen large language model (LLM) agents by selectively managing external memory based on features like success, age, and relevance. Tested on the ALFWorld benchmark with the gpt-5-mini model, TraceRetain demonstrated improved task success and robustness, particularly under noisy conditions where traditional memory approaches degraded significantly. The framework effectively maintains high task performance by evicting less useful memory entries, preventing memory pollution caused by distractors.

In controlled experiments with synthetic noise, TraceRetain preserved task success rates and precision, outperforming unbounded memory and FIFO-based retention methods. Evaluations showed that memory-augmented policies solved more tasks compared to no-memory baselines, highlighting the benefits of bounded retention for efficiency without sacrificing accuracy. The study suggests that selective memory retention is especially valuable in environments with noisy data streams, offering a practical approach to improving long-horizon LLM agent performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When does retention matter for memory-augmented LLM agents? We study this with TraceRetain, a lightweight framework for bounded external memory in frozen LLM agents that scores entries by interpretable features (success, age, access frequency, redundancy, specificity, similarity, downstream utility) and evicts the lowest-scoring ones at capacity. On clean ALFWorld with gpt-5-mini, external memory robustly improves over no memory across two seeds, but differences among bounded retention policies fall within Wilson 95% CIs: clean ALFWorld at T=100 to T=200 does not naturally exhibit the memory pollution retention is designed to address. Under a controlled noisy-write stress (75% synthetic distractors), unbounded memory and FIFO-K50 degrade on Precision@5 (20.2% to 12.4% and 15.8% to 3.8%) while TraceRetain-CEM is essentially unchanged (16.9% to 16.6%) and preserves 97/100 task success. The mechanism: unbounded memory has the highest mean similarity (0.87) but lowest precision, indicating failed distractors close to the query in embedding space. Held-out in-distribution evaluation shows memory-augmented policies solving 47 to 49 of 50 tasks vs. 39/50 for no memory. Bounded retention buys memory and step efficiency on saturated clean benchmarks at no task-success cost, and only differentiates from cache heuristics when streams contain noise.

items.title: Researchers propose evidence-informed belief updates for large language models to improve continual scientific discovery by increasing non-stationary surprisal and reducing spurious rewards in hypothesis search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evidence-Informed LLM Beliefs for Continual Scientific Discovery
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a method to improve continual scientific discovery using large language models (LLMs) by updating their beliefs based on prior evidence. This approach addresses limitations in existing methods like AutoDiscovery, which treat surprisal—a measure of how surprising new information is—as static, whereas human reasoning considers surprisal relative to evolving beliefs. By incorporating evidence-informed belief updates, the researchers enable LLMs to compute non-stationary surprisal, better reflecting the dynamic nature of scientific inquiry.

The study compares different belief-updating mechanisms and finds that embedding-based retrieval augmented generation over prior discoveries most effectively anticipates updated beliefs, identifying a significant portion of static surprisals as spurious. The researchers introduce belief-update filtering and diversity maximization to the hypothesis search process, which together increase accumulated non-stationary surprisal by over 30% across multiple discovery domains. This demonstrates that continual scientific discovery with LLMs benefits from both improved belief measurement and search strategies that reduce redundancy and promote diverse hypotheses.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-ended scientific discovery with large language models (LLMs) increasingly operates as a long-horizon loop of hypothesis search and verification, where a reward signal guides which hypotheses to test next. A notable recent example is AutoDiscovery, which uses "Bayesian surprise" - the belief shift an LLM undergoes after observing evidence for a hypothesis - as both a discovery metric and a reward for search. We first observe that AutoDiscovery treats surprisal as a static quantity, while surprisal in human reasoning is non-stationary - it is defined relative to beliefs that evolve with experience, a prerequisite for continual scientific discovery. We address this mismatch with evidence-informed LLM beliefs: priors updated with evidence from previous hypotheses to compute non-stationary surprisal for new hypotheses. We compare in-context belief-updating mechanisms and find that embedding-based retrieval-augmented generation over prior discoveries best anticipates eventual posteriors, identifying 37.5% of static surprisals as spurious. We then modify search to avoid these spurious rewards and prioritize hypotheses that remain surprising under non-stationary beliefs. Concretely, we introduce two complementary changes to the original search procedure: belief-update filtering and diversity maximization. Across five discovery domains, our method increases accumulated non-stationary surprisal by 30.62% on average compared to the original search procedure, demonstrating that continual scientific discovery with LLMs requires not only better belief measurement but also search procedures that avoid redundancy and encourage diversity.

items.title: Researchers introduce EvalSafetyGap, a hybrid survey and conceptual framework analyzing LLM evaluation-safety failures across eight evidence streams from 2018 to 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EvalSafetyGap: A Hybrid Survey and Conceptual Framework for LLM Evaluation-Safety Failures
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced EvalSafetyGap, a hybrid survey and conceptual framework designed to analyze failures in large language model (LLM) evaluation and AI safety from 2018 to 2026. This work addresses the challenge that improvements in benchmark scores and safety metrics may not accurately reflect the underlying safety properties they intend to measure. EvalSafetyGap synthesizes evidence across eight key areas, including benchmark validity, dynamic evaluation, and governance, and employs a structured audit of ten models to compare evaluation and alignment proxy failures under optimization pressure.

The framework incorporates concepts such as Goodhart's Law, Instability Decomposition, and the Alignment Trilemma to facilitate testable comparisons. The audit reveals that the relationship between model capability and adversarial robustness is statistically inconclusive, with governance and disclosure playing a larger role in the observed safety gaps than behavioral robustness. Due to heterogeneous evaluation protocols, the audit serves as a diagnostic tool rather than a ranking system. This contribution provides a shared vocabulary and evidence map to support more transparent, dynamic, and auditable approaches to LLM safety evaluation and alignment practices.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM evaluation and AI safety face a shared measurement problem: benchmark scores, reward-model signals, and reported safety metrics can improve while the latent properties they are meant to represent remain difficult to verify. This paper combines a hybrid survey - a systematic search paired with narrative synthesis and separately tracked grey evidence - with a conceptual framework and a structured ten-model audit. The synthesis spans eight evidence streams: benchmark validity, dynamic evaluation, LLM-as-judge reliability, safety evaluation, jailbreak/refusal robustness, reward hacking, mechanistic interpretability, and governance/auditability, covering 2018-2026 evaluation-safety measurement work. We introduce EvalSafetyGap as an organizing hypothesis for comparing evaluation-side and alignment-side proxy failures under optimization pressure, using Goodhart's Law together with two constructs we develop here - an Instability Decomposition and an Alignment Trilemma - as tools for generating testable comparisons. The audit shows how conclusions shift when capability, behavioral safety, and governance are measured separately. In this sample (n = 10), the association between capability and sustained adversarial robustness is statistically indeterminate using the displayed Table 3 inputs (Pearson r = +0.232, p = 0.520), and the apparent open-closed safety gap is modest, driven mainly by governance and disclosure rather than behavioral robustness, and sensitive to how a single borderline model is classified; attempt-budget results are protocol dependent. Because the public evidence uses heterogeneous protocols, the audit is diagnostic rather than rank-generating. The contribution is a shared vocabulary and evidence map to support dynamic evaluation, transparent source reporting, multi-attempt safety measurement, and auditable alignment practice.

items.title: Researchers introduce PixelRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation method using web page screenshots in pixel space, outperforming text-based baselines on Wikipedia and open-domain QA tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PIXELRAG: Web Screenshots Beat Text for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PixelRAG, a novel retrieval-augmented generation method that processes web pages as pixel-based screenshots rather than text. This approach preserves the visual layout and formatting of websites, enabling an end-to-end system that retrieves and reads information directly from images. PixelRAG operates on a large-scale dataset of 30 million Wikipedia screenshots and outperforms traditional text-based retrieval methods on various question-answering benchmarks, including text-centric and multimodal tasks.

Built on a visual embedding model fine-tuned with contrastive training on screenshot data, PixelRAG feeds retrieved images directly into a vision-language model without converting them to text. This method not only improves accuracy by up to 18.1% over text-based baselines but also offers efficiency gains through image compression, reducing token costs by up to three times while maintaining performance. The findings suggest that web retrieval can be effectively conducted in the web's native visual form, challenging the conventional reliance on text representations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28344v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Augmenting large language models (LLMs) with retrieved web text has become a dominant paradigm, yet the web is not natively textual: existing systems depend on complex parsing pipelines that linearize HTML and discard layout, visual structure, and formatting. We introduce PixelRAG, a new retrieval-augmented method that represents websites in their native visual form and performs retrieval and reading entirely in pixel space, enabling an end-to-end architecture that eliminates text abstraction. PixelRAG is, to our knowledge, the first pipeline to operate over a full Wikipedia corpus in this form, scaling to a datastore of 30 million screenshot images with an efficient visual retrieval index. Built on an existing visual embedding model (i.e., Qwen3-VL-Embedding), PixelRAG further fine-tunes this model on screenshot data with carefully curated contrastive training data. Retrieved screenshots are then fed directly as pixel inputs to a VLM, without intermediate text conversion. PixelRAG consistently outperforms both no-retrieval and text-based RAG baselines, most surprisingly on widely studied text-centric tasks such as NQ and SimpleQA. It also achieves strong gains on multimodal open-domain QA (e.g., MMSearch), benchmarks over noisy news corpora (e.g., LiveVQA), and agentic benchmarks (e.g., MoNaCo), improving accuracy by up to 18.1% over text-based baselines. Finally, pixel representations enable a new efficiency lever for RAG through image compression, achieving up to 3x token cost reduction at lower resolutions while maintaining accuracy. Our results challenge the necessity of text representations in web retrieval, suggesting that web RAG can operate directly in the web's native visual form while improving both performance and efficiency.

items.title: Researchers propose LoRA-tuned large language model using multi-view speech features for dementia detection, achieving 90.14% F1-score on ADReSSo dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LoRA-Tuned Large Language Models for Dementia Detection via Multi-View Speech-Derived Features
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a low-rank adaptation (LoRA)-tuned large language model (LLM) that integrates multiple speech-derived features to detect dementia with high accuracy. By combining automatic speech recognition transcripts with pause markers, discourse-level topic cues, temporal fluency statistics, and phonological sequences into a unified prompt, the model achieves a 90.14% F1-score on the ADReSSo dataset without relying on separate modality-specific encoders or late-stage fusion.

This approach addresses limitations of previous methods that focused on single speech representations by enabling structured multi-view reasoning within a single LLM. Ablation studies confirm that each speech-derived feature contributes complementarily to the model's performance, highlighting the benefit of integrating diverse speech signals for early, non-invasive dementia screening.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28445v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Early detection of dementia enables timely intervention, and reflecting cognitive impairment, spontaneous speech offers a non-invasive screening modality. Conventional approaches often focus on a single representational dimension -- such as acoustic descriptors, pause modeling, automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcripts, or multimodal fusion -- limiting integrative reasoning across heterogeneous cognitive symptoms. We propose a low-rank adaptation (LoRA)-tuned large language model (LLM) that performs structured multi-view reasoning over four complementary speech-derived signals: ASR transcripts with pause markers, discourse-level topic cues, temporal fluency statistics, and phonological sequences. These cues are encoded within a unified prompt, enabling a single LLM to learn a coherent decision function without modality-specific encoders or late-stage fusion. On ADReSSo, our best model achieves an F1-score of 90.14%, and ablation confirms the complementary contribution of each view.

items.title: Researchers propose an agentic AI pipeline combining deep forecasting, anomaly detection, and LLM reasoning for appliance-level energy anomaly detection and maintenance recommendations in office buildings [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: An Agentic AI Pipeline for Appliance-Level Energy Anomaly Detection and LLM-Driven Recommendations
items.summary: Researchers have developed an integrated AI pipeline that enhances appliance-level energy anomaly detection and maintenance recommendations in office buildings. The system combines deep time-series forecasting, variational anomaly detection, and large language model (LLM) reasoning to provide prioritized, actionable insights for facility managers. It monitors seven office appliances using a hybrid forecasting model and flags abnormal energy consumption with a variational autoencoder, while a multi-stage LangChain pipeline generates structured diagnoses and human-readable reports, incorporating operator feedback through a reflective memory layer.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Appliance-level energy monitoring in office buildings produces noisy alerts that non-expert facility managers struggle to use. This paper proposes an end-to-end agentic pipeline that combines deep time-series forecasting, variational anomaly detection, and LLM-based reasoning to generate prioritized, actionable maintenance recommendations. The system tracks seven office appliances using a hybrid Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) forecasting model, and applies a per-appliance LSTM Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with attention to flag abnormal daily consumption episodes. A three-stage LangChain pipeline begins with a Context Agent that always retrieves three core RAG sources (model reliability, hourly baseline, and expert knowledge) and conditionally adds up to three more (forecast context, anomaly history, global baseline) based on event characteristics, capped at eight reasoning steps. A Diagnosis Agent converts the evidence into a structured JSON diagnosis, and a Report Agent renders a human-readable narrative. A reflective memory layer incorporates operator feedback. The dashboard shows real-time 30-minute forecasts, intraday consumption, the previous day anomaly report, and a feedback form. We evaluate the forecasting model, anomaly detector with appliance-specific thresholds, and LLM reasoning on a 16-scenario benchmark including sustained and transient spikes, unexpected shutdowns, and systemic events, comparing five LLM backends under static vs. dynamic retrieval. Dynamic retrieval matches full static retrieval across all backends while cutting average context from six to three-six sources per event. The best backend scores 90.4/100 with a 100% pass rate at a 70-point threshold, and a fully local 7B-parameter model passes all 16 scenarios.

items.title: Researchers propose SCSuff metric to evaluate sufficiency of large language model explanations based on models' own input beliefs, finding explanations generally insufficient and weakly correlated with size or accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What LLMs explain is not what they believe: Evaluating explanation sufficiency under models' own input beliefs
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a new metric called SCSuff to evaluate the sufficiency of free-text explanations provided by large language models (LLMs). This metric assesses whether explanations contain enough information to justify the model's output by using the model itself to generate alternative inputs based on its explanations, reflecting the model's own beliefs. Their findings indicate that LLM explanations are generally insufficient and show only weak correlations with model size, accuracy, or output entropy.

The study extends the concept of sufficiency from feature attributions to arbitrary explanations and highlights that explanation sufficiency depends on the input distribution, which must be explicitly defined. Experiments demonstrate that SCSuff aligns with targeted perturbation tests and that the metric can be predicted from internal model representations, suggesting its potential to guide the detection and improvement of explanation quality in LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains, where free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought and post-hoc rationales are used to justify model outputs. Yet it remains unclear whether these explanations are sufficient, i.e., if they contain enough information to explain the model's output-generating process. We generalize classical sufficiency from feature attributions to arbitrary explanations and prove that explanation sufficiency can change depending on the input distribution, which must be explicitly defined for LLM explanations. We propose using the LLM itself to generate alternative inputs conditioned on an explanation, capturing its beliefs about possible inputs. We formalize self-consistent sufficiency as a goal for free-text explanations and introduce an information-theoretic metric, SCSuff, that enables evaluation of free-text explanations without relying on predefined biases or shortcuts. Our experiments show that SCSuff agrees with targeted perturbation tests where applicable and demonstrate that explanation sufficiency can vary with the input distribution. We find LLM explanations are generally insufficient and weakly correlated with model size, accuracy, or output entropy. Analysis of final-token hidden states shows that top and bottom SCSuff scores can be predicted from internal representations, suggesting that SCSuff can guide detection and improvement of sufficient LLM explanations. items.title: Researchers identify modal and correlation ceilings in test-time scaling for language models, showing extra sampling can worsen answers and increase costs beyond a few dozen draws [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When More Sampling Hurts: The Modal Ceiling and Correlation Ceiling of Test-Time Scaling
items.summary:
Researchers have identified limits in the effectiveness of test-time scaling for language models, showing that sampling more than a few dozen times can actually degrade answer quality and increase computational costs. While drawing more samples initially raises the chance of generating a correct answer, the ability to select the right one plateaus early, creating an "identifiability gap" where additional samples do not improve final selection and may reinforce confident errors.

The study introduces the concepts of the modal ceiling and correlation ceiling, which mark the points beyond which extra sampling yields no benefit for answer selection or benchmark scoring, respectively. The authors propose a metric called the effective number of samples to quantify this cutoff, emphasizing that the main challenge lies in recognizing the correct answer rather than generating it. This insight suggests that language model systems should limit sampling to optimize performance and resource use.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People overthink; language models over-sample, and the extra effort can talk both into a worse answer. Reasoning systems answer a hard question by sampling it many times (test-time scaling), and the more they draw, the more often a correct answer turns up somewhere, so coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct try, climbs and appears to be progress. But a deployed system must return one answer, and choosing it, not knowing which try is right, is selection; selection is capped, and past a point extra samples only make the model surer of a confident mistake, even as every draw adds cost. The gap between climbing coverage and stalled selection, the identifiability gap, is the answer a model can produce but not pick. So the real question is not whether to sample but how far, and the answer is: not far. For picking an answer, the vote has already settled within a few dozen draws, the modal ceiling; for scoring a benchmark, sooner still, the correlation ceiling. Beyond that, extra draws cost compute and add nothing, and can even make the answer worse. This paper turns the cutoff into a single number, the effective number of samples, that any sampling run already reveals. The bottleneck is recognizing a right answer, not generating one.

items.title: Researchers find clinical evidence strength is encoded in language model representations but not reflected in their stated evidence grades across 22 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The strength of clinical evidence is recoverable from language model representations but not from their stated grades
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed 22 large language models (LLMs) to determine if these models encode the strength of clinical evidence in their internal representations and whether they explicitly convey this information when summarizing clinical claims. Using a dataset of over 45,000 clinical claims harmonized into a four-level evidence grading system, the study found that while a linear estimator could reliably recover evidence strength from the models' activations, the models themselves rarely stated accurate evidence grades. This discrepancy suggests that LLMs carry an implicit signal about evidence strength that is not reflected in their explicit outputs.

The study tested models ranging from 0.6 to 70 billion parameters, including general, medical, and reasoning-focused LLMs, and found that the recoverable evidence strength signal was largely lexical and distinct from factual truth. However, this signal did not generalize well across different topics or grading frameworks. Despite this, the models could still weakly identify claims with weak support. These findings highlight a gap between the internal knowledge of clinical LLMs and their communicated confidence, indicating that current models do not effectively express the strength of evidence in their summaries.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly summarize clinical evidence, where a claim's weight depends on how strongly it is supported. Yet these models convey confidence poorly, and properties they never state, such as truth, are often readable from their activations. Whether a clinical model registers evidence strength, distinct from truth, and states it when asked is untested, and any such signal could be lexical. We compiled 45,134 clinical claims from six public sources, harmonized 20,611 into a four-level evidence grade under three independent frameworks, and tested 22 local, open-weight LLMs from several developers (0.6-70 billion parameters; general, medical, and reasoning), with lexical, truth, and cross-framework controls. A linear estimator recovered the grade in every model (median AUROC 71.8), yet decodability did not rise with scale and was weakest in reasoning models. The grade the models stated fell to chance, 25-27 percentage points below the estimator. The recoverable signal was largely lexical and did not transfer across topics or frameworks, yet it was distinct from factual truth and still flagged weakly supported claims (AUROC 69.2). Clinical LLMs thus carry an ordered evidence-strength signal they do not express, so their stated grades fail to convey a claim's support even when it is recoverable from their representations and text.

items.title: Study compares affective cues in embeddings from 12 text encoders across three psychological emotion theories, finding instruction-aware open-weight models capture strong word-level affective information while proprietary models excel at sentence-level tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Comparative Study on Affective Cues in Text Embeddings Across Psychological Emotion Theories
items.summary: A study evaluated the affective information captured by embeddings from twelve recent text encoders across three psychological emotion theories, using both word- and sentence-level data. The research found that instruction-aware open-weight models contain as much or more word-level affective information compared to proprietary models, while proprietary and task-tuned encoders perform better on sentence-level affective classification tasks. The study also applied a semantic data-leakage prevention technique to enhance robustness and included a qualitative analysis of the affective cues encoded in the latent representations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text encoders are known for their utility in natural language processing, as they are able to efficiently compress inputs into dense vectors while preserving semantics. These models have been applied to affective computing, in particular to help with solving sentiment analysis and emotion recognition tasks. Nevertheless, it remains unclear to what extent the latent representations produced by modern text encoders capture well-defined psychological theories of affect. In this work, we investigate the affective capabilities of twelve recently released text encoders by probing their generated embeddings as input features for solving regression and classification tasks across three established emotion frameworks, using both word- and sentence-level data. Additionally, we apply a semantic data-leakage prevention technique to improve robustness in word-level evaluations. Our main findings show that the latent manifolds of the latest instruction-aware open-weight encoders enclose an equal or even a larger amount of affective information in comparison with proprietary counterparts when evaluated at word level. In contrast, embeddings of task-tuned and proprietary encoders reach the highest scores on sentence-level affective classification. Furthermore, a qualitative analysis of latent representations and their encoded affective cues is provided.

items.title: Researchers introduce Symbolic Mechanistic Data Attribution to trace training data influence on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct's behavioral policies, revealing safety gaps and feature interference in 200 fine-tuning pairs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Symbolic Mechanistic Data Attribution: Tracing Training Influence to Learned Behavioral Policies
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Symbolic Mechanistic Data Attribution (SMDA), a new framework that links training data to the interpretable symbolic policies guiding a model's behavior. Applying SMDA to Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, they analyzed 200 supervised fine-tuning pairs to trace how each example influences the model's refusal behavior, revealing safety gaps and feature interference in the training process.

SMDA uses Ridge regression over sparse autoencoder features to model target behaviors and decomposes the impact of training examples through feature activation and output probability pathways. This approach uncovers systematic weaknesses in the base model's safety responses, explains differing influences of harmful versus harmless training pairs, and identifies cases where training data affects unintended features.

By combining mechanistic interpretability with data attribution, SMDA offers a more detailed and scalable diagnostic tool than existing black-box influence methods or manual circuit analysis, enhancing understanding of how training data shapes high-level model decisions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While existing data attribution methods can identify which training examples build specific mechanistic circuits, they cannot explain how training data shapes the high-level behavioral decisions a model learns to make. To bridge this gap, we introduce Symbolic Mechanistic Data Attribution (SMDA), a framework that attributes training pairs to the interpretable symbolic policies governing model behavior. SMDA fits a closed-form Ridge regression over sparse autoencoder (SAE) features to model a target behavior, then analytically decomposes how each supervised fine-tuning example shifts that policy through feature-activation Delta_X and output-probability Delta_Y pathways. We distill a symbolic policy for refusal behavior in Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and analyze 200 SFT training pairs. Our analysis reveals that (1) the symbolic policy's coefficients expose systematic gaps in the base model's safety behavior for categories like religious stereotyping; (2) per-feature Delta_X/Delta_Y decomposition can mechanistically explain why harmful and harmless pairs exert qualitatively different influences on certain features; and (3) individual training pairs routinely exhibit cross-feature interference, allowing SMDA to identify training pairs whose dominant effect falls on unintended features. These results demonstrate that combining mechanistic interpretability with data attribution yields a diagnostic tool that is both more fine-grained than black-box influence functions and more scalable than manual circuit analysis.

items.title: Researchers identify intervention bias in zero-shot LLM educational advisors and demonstrate supervised policy learning eliminates bias with near-zero calibration error on Open University dataset [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Deterministic Decisions for High-Stakes AI. A Zero-Egress Pipeline with the Deployability of RAG and the Accuracy of Machine Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a previously unquantified issue called intervention bias in zero-shot large language model (LLM) educational advisors, where these models recommend interventions even when an optimal oracle policy suggests no action is needed. In a study using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, zero-shot GPT-4o showed a high false-positive rate, recommending unnecessary actions for 73% of students at a key checkpoint, compared to the oracle's 29.9%. Similar miscalibration was observed in commercial retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and SQL-augmented retrieval systems.

The study demonstrates that supervised policy learning methods, including a trajectory-conditioned Decision Transformer and an XGBoost classifier trained on oracle-labeled data, effectively eliminate this bias, achieving near-zero calibration error and high predictive accuracy across multiple action classes. These supervised models operate with low latency and maintain decision consistency, highlighting their potential for more reliable educational advisory systems.

Additionally, the researchers reveal an evaluation gap where LLM-based scoring methods fail to detect intervention bias, often favoring fluent but excessive recommendations over decision quality. The findings emphasize the importance of task-specific training and careful evaluation to improve the reliability of AI-driven educational interventions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We identify intervention bias as a previously unquantified failure mode of zero-shot large-language-model (LLM) educational advisory agents: without task-specific training, they recommend action when a hindsight-optimal oracle policy mandates inaction. In a six-arm ablation on the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (N=800 students, four temporal cutoffs), at day 56 -- when the oracle designates 70.1% of students as needing no intervention -- zero-shot GPT-4o recommends action for 73%, a 43 percentage-point false-positive rate. Commercial RAG and SQL-augmented retrieval are comparably miscalibrated; at 10,000 students this implies about 4,300 unnecessary advisor contacts per cycle. Supervised policy learning eliminates this bias: a trajectory-conditioned ONNX Decision Transformer (DT) and a snapshot XGBoost classifier, trained on the same oracle-labelled trajectories under strict prefix-only features, both achieve near-zero calibration error. The DT reaches macro-F1 0.79 (macro-recall 0.85) across all five action classes, predicting even the rare load-reduction action without collapsing, at a 0% action flip rate and sub-5 ms CPU decision latency. The two supervised arms are on par; the DT's edge over XGBoost at the final cutoff is indicative only (unpaired across cohorts). Scope: we validate Stage-2 decision-making (EAV state vector to supervised policy) under controlled oracle input from structured OULAD data; high fidelity reflects feature-oracle alignment, not general high-stakes-AI capability. The most robust finding is the intervention-bias contrast, not the absolute accuracies. We also show an Evaluation Gap: LLM-as-judge scoring (DeepEval G-Eval) is blind to intervention bias, rewarding fluent over-prescription rather than decision quality.

items.title: Researchers evaluate five defense methods against five attack types on seven instruction-tuned LLMs, finding prompt-time activation defenses blind to prefilling attacks and introducing response-time probing that eliminates prefilling success [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Closing the Activation-Cone Blind Spot: Response-Time Probing and Unified Defense
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a systematic evaluation of five defense methods against five types of attacks on seven instruction-tuned large language models ranging from 7 to 31 billion parameters. They found that prompt-time activation defenses are inherently ineffective against prefilling attacks, with some methods like AlphaSteer showing zero success against certain attacks but only 50% effectiveness against prefilling. To address this, the team introduced response-time probing, a technique that analyzes the model's hidden states during the first generated tokens, achieving near-perfect detection and eliminating prefilling attack success without false positives.

The study demonstrated that defenses relying on gating interventions based on a single layer's activation alignment are vulnerable to attacks that craft activations within the benign reference space. By combining response-time probing with existing methods like AlphaSteer's null-space steering, the researchers achieved high overall defense success, effectively countering both prefilling and semantic attacks. They also highlighted limitations in current evaluation metrics and showed that diverse negative training data significantly reduce false positives. The researchers have released their code, attack implementations, and evaluation data to support further study.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29441v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Inference-time safety methods for large language models have proliferated, yet no systematic comparison exists. We evaluate five defense paradigms (no defense, static steering, CAST, AlphaSteer, probe-gated) across seven instruction-tuned models (7-31B) and five attack types (GCG, AutoDAN, DeepInception, prefilling, intent laundering). Our central finding: prompt-time activation defenses are structurally blind to prefilling attacks. AlphaSteer achieves 0% attack success on GCG, AutoDAN, and intent laundering but 50% on prefilling. We prove a corollary: any defense that gates intervention on a single layer's activation alignment with a benign reference (cone, subspace, or null-space) is blind to attacks that craft activations to lie inside that reference, whether checked at prompt time or per token. As its constructive contrapositive we introduce response-time probing: a linear probe on the model's hidden state at the first generated tokens, with AUROC 0.97-1.00 across all seven models. Combined with a halt, it cuts prefilling attack success to 0/40 on every model with 0% benign false positives, outperforming Llama Guard 3. Cross-template generalisation depends on probe depth, so we scope the claim to the canonical prefilling-template family. Composing the response-halt with AlphaSteer's null-space steering gives an orthogonal split (the halt catches prefilling, AlphaSteer catches semantic attacks), reaching defense success 0.983 on Mistral and 0.994 on Llama and dominating both components. We further show MMLU fails to capture steering's true utility cost, which appears as behavioral hedging rather than factual loss, and that diverse negative training sets cut probe false positives from 80-100% to near zero. Code, attacks, per-sample results, and the judge prompt are released.

items.title: Researchers introduce LLM4MOF, a closed-loop framework using large language model agents for interpretable inverse design and simulation of metal-organic frameworks across multiple tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Interpretable Inverse Design of Metal-Organic Frameworks with Large Language Model Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LLM4MOF, a closed-loop framework that uses large language model agents to design and simulate metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) across multiple tasks. This system autonomously generates interpretable design hypotheses about metal nodes, linkers, pore geometry, and functional chemistry, then translates these into constraints to select candidate MOFs. Through iterative testing and simulation, LLM4MOF refines its designs, focusing on top-performing structures without prior knowledge of the global property landscape.

LLM4MOF evaluates hypotheses using diagnostic tests that isolate the effects of geometry, chemistry, and metal choice on performance. It efficiently explores six adsorption, separation, and electronic-structure tasks within 400 property evaluations, outperforming random search and genetic algorithms. The framework also generates new MOFs de novo and adapts their geometry to specific conditions during live simulation, demonstrating that language-model agents can conduct interpretable, simulation-based inverse design without needing to train separate models for each objective.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inverse design of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) requires searching a combinatorially vast space where property labels are expensive and most machine-learning models reveal little about why a structure succeeds. We introduce LLM4MOF, a closed-loop framework in which language-model agents reason about chemistry, build candidate MOFs, and test them in simulation, refining hypotheses over ten autonomous iterations. One agent proposes interpretable design hypotheses over metal nodes, linkers, pore geometry, and functional chemistry, and a second translates them into constraints that select candidate MOFs, each made of a metal node, organic linker, and matching topology. Each hypothesis is tested through four diagnostic beams that apply different subsets of its constraints, so comparing them shows whether geometry, chemistry, or metal choice drives performance. Even when blind to the global property landscape of databases, LLM4MOF concentrates its search on top-performing structures across six adsorption, separation, and electronic-structure tasks within 400 property evaluations. The same loop also generates new MOFs de novo and validates them in live simulation, where it adapts the geometry to each requested condition, outperforming random search and a genetic algorithm at roughly $1 per campaign. LLM4MOF shows that language-model agents can run interpretable, simulation-grounded inverse design without training a model per objective.

items.title: Researchers introduce a failure-driven evolution framework enabling a meta-agent to adaptively coordinate diverse retrievers for multimodal document reasoning, achieving up to 19.6-point gains on MMLongBench-Doc and DocBench [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Hybrid Retriever Evolution for Multimodal Document Reasoning Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a failure-driven evolution framework that enables a meta-agent to adaptively coordinate various retrievers—lexical, semantic, and multimodal—for multimodal document reasoning. This approach transforms retrieval from a fixed initial step into an adaptive, step-wise decision process during multi-step document question answering, leading to significant performance improvements. The evolved agent achieved up to 19.6-point gains on benchmarks like MMLongBench-Doc and DocBench, outperforming recent systems such as MACT, MDocAgent, and SimpleDoc.

The meta-agent autonomously analyzes incorrect reasoning paths, probes the environment to identify root causes, and iteratively refines the task agent's instructions. This process allows the agent to learn when and how to invoke different retrievers and effectively combine evidence across modalities and pages. Detailed analyses show that the improvements stem from adaptive routing and evidence composition rather than fixed retrieval strategies, highlighting a shift from narrow lexical methods to rich multi-tool coordination.

These findings suggest that autonomous multi-agent coordination offers a promising new paradigm for multimodal document reasoning, enabling more flexible and effective retrieval orchestration tailored to the demands of individual reasoning steps.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Different retrievers, including lexical, semantic, and multimodal approaches, provide highly complementary strengths for multimodal document understanding, yet most systems combine them through fixed pipelines that cannot adapt to the demands of individual reasoning steps. In this work, we ask whether retrieval orchestration itself can be learned as part of the reasoning process. We introduce a failure-driven evolution framework in which a meta-agent autonomously discovers how a tool-using task agent should coordinate diverse retrievers during multi-step document question answering. The meta-agent analyzes incorrect reasoning trajectories, actively probes the same tool environment to diagnose root causes, and iteratively rewrites the task agent's instructions, turning retrieval from a fixed front-end stage into an adaptive, step-wise reasoning decision. The evolved agent learns when to invoke each retriever, how to combine them, and how to compose evidence across modalities and pages. On MMLongBench-Doc and DocBench, the evolved agent achieves gains of up to +19.6 points over the unevolved baseline and consistently outperforms recent systems including MACT, MDocAgent, and SimpleDoc. Detailed retrieval analyses confirm that these improvements arise from adaptive routing and evidence composition rather than reliance on any hard coded retrieval mode, and evolution dynamics reveal a progressive shift from narrow lexical behavior to rich multi-tool coordination. These findings establish autonomous multi-agent coordination as a promising paradigm for multimodal document reasoning.

items.title: Researchers introduce ARMOR, an adaptive retriever optimization method improving low-resource telecom question answering by enhancing retrieval and generation in domain-specific benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ARMOR: Adaptive Retriever Optimization for Low-Resource Telecom Question Answering
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ARMOR, an adaptive retriever optimization method designed to enhance question answering (QA) in the telecom domain, particularly in low-resource settings. ARMOR improves retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) by focusing on query-side retriever adaptation rather than generator fine-tuning, which can lead to over-specialization. The method jointly optimizes two objectives—the latent-document RAG likelihood and the InfoNCE contrastive objective—to better support evidence retrieval and answer generation across telecom-specific benchmarks.

ARMOR works by learning separate temperature parameters for the RAG retrieval distribution and the InfoNCE softmax, while regularizing the adapted query encoder toward a frozen base encoder. This approach addresses the fragmented and technical nature of telecom data, which includes standards, papers, and specialized protocol language. Evaluations demonstrate that ARMOR enhances both retrieval accuracy and generative QA performance in several in-domain scenarios, offering a promising solution for improving domain-specific QA systems with limited resources.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29706v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Telecom question answering (QA) is a challenging setting for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): evidence is fragmented across standards, papers, encyclopedic resources, and web documents, and answers often hinge on technical tables, equations, and specialized protocol language. In low-resource subdomains, generator fine-tuning can over-specialize and degrade general capability, making query-side retriever adaptation an attractive alternative. To this end, we ask whether a fixed-generator, query-adapted RAG system can outperform generator-side adaptation, and which retriever objectives best support that setting. We motivate retrieval, rather than generator fine-tuning, as the adaptation target through a capacity comparison: under bounded-parameter and soft-retrieval assumptions, query-encoder tuning can have a smaller estimation term than supervised fine-tuning when its effective dimension is smaller. We identify two particularly relevant objectives -- the latent-document RAG likelihood, which optimizes generation utility, and the InfoNCE contrastive objective, which improves semantic retrieval geometry -- and leverage them jointly through a retriever optimization method targeting downstream QA performance in the telecom domain. Specifically, we introduce ARMOR, Adaptive Regularized Mixture Optimization for Retrievers, which learns separate temperatures for the RAG retrieval distribution and InfoNCE softmax and regularizes the adapted query encoder toward the frozen base query encoder. Across telecom-specific retrieval and generative QA benchmarks, we show that ARMOR improves evidence retrieval and answer generation in several in-domain settings. Code is available at https://github.com/heshandevaka/ARMOR.git.

items.title: Researchers present SEVA, a self-evolving verification agent using process rewards to improve fact attribution and produce auditable, structured outputs with multi-round self-refinement [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SEVA: Self-Evolving Verification Agent with Process Reward for Fact Attribution
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SEVA, a self-evolving verification agent designed to improve fact attribution in large language models by producing structured, auditable outputs and enabling multi-round self-refinement. Unlike traditional verifiers that provide only binary labels, SEVA offers detailed evidence alignments, reasoning chains, calibrated confidence scores, and a six-category error diagnosis with actionable fixes, enhancing both agent self-correction and operator auditing.

Training SEVA with reinforcement learning posed challenges due to the complexity of its multi-component outputs, which standard binary rewards could not effectively handle. The team addressed this by introducing a process reward that breaks down verification quality into five components, restoring training gradients and enabling a curriculum where the agent first masters verification behavior before improving outcomes. This approach also revealed that repeated self-refinement rounds produce benchmark-specific specialists rather than generalists. SEVA's 3-billion-parameter model matches the performance of GPT-4o-mini on the ClearFacts benchmark while delivering richer, more transparent verification results, highlighting the importance of aligning reward granularity with output complexity in reinforcement learning tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hallucination is the reliability bottleneck for LLM-based agents, and fact attribution verifiers are the last line of defense -- yet today's verifiers emit only opaque binary labels, leaving agents unable to self-correct and operators unable to audit. We present SEVA, a structured verification agent that emits evidence alignments, step-by-step reasoning chains, calibrated confidence, and a six-category error diagnosis with actionable fixes. Training such an agent with RL is non-trivial: standard binary reward on multi-component output triggers advantage collapse -- within-group reward variance vanishes and the GRPO gradient disappears. We resolve this with a process reward that decomposes verification quality into five independent components weighted 70/30 toward process signals, restoring the gradient and inducing an implicit curriculum -- the agent first masters verification behavior (alignment 0.917 -> 0.997, format 72% -> 100%), then outcomes (F1 64.9 -> 69.0). Structured output further enables a Verify -> Reflect -> Probe -> Refine self-evolution loop, which over four rounds on a 7B model surfaces an unexpected structural finding: each round produces a benchmark-specialist, not a generalist (+15 pp on HaluEval, -10 to -14 pp on TruthfulQA in the same model, persistent at 4x data). On ClearFacts, SEVA-3B matches GPT-4o-mini (69.0 vs. 69.8 F1) while producing substantially richer, auditable output -- confirming a principle that should generalize: for any RL task with multi-component generation, reward granularity must match output granularity.

outputCleanup.description:
Researchers have developed SEVA, a self-evolving verification agent designed to improve fact attribution in large language models by producing structured, auditable outputs and enabling multi-round self-refinement. Unlike traditional verifiers that provide only binary labels, SEVA offers detailed evidence alignments, reasoning chains, calibrated confidence scores, and a six-category error diagnosis with actionable fixes, enhancing both agent self-correction and operator auditing.

Training SEVA with reinforcement learning posed challenges due to the complexity of its multi-component outputs, which standard binary rewards could not effectively handle. The team addressed this by introducing a process reward that breaks down verification quality into five components, restoring training gradients and enabling a curriculum where the agent first masters verification behavior before improving outcomes. This approach also revealed that repeated self-refinement rounds produce benchmark-specific specialists rather than generalists. SEVA's 3-billion-parameter model matches the performance of GPT-4o-mini on the ClearFacts benchmark while delivering richer, more transparent verification results, highlighting the importance of aligning reward granularity with output complexity in reinforcement learning tasks.

items.title: Researchers propose MATCH, a scalable framework that enhances sparse attention in long-context transformers with dynamic in-context retrieval, improving performance on synthetic and real-world language tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MATCH: Modulating Attention via In-Context Retrieval for Long-Context Transformers
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MATCH, a new framework designed to improve the efficiency and scalability of large language models (LLMs) in handling long-context scenarios. MATCH enhances sparse attention mechanisms by dynamically integrating in-context information through an efficient retrieval system, addressing the limitations of traditional attention methods that suffer from high computational costs and performance drops in long-range recall tasks.

The framework avoids rigid structural constraints like local attention windows, which often degrade performance, by augmenting sparsified attention with dynamic retrieval. Empirical tests demonstrate that MATCH significantly boosts the performance of sparse-attention models on both synthetic benchmarks and real-world natural language tasks, making it a versatile solution for improving in-context retrieval while maintaining computational efficiency.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quadratic computational cost of traditional attention mechanisms poses a major bottleneck to the scalability and practical deployment of large language models (LLMs), particularly in long-context scenarios. To improve efficiency, existing approaches often enforce rigid structural constraints such as local attention windows. However, these strategies typically lead to substantial performance degradation on tasks requiring precise long-range recall. In this work, we propose MATCH, a scalable and efficient framework that augments sparsified attention mechanisms with dynamically integrated in-context information through an efficient retrieval system. Empirical results show that MATCH significantly improves the performance of sparse-attention models on both synthetic and real-world natural-language tasks. These findings highlight the versatility of MATCH as a general approach for enhancing in-context retrieval capabilities while maintaining the efficiency benefits of sparse attention architectures.

items.title: Researchers introduce SABER-Math, an automated benchmark for evaluating mathematical information retrieval using 283K high-school math problems and LLM-based relevance ratings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SABER-Math: Automated Benchmark for Information Retrieval Evaluation in Mathematics
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SABER-Math, the first fully automated benchmark designed to evaluate mathematical information retrieval (IR) systems without requiring expert annotations. Utilizing a dataset of 283,000 high-school-level math problems and solutions, SABER-Math creates reranking tasks by extracting solution summaries and topics with large language models (LLMs), identifying relevant documents through topic and lexical similarities, and generating fine-grained relevance ratings via an LLM-based preference tournament. This benchmark addresses the challenge of assessing IR systems' effectiveness in mathematical contexts, where existing benchmarks often fail to capture nuanced relevance.

The study evaluated various retrieval methods, including lexical retrievers, specialized math retrieval systems, and modern embedding models. Results showed that while embedding models outperform traditional and math-specific baselines, they still face difficulties in symbol-intensive areas such as Algebra and Calculus. Additionally, the research highlights that general-purpose IR benchmarks like MTEB do not reliably predict performance in mathematical retrieval tasks, underscoring the importance of math-specific evaluation tools like SABER-Math.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29894v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As agentic AI systems tackle more complex mathematical tasks, they increasingly rely on information retrieval (IR) to search problem databases, theorem libraries, and educational resources. However, choosing the right retriever remains difficult, as it is infeasible to directly isolate its effect on downstream performance. On the other hand, existing retrieval-specific benchmarks often fail to capture fine-grained mathematical relevance, penalizing relevant documents. We address this gap by introducing SABER-Math, the first fully automated benchmark for evaluating mathematical IR without expert annotation. Starting from 283K high-school-level math problems with solutions, SABER-Math builds challenging reranking tasks in three steps: (i) first, LLMs extract concise solution summaries and mathematical topics for each problem; (ii) then, per-query relevant documents are discovered using ontology topic-based and lexical solutions-summary-based similarities, and (iii) finally, a Swiss-style LLM preference tournament produces fine-grained relevance ratings for the documents. We evaluate lexical retrievers, specialized mathematical retrieval systems, and recent embedding models. We find that while modern embedding models substantially outperform classical and math-specific baselines, even the strongest systems struggle in symbol-heavy domains like Algebra and Calculus. Importantly, we show that general-purpose IR benchmarks such as MTEB do not reliably predict mathematical performance, especially for recent embedding models, highlighting the need for math-specific retrieval benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers analyze non-sequential multimodal sentence embeddings in the SONAR model, identifying sensitive dimensions as anomaly detectors and exploring correction methods to improve multimodal representation reliability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Forewarned is Forearmed: When Non-Sequential Embedding Turns Into an Anomaly Detector
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a detailed study of non-sequential multimodal sentence embeddings, focusing on the SONAR model. They found that certain embedding dimensions are particularly sensitive to perturbations and can effectively detect decoding anomalies. By examining the consistency between encoding and decoding processes, they developed an accurate anomaly detector and explored methods to adjust specific embedding dimensions to correct errors.

This analysis highlights the importance of understanding the internal structure of embeddings to improve the reliability of multimodal representations. The findings suggest that targeted modifications to sensitive dimensions can enhance the robustness of models that integrate multiple data modalities.

items.title: Researchers propose permutation-invariant fine-tuning for structured metadata retrieval to reduce field order impact, improving search accuracy across 15 languages with a new benchmark and models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Field Order Should Not Matter: Permutation-Invariant Embedding Model Fine-Tuning for Structured Metadata Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have identified that the order of fields in structured metadata records significantly affects retrieval quality when using text encoders fine-tuned for search tasks. They propose a permutation-invariant fine-tuning method (PI-FT) that randomizes field order and applies field dropout during training, ensuring the model learns to associate meaning with field labels rather than their positions. This approach reduces the retrieval performance drop caused by changes in field order from 7.4 to 0.2 nDCG@10 points with minimal impact on accuracy.

The study focuses on a catalog of nearly 10,000 development indicators searchable in 15 languages, introducing DevDataBench, a benchmark of queries generated by large language models to cover all indicators for training and evaluation. A fine-tuned 118M-parameter encoder using PI-FT outperforms zero-shot baselines, especially in low-resource languages. The researchers have released the benchmark, models, and a reusable PI-FT framework to support improved and robust metadata retrieval across languages.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study retrieval over catalogs of structured metadata, where each record is a small schema whose fields answer different kinds of query. Embedding a record with a text encoder first serializes its fields into a string, which forces a choice of field order. We show this choice, usually treated as an implementation detail, silently controls retrieval quality once the encoder is fine-tuned. A standard fine-tune loses 7.4 nDCG@10 points when the index is rebuilt under a different field order, because it reads absolute position instead of the field labels. We propose permutation-invariant fine-tuning ($\textbf{PI-FT}$), which serializes each record under a freshly sampled field order with random field dropout, so meaning binds to the labels rather than to position. The change is about two lines in the data loader; it costs negligible in-distribution accuracy and cuts the order-change penalty to 0.2 points. We study this in the discovery of development statistics, a catalog of nearly 10,000 indicators that should be searchable in many languages by a model small enough to self-host. As AI assistants and agents increasingly mediate access to public data and statistics, this retrieval step decides whether an answer is grounded in the right indicator or series, making discoverability a precondition for disseminating data through AI. Because usage logs cannot provide training signal for indicators no one has searched, we generate the queries instead. $\textbf{DevDataBench}$ is a fully LLM-generated benchmark of grounded, facet-targeted queries across 15 languages, covering every indicator for both training and evaluation. A fine-tuned 118M-parameter CPU encoder outperforms every zero-shot baseline, including $\texttt{text-embedding-3-large}$ (0.707 vs.\ 0.556 nDCG@10), with the largest gains in low-resource languages. We release the benchmark, pipeline, models, and a reusable PI-FT framework.

items.title: Researchers introduce Co-Scientist, a multi-agent AI system built on Gemini that generates and refines novel scientific hypotheses, validated in biomedical applications including drug repurposing for acute myeloid leukemia [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Co-Scientist, a multi-agent AI system built on the Gemini platform designed to generate and refine novel scientific hypotheses. This system supports scientists by formulating new research hypotheses based on their objectives and existing scientific evidence, with a focus on accelerating discovery through continuous hypothesis generation, critique, and refinement. Co-Scientist's architecture includes an asynchronous task execution framework and a tournament evolution process that improves hypothesis quality over time.

The system has been validated in biomedical applications such as drug repurposing, novel target discovery, and understanding antimicrobial resistance mechanisms. Notably, Co-Scientist identified new drug repurposing candidates and synergistic combination therapies for acute myeloid leukemia, which were confirmed through in vitro experiments. These results demonstrate Co-Scientist's potential to enhance scientific discovery and support AI-empowered research efforts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2502.18864v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific discovery is driven by scientists generating novel hypotheses for complex problems that undergo rigorous experimental validation. To augment this process, we introduce Co-Scientist, a multi-agent AI system built on Gemini for structured scientific thinking and hypothesis generation. Co-Scientist aims to help scientists discover new original knowledge. Conditioned on their research objectives and prior scientific evidence, it formulates demonstrably novel research hypotheses for experimental verification. The system's design involves agents continuously generating, critiquing and refining hypotheses accelerated by scaling test-time compute. Key contributions include: (1) a multi-agent architecture with an asynchronous task execution framework for flexible compute scaling; (2) a tournament evolution process for self-improving hypotheses generation. Automated evaluations show continued benefits of test-time compute scaling, improving hypothesis quality over time. While general purpose, we focus the validation in three biomedical applications: drug repurposing, novel target discovery, and explaining mechanisms of anti-microbial resistance. Specifically, Co-Scientist helped identify new drug repurposing candidates and synergistic combination therapies for acute myeloid leukemia, which were validated through in vitro experiments. These real-world validations demonstrate the potential of Co-Scientist to accelerate scientific discovery and usher in an era of AI empowered scientists.

items.title: Researchers propose distributionally robust reinforcement learning from human feedback to improve large language model fine-tuning and out-of-distribution task performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Distributionally Robust Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a distributionally robust reinforcement learning approach from human feedback (RLHF) to enhance the fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) and improve their performance on tasks that differ from the training data. This method aims to maintain model effectiveness even when the prompt distribution during deployment varies significantly from that seen during fine-tuning. The team formulated distributionally robust optimization versions of two common fine-tuning techniques—reward-based RLHF and reward-free direct preference optimization (DPO)—and proposed minibatch gradient descent algorithms with proven convergence guarantees.

The researchers evaluated their approach by training models on the Unified-Feedback dataset and testing them on out-of-distribution tasks across different datasets. Results demonstrated that the robust training improved the accuracy of learned reward models overall, with notable gains in reasoning tasks. Additionally, the robust policy optimization methods showed enhanced performance on out-of-distribution tasks, suggesting that this approach can make LLM fine-tuning more reliable across diverse applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2503.00539v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has evolved to be one of the main methods for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). However, existing RLHF methods are non-robust, and their performance deteriorates if the downstream task differs significantly from the preference dataset used in fine-tuning. In order to mitigate this problem, we introduce a distributionally robust RLHF for fine-tuning LLMs. In particular, our goal is to ensure that a fine-tuned model retains its performance even when the distribution of prompts significantly differs from the distribution encountered during fine-tuning. We formulate distributionally robust optimization (DRO) version of two popular fine-tuning methods -- (1) reward-based RLHF and (2) reward-free DPO (direct preference optimization). We propose a minibatch gradient descent based algorithms for both of them, and theoretically prove convergence guarantees for the algorithms. Subsequently, we evaluate our algorithms on an out-of-distribution (OOD) task by first training the model on the Unified-Feedback dataset and evaluating its performance on two different datasets. The experimental results show that our robust training improves the accuracy of the learned reward models on average, and markedly on some tasks, such as reasoning. Furthermore, we show that the robust versions of policy optimization methods, similarly improve performance on OOD tasks.

items.title: Researchers develop post-training fine-tuning method to improve large language models' convention formation and communication efficiency, validated on two new benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Post-training for Efficient Communication via Convention Formation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a post-training fine-tuning method to enhance large language models' ability to form ad-hoc conventions and communicate more efficiently in multi-turn interactions. This approach targets demonstrations of convention formation identified through heuristics and has been validated using two newly designed benchmarks that focus on this capability.

The first benchmark is a cognitively motivated interaction task that reliably elicits convention formation trends observed in humans, while the second is a document-grounded reference completion task reflecting real-world convention formation behavior. The studies demonstrate that language models subjected to this post-training process show significant improvements in their convention formation abilities across both evaluation methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2508.06482v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Humans communicate with increasing efficiency in multi-turn interactions, by adapting their language and forming ad-hoc conventions. In contrast, prior work shows that LLMs do not naturally show this behavior. We develop a post-training process to develop this ability through targeted fine-tuning on heuristically identified demonstrations of convention formation. We evaluate with two new benchmarks focused on this capability. First, we design a focused, cognitively-motivated interaction benchmark that consistently elicits strong convention formation trends in humans. Second, we create a new document-grounded reference completion task that reflects in-the-wild convention formation behavior. Our studies show significantly improved convention formation abilities in post-trained LLMs across the two evaluation methods.

items.title: Researchers train small attention-only transformers achieving perfect indirect object identification with minimal circuits specialized into additive and contrastive subcircuits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Emergence of Minimal Circuits for Indirect Object Identification in Attention-Only Transformers
items.summary:
Researchers have trained small, attention-only transformer models from scratch to perform the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task, achieving perfect accuracy with minimal architecture. A single-layer model with just two attention heads, lacking multilayer perceptrons and normalization layers, successfully resolves IOI by specializing its heads into additive and contrastive subcircuits. This demonstrates that task-specific training can produce highly interpretable and minimal computational circuits within transformers.

The study employed techniques such as residual stream decomposition, spectral analysis, and embedding interventions to analyze how these attention heads function. Additionally, a two-layer, one-head model was shown to integrate information primarily through query-key interactions, highlighting the simplicity of the mechanisms involved. These findings provide a controlled framework for understanding the computational foundations of transformer reasoning and contribute to the field of mechanistic interpretability.
