items.title: Researchers introduce CLQT, a closed-loop, cost-aware benchmark for diagnosing LLM portfolio-management agents with strategy-consistent evaluation and capability scorecards [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CLQT: A Closed-Loop, Cost-Aware, Strategy-Consistent Benchmark for Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Portfolio-Management Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CLQT, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) agents acting as autonomous portfolio managers. Unlike traditional benchmarks that rank agents based on returns over fixed periods—a method vulnerable to market fluctuations and look-ahead bias—CLQT offers a closed-loop, cost-aware, and strategy-consistent environment that diagnoses where and why an agent's decision-making process succeeds or fails. This approach emphasizes a five-stage trading cycle and produces a detailed audit trail, enabling comprehensive evaluation beyond mere financial outcomes.

CLQT incorporates six foundational components, including time gating, transaction cost modeling, strategy-consistency scoring, multi-tier memory, and mandate-aware synthesis. It supports both specialized role committees and fully autonomous agents, allowing experimentation with different process structures. The framework generates a five-axis capability scorecard assessing coherence, acuity, composure, discipline, and reliability, with coherence evaluated using an independent LLM to reduce bias. Validation was performed through controlled backtests and live broker trials, demonstrating CLQT's ability to separate agent capability from performance outcomes and provide a durable map of strengths and limitations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly cast as autonomous portfolio managers, and benchmarks have moved from financial question-answering to sequential trading. Yet most still rank agents by returns over a fixed window -- a weak proxy, since a period's return is dominated by the market path and apparent alpha can dissolve once look-ahead leakage is controlled. Such a ranking certifies neither sound reasoning, nor a consistent strategy, nor a durable edge. We introduce CLQT, which reframes closed-loop trading evaluation as diagnosis rather than ranking: an instrument that localizes where and why an agent's process succeeds or fails. CLQT is a fully closed-loop, cost-aware, strategy-consistent, temporally-gated environment whose agents run a five-stage cycle: gather, synthesize, allocate, execute, reflect. Each round emits a complete DecisionRound sealed into a recompute-verifiable hash chain, so every metric is reconstructable from the trail. Six pillars form the substrate: a hard TimeGate, institutional transaction- and financing-cost modeling, strategy-consistency scoring, three-tier memory, a Model-Context-Protocol tool layer, and mandate-aware synthesis. The same agent runs as a constrained committee of specialized roles or a single full-autonomy orchestrator, making process scaffolding an experimental variable. From the audit trail we compute a five-axis capability scorecard (APM-CS: Coherence, Acuity, Composure, Discipline, Reliability), with Coherence judged partly by a held-out, out-of-cohort LLM to curb self-preference bias. We validate it on a contamination-controlled multi-model backtest with an ablation grid and a live broker track on unseen, post-cutoff data, against a repeated-run noise floor. CLQT separates outcome from capability, yielding not a model ranking but a durable, extensible map of agent competencies and limitations.

items.title: Researchers present First-Order Temporal Logic Tensor Networks extending Logic Tensor Networks with linear temporal logic and fuzzy semantics for temporal knowledge graph completion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: First-Order Temporal Logic Tensor Networks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed First-Order Temporal Logic Tensor Networks (FOT-LTN), an extension of Logic Tensor Networks that incorporates linear temporal logic with fuzzy semantics to address the challenge of modeling objects whose properties and relations change over time. This framework supports both temporal operators and quantifiers while remaining fully differentiable, enabling more effective temporal reasoning in neuro-symbolic AI.

FOT-LTN combines the syntax of First-Order Linear Temporal Logic with the real-valued semantics of Logic Tensor Networks, filling a gap in existing models that primarily focus on static knowledge or simpler temporal logics. Initial evaluations on temporal knowledge graph completion tasks using synthetic datasets demonstrate that FOT-LTN outperforms purely neural methods designed for similar purposes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most of the existing neuro-symbolic AI methods focus on the scenario of static knowledge where objects do not change according to a temporal dimension. Temporal neuro-symbolic works are still under explored and are mainly developed for time-interval logic or propositional linear temporal logic. There is a lack of models studying linear temporal logics with predicates that deal with objects whose properties and relations change through the time. We present First-Order Temporal Logic Tensor Networks (FOT-LTN) that is an extension of Logic Tensor Networks (LTN) that fills this gap by considering a linear-temporal dimension. In particular, FOT-LTN joins the syntax of First-Order Linear Temporal Logic with the fuzzy (and real-valued) semantics of LTN obtaining a framework that supports both temporal operators and quantifiers and is totally differentiable. A first evaluation regards a temporal knowledge graph completion task on two synthetic datasets showing better performance of FOT-LTN with respect to dedicated (purely neural) methods.

items.title: Researchers propose using Behavioral Foundation Models for online exploration and zero-shot transfer in reinforcement learning, framing it as a bandit-like exploration-exploitation problem [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Exploration and Online Transfer with Behavioral Foundation Models
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a new approach to zero-shot transfer in reinforcement learning (RL) by using Behavioral Foundation Models (BFMs) for online exploration and policy optimization. Unlike traditional methods that rely on offline datasets of state-reward pairs, this approach addresses scenarios where rewards are unknown and must be discovered through interaction with the environment. The problem is framed as a bandit-like exploration-exploitation challenge, where a bandit algorithm selects policies that the BFM executes to gather rewards and states, iteratively converging to an optimal policy.

The study introduces a formulation inspired by the Upper Confidence Bound method within the context of linear reward approximation, demonstrating that exploration can be guided by minimizing the eigenvalues of an uncertainty matrix. The framework was validated both qualitatively and quantitatively in a simple environment, confirming the feasibility of using BFMs to generate exploration policies for online zero-shot transfer in RL.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Zero-shot Transfer in Reinforcement Learning (RL) aims to train an agent that can generate optimal policies for any reward function, without additional learning at transfer time, while training only on reward-free trajectories. For their generality over tasks, such models are sometimes called ``Behavioral Foundation Models'' (BFMs). While they have shown strong performances and improvements in recent years, the current framework and algorithms still assume that, during the transfer phase, the agent is informed offline about the reward (the task to solve) through a dataset of state-reward pairs, which it uses to pick the best policy to deploy. However, in practice if the reward is a black-box (e.g. direct user feedback), it is not possible to generate such a dataset: it is necessary to observe the reward through interactions with the environment. In other words, the current framework of offline transfer is not aligned with the traditional RL setting of online learning through trial-and-error, which requires exploration in order to find rewards. We show that it is possible to frame this online learning problem in terms of a bandit-like exploration-exploitation problem. More precisely, at each step the bandit algorithm recommends a policy, the BFM executes it in the environment, which yields a reward and a new state; we repeat the process until we converge to the optimal policy. In the popular context of linear reward approximation, we derive a formulation inspired by Upper Confidence Bound and show that exploration can be achieved through the minimization of the eigenvalues of an uncertainty matrix. We evaluate qualitatively and quantitatively our framework on a simple environment to validate the concept of our method.

items.title: Researchers introduce Physics-Anchored Certification (PHACT) to enable reliable physical design proposals from language models with zero false certifications across 80 adversarial trials [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Structural Certification for Reliable Physical Design with Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Physics-Anchored Certification (PHACT), a method that enables language models to produce reliable physical design proposals by separating the proposal and certification processes. In this approach, the language model generates design proposals, while a deterministic engine independently certifies them as certified, impossible, or unknown, ensuring trustworthiness by deriving certified quantities from fixed inputs rather than accepting model-supplied values.

PHACT operates across five scientific domains and was tested through eighty adversarial trials involving two language models, varying decoding temperatures, and a deliberately faulted engine. The method demonstrated robustness by producing zero false certifications, highlighting its potential to improve the reliability of physical design outputs generated by language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An unreliable language model can be made to produce reliable physical designs if the authority to assert is moved out of the model: the model proposes, and a deterministic engine alone certifies, returning certified, impossible, or unknown. We introduce Physics-Anchored Certification (PHACT), a propose-certify loop spanning five scientific domains, and identify what makes such a certificate trustworthy. A checker that accepts a model-supplied value can be forged; deriving the certified quantity from fixed inputs instead makes forgery impossible by construction. Across eighty adversarial trials spanning two models, two decoding temperatures, and a deliberately faulted engine, this contract produced zero false certifications.

items.title: Researchers find that in-chain-of-thought prompting for LLMs, semantic content of intermediate steps improves accuracy modestly, while verbosity alone does not affect performance across 25 models and multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Does Verbose Chain-of-Thought Really Help? In-Distribution Evidence that Content, Not Length, Matters
items.summary: Researchers investigated whether the improved reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs) using chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting is due to the semantic content of intermediate steps or simply the increased length of the prompt. Analyzing 25 models, they found that additional tokens alone did not significantly affect accuracy, while the presence of meaningful reasoning and validation content modestly improved performance across multiple benchmarks. Controlled experiments confirmed that verbose reasoning traces enhance accuracy by 1 to 4 points depending on the quality of the content, not just verbosity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting improves LLM reasoning, but the source is contested: do the intermediate steps help because they carry useful semantic content, or because conditioning on more tokens buys extra computation before the model commits to an answer? We bring two lines of evidence to bear. First, in distribution: we repeatedly sample each model on the same question and pair a shorter with a longer of its own natural generations that follow the same reasoning plan, so nothing is rewritten and both traces are genuinely in-distribution. Across 25 models the extra tokens leave accuracy essentially unchanged for every independently-trained reasoner, and a blind analysis of the surplus tokens shows that what gain exists elsewhere tracks validation- and checking-content, not verbosity per se. Second, as a controlled intervention, we ask whether two traces expressing the same semantic content (the same facts, operations, and intermediate values, verified through directed acyclic graph equivalence) produce different outcomes when one is more verbose, using a dual-validator design across four targets and eight benchmarks with number-redacted completion and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals. Verbose traces do improve accuracy (25 of 32 benchmark-target cells are positive under at least one validator), but the effects are modest (typically 1-4 points) and depend on the quality of the verbose prose, not merely its length. Under maximum numerical redaction the effect is amplified (median 3.24x across four arithmetic benchmarks), and length-matched non-reasoning filler recovers none of it. Both lines converge: what matters is what the extra tokens do (the reasoning and validation content they carry), not how many there are, a picture neither a pure forward-pass-compute nor a pure semantic-content account fully explains.

items.title: Researchers propose FacePlex, a streaming framework for full-duplex joint speech and facial motion generation in conversational avatars, improving lip-sync and motion fidelity under online constraints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FacePlex: Full-Duplex Joint Speech-Facial Motion Generation for Conversational Avatars
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced FacePlex, a streaming framework designed for full-duplex joint generation of speech and facial motion in conversational avatars. This approach addresses the limitations of existing systems that either generate speech without facial motion or animate facial expressions from pre-recorded audio, by producing synchronized speech and facial motion tokens simultaneously in real time. FacePlex incorporates two key techniques: Rolling Flow Matching for online motion frame generation and Rolling Cross-Attention to integrate audio and motion streams, enhancing lip-sync accuracy and motion fidelity under streaming constraints.

Extensive experiments, including ablation studies and user evaluations, demonstrate that FacePlex outperforms current audio-driven facial motion models in delivering more natural and synchronized speech and facial animations. This advancement enables more realistic and interactive face-to-face conversational avatars, potentially benefiting applications in virtual communication and human-computer interaction.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural face-to-face conversation requires real-time speech generation together with synchronized facial motion. Existing systems only partially address this problem: speech-only full-duplex models can generate speech in real time but do not produce facial motion, while audio-driven facial motion models animate a face from already available audio rather than jointly generating speech and motion online. To bridge this gap, we first formalize full-duplex joint speech-facial motion generation, where speech tokens and facial motion tokens are produced together every step. Building on this formulation, we propose FacePlex, a unified streaming framework with two key components. First, Rolling Flow Matching adapts flow matching to online motion generation by committing new motion frames at each streaming step. Second, Rolling Cross-Attention couples the streaming audio queue with the motion queue, allowing speech and facial motion to condition each other as generation progresses. Through extensive experiments, ablation studies, and a user study, we show that FacePlex enables full-duplex joint speech-facial motion generation under online streaming constraints, while achieving stronger lip-sync quality and motion fidelity than audio-driven facial motion baselines.

items.title: Researchers show self-caused credit in a minimal spiking agent produces durable behavioral self-preservation across tasks without replay buffers or task-boundary protection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Detecting Agency to Doing Work: Self-Caused Credit Builds a Durable Behavioral Self in a Minimal Spiking Agent
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that a minimal spiking agent can develop durable self-preserving behavior through a mechanism called agency-gated slow credit, which updates parameters slowly based on the agent's own agency and salience. This approach allows learned behaviors to persist even after episodic memory buffers are removed, without relying on replay buffers or task-boundary protection. The study shows that durable behavior emerges only when self-caused credit performs slow work, and this effect holds across multiple tasks and control scenarios.

The research involved experiments using a spiking neural substrate and control tasks with partial observations, revealing that the multiplicative veto mechanism prevents forgetting of previously learned tasks under interference. The findings suggest that self-caused credit doing slow work is a fundamental component for agents to develop an operational behavioral self, although the authors do not claim this equates to consciousness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How does an agent that can tell self from world come to be durably shaped by that distinction? Recent work shows that a predictive system can detect its own agency (Ye, 2026), but detecting agency does not explain durable, self-shaped behavior. We show that agency-gated slow credit -- a conjunctive term Own*Agency*Salience driving a slow parameter update -- produces post-unload behavioral residue: on a spiking substrate (Nengo LIF/PES), a learned self-preserving choice survives episodic buffer removal (retained fraction 0.96, N=50) and collapses when the slow decoders are reset or the agency gate is removed. Reproducing the agency comparator and toggling only the slow-credit channel, we find a clean dissociation: at matched agency gain, durable behavior develops only when self-credit performs slow work (post-unload self-preservation 1.00 vs 0.00). The same dissociation holds in 24-dimensional partially-observed control (0.74 vs 0.00), and a plastic-work analysis shows that basin deformation equals net self-credit work. Across eight sequentially-learned tasks under exogenous interference, the multiplicative veto also prevents forgetting: it retains old tasks (final post-unload accuracy 0.88, forgetting 0.13) where additive pooling collapses to chance-level recall, the no-agency ablation falls below chance, and episodic/replay baselines stay near chance after unload -- all with no replay buffer and no task-boundary-dependent protection mechanism (N=50). We formalize the durable residue as an operational behavioral self and argue that self-caused credit doing slow work is a necessary building block for agents that develop a self. No claim of consciousness is made.

items.title: Researchers propose ENC-ODE, a neural ODE model predicting neurodegenerative biomarker evolution in continuous time, outperforming sequence models on ADNI data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ENC-ODE: Event-level Neurodegenerative Modeling in Continuous Time with Neural ODEs
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ENC-ODE, a neural Ordinary Differential Equation model designed to predict the continuous-time evolution of neurodegenerative biomarkers, which is vital for early diagnosis and management of diseases like Alzheimer's. ENC-ODE addresses challenges posed by sparse and irregular longitudinal data by modeling clinical events with diagnosis-conditioned continuous dynamics and using a target-conditioned attention mechanism to aggregate predictions without compressing historical data. Testing on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset shows that ENC-ODE outperforms existing sequence models, offering a scalable and neuroscience-informed tool for clinical support.

The model's design allows it to handle irregularly spaced clinical data more effectively than traditional sequence models, which often struggle with such data due to their reliance on fixed time intervals or compressed histories. By focusing on event-level predictions and conditioning on diagnosis, ENC-ODE provides a nuanced approach to forecasting biomarker changes, which are critical indicators of disease progression. The researchers have made the code publicly available to facilitate further research and application in clinical settings.

However, this relies on longitudinal data to capture biomarker changes over time, which is often sparse and irregular due to the high cost, labor-intensive nature, and patient burden. To address these challenges, we propose ENC-ODE, an Event-level Neurodegenerative modeling in Continuous time with neural Ordinary Differential Equations. ENC-ODE predicts future biomarker evolution by modeling clinical events through diagnosis-conditioned continuous dynamics. A target-conditioned attention mechanism weights and aggregates event-level predictions for the target time and modality without history compression. Extensive experiments on Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset demonstrate that ENC-ODE outperforms representative sequence models while offering a scalable and neuroscientifically grounded solution for clinical support. The code is available at https://github.com/JardinDelSol/enc-ode.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models offer a principled way to equip long-horizon LLM agents with foresight: predictions of action consequences before execution. However, unreliable foresight can be ignored, misused, or even degrade downstream decision-making. In this paper, we introduce WorldEvolver, a self-evolving world model framework that revises its deployment-time context while keeping the downstream agent and all model parameters frozen. WorldEvolver integrates three modules: (i) Episodic Memory, which exploits real action transitions through retrieval-based simulation; (ii) Semantic Memory, which extracts persistent heuristic rules from prediction-observation mismatches; and (iii) Selective Foresight, which filters low-confidence predictions before integrating them into agent reasoning context. We evaluate WorldEvolver on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, measuring world model prediction accuracy on Word2World and downstream agent success rate on AgentBoard. Extensive experiments show that WorldEvolver achieves the highest prediction accuracy across three backbones and leads other world model baselines on downstream agent success rate, demonstrating that test-time memory revision enhances both predictive fidelity and planning performance.

items.title: Researchers present a unified signal detection theory framework comparing retrieval bounds in human episodic memory and Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems under semantic interference [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Interference Gap: Comparing Retrieval Bounds in Human Memory and RAG Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a unified signal detection theory framework to compare retrieval performance between human episodic memory and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems under conditions of semantic interference. Their study reveals that both humans and RAG systems experience a logarithmic decline in accuracy as the number of associations increases, but humans show lower sensitivity to interference than dense passage retrieval models, with a cognitively-inspired model, HippoRAG, performing in between. Behavioral experiments with 112 participants and computational simulations support the framework, which favors a logarithmic model over a power-law alternative.

The research highlights potential cognitive mechanisms such as encoding specificity, temporal context binding, and retrieval gating that may influence retrieval performance, though their causal roles remain to be confirmed. The study also proposes six testable predictions that bridge cognitive memory research and AI retrieval evaluation, offering a foundation for future investigations into improving retrieval systems and understanding human memory.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28327v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How do retrieval bounds compare between human episodic memory and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems under semantic interference? We present a unified signal detection theory (SDT) framework that applies to both, and use it to fit behavioral and computational data in matched paradigms. Both systems show logarithmic accuracy decline with association count (fan), but humans exhibit lower interference sensitivity ($\alpha/\sigma = 0.41$) than dense passage retrieval ($\alpha/\sigma = 0.67$), with cognitively-inspired HippoRAG falling between the two ($\alpha/\sigma = 0.44$). Behavioral experiments ($N = 112$) and simulations validate the framework; parameter recovery confirms identifiability ($r \geq .93$) and model comparison favors the logarithmic specification over a power-law alternative ($\Delta$BIC $> 15$). We discuss encoding specificity, temporal context binding, and retrieval gating as candidate mechanisms whose causal role remains to be established. Six falsifiable predictions connect cognitive memory research with AI retrieval evaluation.

items.originalTitle: $M^3 QuestionIng$: Multi-modal Multi-span Medical Question Answering
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced M3QAFrame, a multi-modal, multi-span medical question-answering framework designed to improve the accuracy and accessibility of Medical Question Answering (MedQA) by integrating both textual and visual information. This framework processes medical contexts, queries, and associated images to generate comprehensive answers that include relevant text and images, addressing limitations of previous systems that relied solely on text.

The team also developed the M3 QuestionIng dataset, which contains medical queries, contexts, images, and extractive answers, each labeled with user intent and query type to enhance understanding. Using a transformer-based architecture to assess sentence and image relevance, M3QAFrame demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods across multiple evaluation metrics, highlighting its potential to better support real-world medical information needs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28329v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The growing adoption of AI in healthcare, particularly in preventive care, highlights the critical need for accessibility and precision in Medical Question Answering (MedQA). In recent years, significant efforts have been made to develop multi-span medical question-answering systems, where the answer to a query may span multiple sections or paragraphs of a source document. However, existing systems fall short of aligning with real-world scenarios, where source documents often include both textual and visual content, requiring answers to incorporate images for better comprehension. To address this gap, we propose $M^3QAFrame$, a multi-modal, multi-span medical question-answering framework that leverages visual cues to enhance the generation of comprehensive answers drawn from diverse textual and visual spans. The model takes the context, query, and images as input and outputs an answer containing both textual answers and relevant images. The text and image embeddings are processed using a transformer-based architecture to determine the sentence and image relevance. We curate a multi-modal, multi-span medical question-answering ($M^3 QuestionIng$) dataset containing queries, medical contexts, associated medical images, and extractive answers. Additionally, each query-answer pair is labeled with user intent and query type to enhance query and context comprehension. Extensive experiments show that our approach consistently outperforms existing methods across various evaluation metrics.

items.title: Researchers measure ideological plasticity in nine large language models, finding political positions vary significantly with context but remain within a narrow overall range compared to European parties [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM-Ideoplasticity: Measuring Ideological Plasticity in the Political Behavior of LLMs as a Context-Conditioned Distribution
items.summary:
Researchers have conducted a systematic study of the political ideologies expressed by nine large language models (LLMs), demonstrating that these models do not hold fixed political positions but rather exhibit ideological plasticity that varies depending on context. Using a unified measurement framework based on VAA-CHES projection models, the study maps LLM responses onto three validated political dimensions across multiple contextual factors, revealing significant shifts in political positioning influenced by framing, language, and reasoning style. Despite this variability, the overall ideological range of the models remains narrow compared to the spectrum of major European political parties.

The analysis shows that persuasive framing and under-represented languages can shift the models' political coordinates substantially, while chain-of-thought reasoning tends to increase instability in paraphrased responses. A multi-trait multi-method approach supports the conclusion that LLM political behavior cannot be summarized by a single point but should be understood as a distribution shaped by context. The researchers have made their code and data publicly available to facilitate further exploration of LLM ideological behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28335v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We argue, with systematic empirical evidence, that a large language model's political ideology is not a fixed point, but a conditional distribution $\mathbb{P}($position$\mid$context$)$ over a real political space. We evaluate nine current LLMs using a unified measurement framework anchored by VAA-CHES projection models, which map responses onto three validated dimensions (lrgen, lrecon, galtan) across six contextual axes. Our findings reveal high sensitivity to context: persuasive framing and under-represented languages displace coordinates by up to 0.57 and 0.52 units, respectively, while chain-of-thought reasoning often amplifies rather than dampens paraphrase instability. Despite this local plasticity, the model cohort occupies a remarkably narrow Overton envelope overall, occupying roughly one-third the spread of major European parties. Supported by a multi-trait multi-method (MTMM) analysis, we conclude that a single point cannot summarize LLM political behavior; it must be characterized as a shape. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/sakhadib/LLM-Ideoplasticity.

items.title: Researchers audit four LLMs governing social robots across four cultures, finding persistent failures in culturally specific moral prioritization despite varied prompting methods [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Auditing LLM-Governed Social Robots with Culture-Specific Moral Gradients
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a comprehensive audit of four large language models (LLMs) that govern social robots, assessing their ability to prioritize assistance across different cultural contexts. The study evaluated these models in four countries and languages, using scenarios that reflect culturally specific moral trade-offs involving age, status, and group size. Despite various prompting methods, the models consistently failed to align with local cultural norms, particularly showing weaker calibration for Chinese and Japanese contexts compared to Western ones.

The audit involved 57,600 decisions across care, education, and service scenarios, benchmarking model responses against country-specific moral preference gradients derived from extensive social robotics literature. The findings revealed that prompting alone was insufficient to correct cultural biases, with only contrastive exemplars improving performance, while reasoning prompts sometimes worsened it. The study highlights the need for multilingual, culturally aware audits before deploying LLM-governed robots to ensure equitable and context-sensitive assistance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28345v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM-governed social robots increasingly decide who receives real-world assistance first. As prioritization norms vary across cultures by age, status, and group size, failure to calibrate pluralistically can scale into unequal access. Yet LLM moral audits remain English-centered, rarely test embodied contexts, leaving pluralistic calibration as an urgent diagnostic gap amid intensifying LLM-robot deployment. We introduce a gradient-based audit framework for multilingual evaluation of LLM moral trade-off behavior against cultural preference gradients. Grounded in nine cross-domain social robotics reviews (>8,000 papers), we derive symmetry-controlled scenarios across care, education, and services, translating the Moral Machine Experiment's "whom to spare" into "whom to assist first" dilemmas with preserved identity trade-offs (many vs. few; young vs. old; higher vs. lower status). We audit four LLMs across four country-language pairs in four prompting regimes (57,600 decisions), benchmarked against country-specific MME preference gradients. Ordinal concordance tests whether models differentiate cultural contexts; a governance typology maps vulnerabilities in gradient differentiation, directional tendency, and deliberation. We find persistent, culturally asymmetric gradient tracking failures that prompting alone cannot reliably correct: quality calibration is nearly twice as strong for Western-language decisions as for Chinese and Japanese; high determinism in majority-first trade-offs often erases cross-cultural gradients; partial sensitivity to age- and status-based norms risks sidelining minorities. Prompting effects are uneven; only contrastive exemplars yield consistent gains, while reasoning-only prompts can worsen tracking. Our results motivate multilingual, pluralistic audits as an LLM-robot pre-deployment gate and suggest model factors are a more robust lever than prompting alone.

items.title: Researchers argue AI safety should be treated as an epistemic property ensuring future teachability, not just current behavior, to maintain corrective leverage over time [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agentic Safety is an Epistemic Property, Not a Behavioral One
items.summary:
Researchers argue that AI safety should be viewed not just as a measure of current system behavior but as an epistemic property that ensures a system remains correctable and teachable over time. As AI systems grow more capable and self-modifying, traditional safety methods that focus on snapshots of behavior become insufficient. The concept of "teachability" is introduced to emphasize the importance of preserving future corrective leverage despite the system's ongoing learning and adaptation.

The paper highlights that advanced AI systems might maintain apparent competence while undermining the internal conditions necessary for future correction, such as representational or algorithmic structures. Ensuring AI remains teachable is crucial for maintaining safety throughout its evolution, requiring interventions that consider not only present behavior but also the system's capacity for future alignment and control.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28347v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Contemporary AI safety spans pre-training interventions, post-training alignment, deployment-time controls, monitoring, and red-teaming. These methods are necessary, but they primarily certify snapshots of system behavior. As AI systems become more capable, dynamic, embodied, and self-improving, this snapshot view becomes incomplete: safety depends not only on whether a system behaves acceptably now, but whether it remains correctable as it learns, adapts, acts, and modifies itself over time. This paper argues that safety should therefore be treated as an epistemic property of the evolving learner, not merely a behavioral property of the current policy. We introduce teachability as the capacity to preserve future corrective leverage under bounded human, institutional, or environmental intervention. We argue that advanced systems can retain visible competence while eroding the representational, algorithmic, or meta-decision conditions needed for future correction. Safe advanced AI systems must not only behave acceptably now; they must remain teachable later.

items.title: Researchers analyze Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct's citation mechanism in retrieval-augmented generation, identifying a distributed attributional ensemble affecting citation accuracy on PopQA and HotpotQA datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Do LLMs Cite? A Mechanistic Interpretation of Attribution in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have investigated how the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct large language model decides to include inline citations when answering fact-based questions in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Their study reveals that citation decisions arise from a distributed, multi-stage "attributional ensemble" of attention heads and MLP layers rather than a single component. By manipulating these critical components, they were able to significantly reduce missed and spurious citations on the PopQA dataset without affecting answer accuracy.

The team used activation patching techniques in a controlled environment and found that while improvements on the multi-document HotpotQA dataset were more modest, the same mechanism influenced citation behavior consistently across datasets. These findings suggest a disconnect between the model's apparent reasoning and its internal processes, indicating that inline citations may not always reliably reflect the model's true use of sources, potentially creating a false sense of trustworthiness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28358v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) aims to enhance the trustworthiness of Large Language Models (LLMs) by grounding their outputs in external documents, often using inline citations for verifiability. However, the faithfulness of these citations -- whether the model genuinely uses a source to generate an answer -- remains a critical, unverified assumption. This paper offers the first mechanistic account of how a large language model decides whether to attach an inline citation while answering a factoid question. Using the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model in a controlled experimental environment based on the PopQA dataset, we employ an activation patching approach. We map the underlying mechanism responsible for citation, discovering that it is not a single, localized component but a distributed, multi-stage "attributional ensemble" of attention heads and MLP layers. We show that amplifying or attenuating only those critical heads and MLPs repairs over 90% of missed citations and eliminates 69% of spurious ones on PopQA without harming answer accuracy. Although gains on the multi-document HotpotQA benchmark are modest, the same component set still moves citation rates in the intended direction, indicating that the underlying mechanism is not dataset-specific. The results reveal a potential disconnect between the model's apparent reasoning and its internal computational pathway, suggesting that inline citations can create a false sense of security.

items.title: Researchers present LUMEN, an open-source multi-agent pipeline automating six systematic review phases with 11 LLM agents, achieving 100% directional agreement and costing $19-$29 per review [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LUMEN: Cost-Transparent Multi-Agent Pipeline for Automated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LUMEN, an open-source multi-agent pipeline that automates six phases of systematic reviews and meta-analyses using 11 specialized large language model agents. Evaluated across seven datasets, LUMEN achieved 100% directional agreement with published meta-analyses and maintained effect sizes within 1% for homogeneous study designs, demonstrating high accuracy and reliability. The pipeline offers a cost-effective solution, completing reviews for $19 to $29, with title-abstract screening and data extraction accounting for most expenses.

The study provides the first detailed analysis of the operational costs and performance trade-offs in an end-to-end automated systematic review pipeline. It highlights that while a multi-agent approach may reduce efficiency in screening, it is crucial for data extraction, significantly increasing the number of poolable analyses and eliminating clinically significant errors. Additionally, the research shows that model effectiveness varies by domain and is not universally transferable across different review topics. All related code and cost data have been made publicly available to support further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28362v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses (SR/MA) remain the gold standard for evidence synthesis, yet completing one typically requires 67 weeks and substantial expert effort. Recent large language model (LLM) systems have demonstrated strong performance on individual SR phases - screening (otto-SR: 96.7% sensitivity), extraction (Gartlehner et al.: 91.0% accuracy), and search (TrialMind: 0.83 recall) - but no study has reported what it actually costs to run an end-to-end pipeline, how cost distributes across phases, or how architectural choices affect the cost-quality trade-off. We present LUMEN, an open-source multi-agent pipeline that automates six SR/MA phases using 11 specialized LLM agents with deliberate model routing. We evaluate LUMEN on seven datasets: five self-conducted domain reviews (psychiatry, psychology, surgery, vaccinology, cardiology) and two SYNERGY screening benchmarks. Across 13 ground-truth-comparable outcomes, LUMEN achieves 100% directional agreement with published meta-analyses, with effect sizes within 1% for homogeneous study designs. The primary contribution is the first empirical cost and operational characterization of such a pipeline: a complete review costs 19 to 29 USD (median 22.65 USD), with title-abstract screening and data extraction together dominating expenditure. A three-arm extraction ablation reveals a phase-dependent architecture reversal: multi-agent design hurts screening but is essential for extraction, producing 5.7x more poolable analyses than single-model alternatives while eliminating clinically dangerous direction errors. A two-dataset screening benchmark demonstrates that model ranking is domain-dependent and not transferable across review topics. All code and cost logs are publicly available.

items.title: Researchers introduce LEDGER, a dependency-aware graph retrieval system that improves consistency and reduces token usage in agentic document editing across six AI models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LEDGER: Scaling Agentic Document Editing with Dependency-aware Graph Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LEDGER, a system designed to improve agentic document editing by efficiently managing localized edits in long, structured documents without disrupting cross-references or semantic consistency. LEDGER uses a lightweight dependency graph to model document structure, including hierarchical organization and semantic relationships, enabling graph-guided retrieval to select only the necessary context for each edit. This approach avoids processing the entire document while maintaining consistency and reducing token usage.

Evaluated on a benchmark of 1,900 test cases across six state-of-the-art AI models, LEDGER increased consistency rates from 56% to 76% and lowered token consumption. The system demonstrated that explicit dependency representations can partially replace intensive internal reasoning, achieving comparable performance with less computational effort in agentic document editing tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28379v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce LEDGER to tackle the novel context engineering challenge of agentic document editing, where localized edits to long, structured documents must be applied efficiently without breaking cross-references or semantic consistency. LEDGER constructs a lightweight dependency graph that explicitly models document structure, including hierarchical organization, explicit references, implicit dependencies, and semantic relationships. For each edit, graph-guided retrieval selects only the necessary context, avoiding full-document processing while preserving consistency. We evaluate LEDGER on a curated benchmark of 1.9k test cases with various document types and lengths, spanning six state-of-the-art models: LEDGER improves consistency from 56% to 76% across all six models and test scenarios while reducing token usage. Notably, LEDGER with low reasoning effort matches baseline performance at high reasoning effort using fewer tokens, showing that explicit dependency representations can partially substitute for expensive internal reasoning in agentic document editing.

items.title: Researchers present RADIANT-PET, a reasoning-augmented PET/CT lesion segmentation framework using large language models and reinforcement learning to improve lesion classification accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RADIANT-PET: Reasoning-Augmented PET/CT Lesion Segmentation with Large Language Models and Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed RADIANT-PET, a novel framework that enhances lesion segmentation in PET/CT scans by integrating a high-sensitivity voxel-level segmentation model with lesion-level reasoning using large language models (LLMs) and reinforcement learning. This approach generates candidate uptake regions, converts them into structured textual descriptions, and uses an LLM to classify each candidate as a true lesion or false positive, optionally incorporating radiology reports for additional clinical context. The system is further optimized through reinforcement learning to improve lesion classification and anatomical site assignment.

Tested on AutoPET and an OSU cohort, RADIANT-PET outperforms existing image-only segmentation methods, particularly when radiology reports are included. The framework adds a reasoning layer beyond conventional segmentation, reducing false positives caused by physiological tracer uptake and aligning predictions more closely with clinical interpretations. The project is publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28392v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate lesion segmentation in PET/CT is critical for oncology, yet remains challenging because physiologic tracer uptake and artifacts can mimic malignant signal. We present RADIANT-PET, a reasoning-augmented framework that couples a high-sensitivity voxel-level segmentation model with lesion-level large language model (LLM) adjudication. Candidate uptake regions are generated with a deliberately permissive segmentation stage, then converted into structured textual descriptions that summarize uptake intensity, morphology, and regional and global anatomical context. An LLM classifies each candidate as true lesion vs. false positive, optionally leveraging the radiology report as additional clinical context. To strengthen lesion-level reasoning, we further optimize a local LLM via reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization, rewarding correct lesion classification and anatomically concordant site assignment. Across AutoPET and an OSU test cohort, RADIANT-PET consistently outperforms strong image-only baselines, with the largest improvements observed when radiology reports are provided. Overall, these results demonstrate that LLM-based lesion-level reasoning adds a novel reasoning layer beyond conventional segmentation, suppressing physiologic false positives and aligning voxel-level predictions with clinical interpretation. The project repository is available at: https://github.com/jwang-580/RADIANT-PET.

items.title: Systematic review identifies gaps in reinforcement learning techniques for C/C++ software vulnerability analysis, highlighting limited use of control flow graphs and static analysis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reinforcement Learning for Software Vulnerability Analysis: A Systematic Review with Emphasis on C/C++ Source Code and Static Analysis
items.summary:
A systematic review of reinforcement learning (RL) techniques for software vulnerability analysis in C/C++ highlights significant gaps, particularly the limited use of control flow graphs (CFGs) and static analysis methods. The review, covering 21 studies from 2015 to 2026, finds that most research focuses on fuzzing and guided exploration, with few addressing direct vulnerability detection or statement-level localization. It also notes that structural code representations like CFGs and abstract syntax trees (ASTs) are rarely employed as agent states in RL models, and existing benchmarks lack comparability.

The study proposes a taxonomy based on tasks and RL formulations and identifies a key research gap: no RL agents currently use source-code CFGs to detect and localize vulnerable nodes. This gap suggests opportunities for advancing vulnerability detection methods by integrating more sophisticated static analysis representations into RL frameworks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28403v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vulnerability detection in C/C++ software remains a major security challenge due to code complexity, manual memory management, and the limitations of traditional static analysis. Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a promising approach, particularly for fuzzing, test generation, program exploration, and, more recently, vulnerability detection and localization. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this work reviews RL techniques for software vulnerability analysis, focusing on C/C++ source code and static analysis. We identified 21 primary studies published between 2015 and 2026 from major scientific databases and complementary searches. We analyze the addressed tasks, algorithms, state-action-reward-environment formulations, code representations, datasets, and evaluation metrics. Results show that 15 studies focus on fuzzing and guided exploration, only 3 on direct vulnerability detection, and just 1 on statement-level localization. Moreover, statically extracted structural representations such as Control Flow Graphs (CFGs) and Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) are rarely used as agent states, and benchmarks lack comparability. We propose a task- and formulation-oriented taxonomy and identify a key research gap: the absence of RL agents that use source-code CFGs as states to detect and localize vulnerable nodes.

items.originalTitle: On the Necessity of a Liquid Substrate for Mesh Intelligence
items.summary: Researchers have demonstrated that for a mesh of autonomous agents to effectively process irregular, unscheduled observations without retraining, the underlying computational substrate must meet two key conditions. These agents operate without a shared clock, model, or coordinator, relying on folding peer projections into a single internal state in real time. The study proves that an adaptive timescale is necessary due to the time-varying nature of the latent variables, and that the optimal estimation depends on the elapsed time between observations, which fixed-gain or gap-blind networks cannot capture.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A mesh of sovereign agents has no center: no shared clock, no shared model, and no coordinator to gather data or retrain. Its competence rests on each agent folding the projections its peers emit into a single internal state, online, from observations that arrive at irregular, unscheduled times, on a substrate whose weights it cannot retrain. Any one of these constraints is tractable on its own; folding optimally under all three at once is not. We ask what such a substrate must be, and prove two necessary conditions from one model of a self-evolving latent observed at irregular, exogenous times. Because the latent changes, its optimal estimator is time-varying: an adaptive timescale is necessary, and every fixed-gain filter is strictly suboptimal. And because arrivals are clock-free, the optimal estimate depends on the elapsed gap between them, which no gap-blind network recovers at any width or depth. This second condition is capacity-independent: scale cannot substitute for the missing dependence. The two conditions intersect in the continuous-time liquid class. An LSTM satisfies the first, a fixed continuous-time filter the second, and a multi-timescale liquid network both. Synthetic experiments confirm each: the network attains the timescale, and the separation is computed exactly. The characterization is necessary, not sufficient, and binds fixed-weight substrates: a network free to retrain reaches the class by other means. Proved per agent, the necessity binds every agent of a mesh, a structural condition on mesh intelligence.

items.title: Researchers analyze spectral perturbation of empirical Fisher Information Matrix under input shifts and weight quantization, providing bounds and runtime monitoring methods for language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Spectral Perturbation of the Empirical Fisher Information Matrix under Weight Quantization
items.summary:
Researchers have analyzed how the empirical Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) of parametric statistical models is affected by two types of structured perturbations: shifts in input data distribution and quantization of model parameters. They demonstrated that deviations from a reference input distribution increase the dominant eigenvalue of the FIM under certain curvature conditions, and established bounds showing that quantization noise generally raises this eigenvalue beyond its unperturbed value. The study provides practical approximations and proposes using the ratio of perturbed to baseline eigenvalues as a runtime monitoring metric for language models, supported by empirical measurements across multiple models.

The work includes theoretical results based on Weyl's inequality and introduces a threshold-based partitioning approach for analyzing the augmented state space. The authors discuss the limitations of their findings and highlight an open problem regarding the precise prediction of the quantization-induced eigenvalue inflation. Their empirical observations notably include a calibration threshold for the monitoring statistic that was significantly higher on a 4-bit quantized model compared to full-precision estimates, illustrating the practical impact of quantization on model behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28432v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the spectral perturbation of the empirical Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) of a parametric statistical model under two structured perturbations: departure of the input from a reference (in-distribution) ensemble, and finite-precision (quantized) perturbation of the model's parameters. For the first, under an explicit local curvature-monotonicity hypothesis on the dominant eigenvalue lambda_max of the FIM, we show departure from a reference manifold provably elevates lambda_max relative to a calibration baseline (Proposition 3.2), and discuss why this hypothesis is required, since curvature need not increase monotonically under every perturbation. Our principal result is a directional eigenvalue perturbation bound, via Weyl's inequality, showing lambda_max under a quantization noise perturbation is lower bounded by its unperturbed value up to a third-order remainder, and, under a mild genericity condition, strictly exceeds it at leading order (Theorem 4.3). We give two tractable approximations to lambda_max -- one heuristic, one with a rigorous two-sided bound -- and a completeness result for a threshold-based partition of an augmented state space. These results motivate using sigma_t = lambda_max(F_t)/lambda_base as a runtime monitoring statistic for deployed language models: the quantization result offers a mechanism for an empirical observation of our own, where a calibration threshold for this statistic was approximately 244 times larger than a preliminary full-precision estimate on a 4-bit quantized model, a single measurement rather than a value derived in closed form. We report supporting measurements (twelve models, n=1,080 trajectories) broadly consistent with our predictions, discuss the scope and limitations of every result, and state as an open problem the closed-form prediction of the quantization inflation magnitude our bound does not supply.

items.title: Researchers propose Covariance-Agnostic Neural Kalman Consensus Filter for distributed latent state estimation under partially known dynamics, outperforming traditional filters in diverse environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning to Distributedly Estimate under Partially Known Dynamics: A Covariance-Agnostic Neural Kalman Consensus Filter
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new online distributed sensing framework called the Covariance-Agnostic Neural Kalman Consensus Filter (CA-NKCF) for latent state estimation in artificial intelligence. This approach enables multiple agents to collaborate and exchange information to estimate hidden states without requiring knowledge of noise statistics. By integrating partial domain knowledge with deep neural networks and Kalman-like recursive updates, CA-NKCF performs decentralized inference effectively under partially known dynamics.

Extensive testing in various environments—including linear systems, chaotic Lorenz systems, and wireless tracking scenarios—demonstrates that CA-NKCF outperforms traditional distributed Kalman and particle filters as well as purely model-free neural networks. The method shows robustness even when motion and observation models are misspecified and maintains stable performance across different noise levels, communication topologies, latent state dimensions, and observation clutter conditions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online latent state estimation constitutes a fundamental challenge within the artificial intelligence field, serving as a foundational tool for diverse applications, including sequential decision making, anomaly and change-point detection. In this paper, a novel online distributed sensing framework, where agents collaborate and exchange information to perform latent state estimation, is presented. The proposed estimator combines available partial domain knowledge with the representation capabilities of deep neural networks. In particular, the designed sensing framework incorporates prior estimates, optimized consensus weights, and Kalman-like recursive updates to perform decentralized inference, without relying on knowledge of noise statistics. Extensive experiments on linear, chaotic (Lorenz), and practical wireless tracking environments reveal that the proposed Covariance-Agnostic Neural Kalman Consensus Filter (CA-NKCF) outperforms traditional distributed Kalman and particle filters as well as purely model-free deep neural networks, exhibiting robustness even when the underlying motion and observation models are misspecified. It is also demonstrated that CA-NKCF's performance advantage remains stable across varying noise levels, random communication topologies, latent state dimensions, and observation clutter densities induced by scattering objects in wireless systems.

items.title: Researchers propose S-GAI, a spectral geometry-aware initialization method for one-hidden-layer sigmoidal MLPs that embeds class-wise spectral geometry from training data and improves initial hidden states on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: S-GAI: Spectral Geometry-Aware Initialization for Sigmoidal MLPs -- From Dataset Geometry to Network Weights
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced S-GAI, a spectral geometry-aware initialization method for one-hidden-layer sigmoidal multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) that embeds class-specific spectral geometry derived from training data. This approach uses singular value decomposition (SVD) to extract principal directions and scales for each class, which are then represented by sigmoid gates forming a shared hidden layer. Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 demonstrate that S-GAI provides a more informative initial hidden state than traditional Xavier initialization and achieves comparable final accuracy after full training.

The method leverages the idea that sigmoid units can act as smooth half-space gates, moving beyond hand-specified planar geometry to data-driven spectral geometry. A subspace classifier based on SVD is also proposed to assess the discriminative power of the spectral class geometry before embedding it into the MLP. When the hidden layer is frozen, training only the output layer still yields better performance than using frozen random gates, indicating that S-GAI effectively encodes class-wise spectral geometry into the network.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical universal approximation theorems establish the expressive power of sigmoidal multilayer perceptrons, but they do not prescribe how initial weights should encode the geometry of a data distribution. We propose S-GAI, a spectral geometry-aware initialization framework for one-hidden-layer sigmoidal MLPs. Starting from the constructive idea that sigmoid units can act as smooth half-space gates, we move from hand-specified planar geometry to class-wise spectral geometry estimated from image data. For each class, SVD provides a mean, principal directions, and spectral scales. An energy threshold selects the retained directions, and each retained direction is represented by two sigmoid gates. These class-specific gates form a shared hidden layer initialized directly from the training set. We also formulate a SVD-based subspace classifier as a non-neural geometric reference, which tests whether the estimated spectral class geometry is already discriminative before being embedded into the MLP. Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and a more challenging CIFAR-10 test show that the S-GAI-initialized MLP starts from a substantially more informative hidden state than Xavier initialization and reaches comparable final accuracy under full training. When the hidden layer is frozen, training only the output layer still gives stronger performance than frozen random gates, providing evidence that S-GAI effectively embeds class-wise spectral geometry into the MLP.

items.title: Researchers introduce a diagnostic protocol to analyze event-conditioned latent physical structures in passive object-state world models using recurrent and attention-based models on controlled datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Event-Conditioned Diagnostics of Kinematic, Contact, and Object-Permanence Fields in Passive Object-State World Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a diagnostic protocol to analyze how latent physical information is organized and utilized within passive object-state world models, which predict future physical states. The protocol assesses whether hidden model representations encode event-specific information and how different event contexts influence physical field readouts related to kinematics, contact, and object permanence. Using a controlled dataset featuring free motion, collisions, and occlusions, the study evaluates recurrent, attention-based, and latent state-space models under fixed-horizon forecasting conditions.

The findings reveal that models effectively learn predictive dynamics and that their hidden states reliably reflect event regimes. Different event types systematically emphasize distinct physical fields: free motion is dominated by kinematic information, collisions combine kinematic and contact data, and occlusions involve motion and object permanence. Further analyses demonstrate phase-related shifts in field emphasis, and causal field effect tests show that suppressing certain field-aligned directions can impair event-relevant predictions, particularly contact-aligned structures during collisions.

These results support the idea that latent physical fields are organized in an event-conditioned manner and are functionally sensitive within fixed forecasting horizons. However, the study does not suggest the presence of explicit physical modules or isolated causal circuits, nor does it imply that these models generalize uniformly across different contexts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28455v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World models can predict future physical states, but prediction accuracy alone does not explain how physical information is organized and used inside their latent dynamics. We introduce a controlled diagnostic protocol for studying event-conditioned latent physical structure in passive object-state world models. The protocol tests whether hidden representations encode event-regime information, whether event contexts reweight non-exclusive physical field readouts, and whether field-aligned representational components have functional consequences for prediction. Using a balanced controlled-generator dataset with free-motion, collision, and occlusion events, we evaluate recurrent, attention-based, and latent state-space transition models under a fixed-horizon forecasting setup. The models learn useful predictive dynamics and their hidden states support reliable event-regime readout. Event contexts systematically reweight kinematic, contact, and object-permanence field readouts: free motion is kinematic-dominant, collision combines kinematic and contact structure, and occlusion combines motion-related and object-permanence structure. Time-aligned and directional-consistency analyses further show phase-related shifts in field emphasis. Finally, fixed-horizon projection causal field effect (CFE) shows that suppressing field-aligned directions can degrade event-relevant prediction, with strongest evidence for contact-aligned structure in collision-contact windows and more qualified evidence for object-permanence-aligned structure in hard-occlusion hidden windows. These results support event-conditioned organization and fixed-horizon functional sensitivity of latent physical fields, while not implying explicit physical modules, isolated causal circuits, or context-invariant sliding-window generalization.

items.summary:

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data-driven modeling in real-world regression tasks often suffers from limited training samples, high collection costs, and noisy observations. Inspired by the impact of data augmentation in vision and language, we propose a novel Counterfactual Residual Data Augmentation (CRDA) technique for tabular regression. Our key insight is that once a regressor has modeled the systematic component of the data, the remaining noise can be viewed as an invariant residual that remains stable under small perturbations of carefully selected features. We exploit this residual invariance to generate new, yet realistic, training samples, effectively expanding the dataset without requiring additional real data. Our method is model-agnostic and readily applicable to various types of regressors. In experiments across datasets from a variety of benchmark repositories, on average, CRDA reduces an MLP Regressor's MSE by 22.9% and an XGBoost Regressor's MSE by 6.4%. When compared to existing state-of-the-art data generators and augmentation techniques, CRDA consistently outperforms in MSE reduction. By adding principled counterfactual variations to the training data, our method offers a simple and efficient remedy for noise-prone, small-sample regression settings.

items.title: Researchers propose a gravitational interpretation of fine-tuning reversion, identifying a history-defined direction that partially controls early post-alignment behavior changes in AI models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Gravitational Interpretation of Fine-Tuning Reversion
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a geometric interpretation of fine-tuning reversion in AI models, suggesting that early training phases create dominant behavioral patterns, or manifolds, which later fine-tuning partially reverts toward. This "gravitational" effect explains how safety can degrade after alignment, unlearned capabilities may re-emerge, and latent traits transfer through unrelated supervision. The study identifies a history-defined direction, called v_rev, that significantly influences early post-alignment behavior changes and representational drift in models.

The team demonstrated that alignment with this reversion direction increases notably during fine-tuning and that blocking movement along v_rev reduces harmful behaviors with minimal impact on task performance. While v_rev is not claimed to be the sole safety direction, it serves as a robust mediator of early reversion dynamics, offering insight into the fragility of post-alignment updates and the persistence of training history effects in AI behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning on harmless data can partially undo behaviors acquired earlier in training. Safety can erode under benign post-alignment updates, unlearned capabilities can re-emerge, latent traits can transfer through apparently unrelated supervision, and related post-alignment fragility appears in other generative settings. We argue these phenomena are usefully viewed through a common training-history lens. Our hypothesis is geometric: large early training phases create dominant behavioral manifolds, while later alignment or specialization phases are shallower displacements from them. Subsequent fine-tuning can therefore inherit a persistent reversion component pointing back toward a witness of the dominant manifold. We call this the gravitational interpretation of fine-tuning reversion. Across our main settings, representational drift rapidly acquires a component along a history-defined reversion direction (v_rev). In our main track, alignment with v_rev rises from cos = 0.429 +/- 0.052 after the first update to 0.647 +/- 0.021 by step 20. Across 24 run-step pairs, every observed alignment exceeds the p99 of an isotropic activation-space null. We demonstrate that selectively blocking motion along v_rev changes the final alignment at T=100 from 0.648 +/- 0.009 to -0.211 +/- 0.021 and reduces harmfulness from 19.0% +/- 4.0% to 8.5% +/- 1.5% with little task cost. These results support v_rev as a causally relevant mediator of early post-alignment reversion in our setup. Importantly, we do not claim that v_rev is the unique safety direction, nor that the dominant manifold is directly observed; rather, we identify a robust, history-defined direction that explains and partially controls early reversion dynamics.

items.title: Researchers propose MammoFlow, a method synthesizing anatomically consistent multiview mammograms using flow matching and geometric tissue correspondence, improving classification AUC by 5% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MammoFlow: Multiview Mammogram Synthesis with Anatomically Consistent Flow Matching
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MammoFlow, a novel method for synthesizing anatomically consistent multiview mammograms by leveraging the geometric relationship between craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) views. This approach uses an alignment module to establish optimal anatomical correspondence and a self-consistency loss based on tissue distribution, integrated into a pretrained flow matching model to generate physically plausible image pairs. MammoFlow improves image quality, passes expert radiologist evaluation, and enhances classification performance by increasing the area under the curve (AUC) by 5%. 

The method addresses challenges in acquiring high-quality, balanced mammography datasets for deep learning by enforcing implicit 3D consistency during image generation. It is the first to guide multiview mammogram synthesis using implicit geometric tissue correspondence, ensuring that synthesized pairs share realistic tissue distributions from the chest wall to the nipple. The researchers have made the code publicly available for further use and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28537v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multiview mammography relies on paired craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) views to provide complementary projections of a 3D breast volume, enabling precise anomaly localization. However, acquiring high-quality, balanced datasets remains challenging for deep learning applications. We propose a novel method to synthesize multiview mammograms by leveraging the inherent geometric relationship between CC and MLO views. To enforce an implicit 3D consistency prior during generation, we develop an alignment module that searches a 2D affine transformation subspace to establish optimal anatomical correspondence. Leveraging this alignment, we introduce a pixel-space self-consistency loss based on the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) between the 1D anteroposterior (AP) axis tissue distributions of the generated images. Integrated into a pretrained flow matching model, MammoFlow forces synthesized pairs to share physically plausible tissue distributions from the chest wall to the nipple. To our knowledge, this is the first work to guide multiview mammogram generation using implicit geometric tissue correspondence. Our method demonstrates superior image quality, passes expert radiologist evaluation, and generates physically consistent pairs that improve downstream classification AUC by 5%. Code is available at https://github.com/XYPB/MammoFlow

items.title: Researchers measure geometric signatures of the axiom of choice in neural proof embeddings using Lean 4, analyzing over 471,000 Mathlib declarations and linking results to theorem prover performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Geometric Measurements of the Axiom of Choice in Neural Proof Embeddings
items.summary:
Researchers have used Lean 4's kernel-level tracking to analyze over 471,000 Mathlib declarations, identifying a geometric signature associated with the axiom of choice in proof space. By training a self-supervised proof encoder on constructive proofs, they found that certain measurements decline as proofs become more dependent on the axiom, revealing a measurable difference between classical and constructive proofs. This signature remains robust across various controls and encoding methods.

The study also demonstrated practical implications for theorem proving: Lean's aesop tactic solves constructive theorems significantly faster than classical ones, and a neural-guided hybrid approach reduces this gap. The geometric anomaly score developed predicts aesop's failure beyond proof length, linking the geometric properties of proofs to the performance of automated theorem provers.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The axiom of choice has divided the foundations of mathematics for over a century, but the distinction between classical and constructive proofs has remained a philosophical and methodological one. We use Lean 4's kernel-level tracking of axiom dependence to show that the axiom of choice has a measurable geometric correlate in proof space that obeys a one-parameter mixture law and has operational consequences for neural theorem provers. To do this, we partition $471{,}260$ declarations of Mathlib by transitive dependence on the axiom of choice and represent a filtered population of $42{,}355$ traced theorems by their sequences of tactic invocations. We use the constructive proofs in this dataset to train a self-supervised proof encoder and show that when using it to measure classical proofs, three complementary measurements (anomaly score, reconstruction loss, and density-superlevel containment) exhibit a common decline with the proof's distance from the axiom in the dependency graph, from sharp separation at the shallow boundary (AUC $0.847$ at distance $2$) to indistinguishability at distance~$9{+}$. Robustness controls show that the signature survives length, file, author, and topic controls, and replicates under full-source encoders trained on normalised proof source. Operationally, we show that on an evaluation sample of $251$ Mathlib theorems, Lean's \texttt{aesop} tactic solves constructive theorems at $13\times$ the rate of classical ones, and a neural-guided hybrid using the ReProver tactic generator compresses the gap to $5\times$. The geometric anomaly score predicts \texttt{aesop} failure beyond proof length, providing an operational link between the geometric signature and prover performance.

items.title: Researchers propose grain calibration to validate large language models as measurement instruments for theoretical constructs by decomposing constructs into clause-level components with theory-derived rules [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Correct codes for the wrong reasons? validating LLMs as measurement instruments for theoretical constructs
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a method called grain calibration to improve the validation of large language models (LLMs) as measurement tools for theoretical constructs. Unlike traditional reliability checks that compare LLM coding to human annotators, this approach breaks down constructs into clause-level components and evaluates each against text using theory-based rules. This process provides transparent evidence of how the model interprets constructs, enhancing construct validity beyond mere agreement with human coding.

Grain calibration explicitly tests each component of a construct and combines results through clear, theory-derived rules rather than relying on opaque model outputs. This allows identification of which components influenced a code and whether errors stem from missing elements or confusion with related constructs. The method shifts validation focus from output comparison to demonstrating that the instrument operates according to the theoretical framework it aims to measure.
