items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a large language model (LLM) codes a construct in text as a human annotator would, that agreement makes the LLM a reliable coder. Yet reliability leaves construct validity untouched. The instrument may be theory-naive, reaching the code through a correlate that meets none of the demands the construct's theory makes, and no current method tells that apart from genuine measurement. We propose grain calibration as a method that closes the gap. It decomposes a construct into clause-level components, tests each against the text with extractive evidence, and combines the results through an explicit, theory-derived rule. Because the rule is stated rather than lodged in one opaque pass, its structure is evidence about the process rather than the output. It shows which components settled a code, and, when the code is wrong, whether a component was missed or an adjacent construct mistaken for it. Validation shifts from scoring an instrument's outputs against an annotator to showing that the instrument runs on the construct its theory specifies.

items.title: Researchers introduce Animation2Code benchmark to evaluate temporal visual reasoning in video-to-code generation, revealing current vision-language models struggle with temporal consistency despite high appearance similarity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Animation2Code: Evaluating Temporal Visual Reasoning in Video-to-Code Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Animation2Code, a new benchmark designed to evaluate temporal visual reasoning by reconstructing executable web animation code from videos. The dataset includes 1,069 web animation videos paired with their corresponding HTML, CSS, and JavaScript implementations, enabling assessment of both visual appearance and motion dynamics. Two human-aligned metrics, appearance similarity and temporal similarity, help distinguish between visual fidelity and temporal alignment in generated animations.

Testing state-of-the-art vision-language models on Animation2Code revealed that while these models can achieve high appearance similarity, they struggle to maintain temporal consistency in their reconstructions. This limitation persists even with finetuning and iterative refinement, highlighting challenges in capturing motion dynamics accurately. The benchmark and associated code are publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28593v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While recent vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved significant improvements on static visual-to-code tasks such as generating code for webpages, charts, or SVGs, it remains unclear whether they can recover temporal dynamics when motion is present. To this end, we introduce Animation2Code, a benchmark for evaluating temporal visual reasoning via reconstructing executable web animation code from videos. items.title: Researchers introduce energy-aware reinforcement learning for adaptive deep brain stimulation, reducing stimulation charge by 80% and inference energy by 28x on neuromorphic hardware [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Neuromorphic Energy-Aware Learning for Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an energy-aware reinforcement learning approach for adaptive deep brain stimulation (DBS) in Parkinson's disease, significantly reducing both stimulation energy and computational inference costs. Using a deep spiking Q-network trained on a biophysical brain circuit model, the system suppresses pathological brain oscillations by 45.2% while cutting stimulation charge by 80% compared to continuous DBS. The learned policy is efficiently compressed onto a neuromorphic processor, achieving 28 times lower energy per inference than traditional neural networks on standard hardware.

This method integrates actuator energy consumption directly into the reinforcement learning reward, addressing the combined energy demands of both the neural controller and the stimulation actuator in closed-loop neuromodulation systems. By co-optimizing these factors, the framework offers a promising solution for energy-efficient, implantable brain stimulation devices.

Here, we introduce energy-aware learning, an approach that incorporates actuator energy directly into the reinforcement learning reward, and demonstrate it in closed-loop deep brain stimulation (DBS) for Parkinson's disease. Sparsity-constrained knowledge distillation compresses the policy onto the SynSense XyloAudio 3 neuromorphic processor at 0.52 mW inference power, yielding 28.1x lower energy per inference than an equivalent artificial neural network on conventional edge hardware. By co-optimizing stimulation energy and inference efficiency, the framework addresses both major power demands in implantable neuromodulation.

items.title: Researchers prove fundamental mathematical limits of AGI alignment, establishing structural unverifiability and containment failures that challenge current AI safety engineering approaches [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Undecidability of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) Alignment
items.summary:
A recent study establishes fundamental mathematical limits on the safety of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), demonstrating that the main challenge is not achieving alignment but the structural unverifiability of such alignment. The researchers present two key impossibility theorems that show current engineering approaches relying on finite hardware or halting architectures cannot overcome inherent logical barriers, leading to unavoidable containment failures in AGI systems.

The study identifies a triad of containment issues rooted in undecidability and algorithmic incomputability, and introduces the Soundness--Completeness--Tractability Trilemma, which reveals that these properties cannot coexist due to descriptive complexity. The findings suggest that modern AI containment strategies are not temporary fixes but necessary compromises that limit logical expressivity to maintain decidable and safe AI behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28639v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This article establishes the foundational mathematical limits of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) safety, proving that the core barrier is not the impossibility of an aligned state, but its structural unverifiability. We formalize this boundary through two central impossibility results: the Unverifiability Theorem of Alignment and the Theorem of Finite Structural Unverifiability of AGI Alignment. We ground this boundary at Trakhtenbrot's Wall, demonstrating that contemporary engineering defenses relying on finite hardware or halting architectures fail to escape logical obstructions. This failure manifests as an inescapable triad of containment failures: open domains yield fundamental undecidability (Rice and G\"odel); universal finite verification collapses into algorithmic incomputability (Trakhtenbrot); and particular bounded environments trap the supervisor within intractable bounds in the worst case. As a direct structural corollary of these results, we derive the Soundness--Completeness--Tractability Trilemma, establishing that the mutual incompatibility of these three properties is a necessary consequence of descriptive complexity rather than an empirical anomaly. Finally, we map these theoretical bounds onto practical AI engineering, demonstrating that modern containment strategies are not temporary patches, but mandatory sacrifices of logical expressivity required to secure decidable fragments of safety.

items.title: Researchers analyze parameter settings for the bat algorithm using variance evolution theory, confirming theoretical bounds with numerical experiments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Analysis of Parameter Settings for the Bat Algorithm Using Variance Evolution
items.summary:
Researchers have conducted a theoretical analysis of parameter settings for the bat algorithm, an evolutionary algorithm, using dynamical systems theory and the evolution of population variance. Their study establishes parameter ranges that influence the algorithm's performance and confirms these theoretical bounds through numerical experiments. This approach offers insights into key algorithmic behaviors such as variance evolution, the balance between exploration and exploitation, and convergence patterns.

The analysis addresses a common gap in evolutionary algorithm research, where practical effectiveness is often demonstrated through experiments but lacks rigorous theoretical backing. By linking theoretical predictions with empirical results, the study enhances understanding of how parameter choices affect the bat algorithm's dynamics and effectiveness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28644v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Parameter settings in evolutionary algorithms and metaheuristics are important because such parameter values can influence the performance of algorithms under evaluation. For a given algorithm, there are many different numerical experiments to show that the algorithm can work well in practice; however, in most cases there is no theoretical analysis of parameter settings. In this work, we show that theoretical analysis using the theory of dynamical systems and evolution of population variance can give some good results in terms of parameter ranges for the bat algorithm. We also show that results from numerical experiments are consistent with theoretical bounds. Such analyses can provide good insights from different perspectives about the algorithmic characteristics such as variance evolution, transition between exploration and exploitation as well as convergence behaviour.

items.title: Researchers propose FedLAS, a feature-modulated bidirectional label smoothing algorithm to improve neural network calibration by addressing both overconfidence and underconfidence in training samples [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FedLAS: Feature-Modulated Bidirectional Label Smoothing for Neural Network Calibration
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced FedLAS, a novel algorithm designed to improve the calibration of deep neural network classifiers by addressing both overconfidence and underconfidence in predictions. Unlike traditional label smoothing methods that apply uniform adjustments and mainly target overconfidence, FedLAS uses a Feature Norm-based Confidence Indicator and a Bidirectional Calibration Gating module to tailor smoothing dynamically for each training sample. This approach enhances model calibration while maintaining accuracy.

FedLAS integrates seamlessly with existing label smoothing techniques and has been tested extensively on standard and fine-grained high-resolution vision benchmarks. The results demonstrate consistent improvements in calibration metrics such as Expected Calibration Error and Adaptive ECE compared to current methods, without sacrificing Top-1 accuracy. The algorithm is available as a plug-and-play solution for standard deep neural networks, offering a practical advancement in neural network training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28654v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep Neural Network (DNN) classifiers suffer from poor calibration when their softmax outputs (predictive confidence) deviate from the empirical likelihoods. This manifests itself as either overconfident incorrect predictions or under-confident correct predictions. Label smoothing (LS) enhances model calibration by introducing entropy regularization during training through redistributing probability mass from the ground-truth label to the remaining classes. LS, including Margin-based LS (MbLS), have restrictive assumptions: they rely on predefined, uniform smoothing rules and only tackle overconfidence. In reality, samples exhibit diverse characteristics, such as difficulty/ambiguity, that interact with the evolving nature of the model being trained. In training, samples may have various degrees of under- or overconfidence. To overcome this, a mechanism that identifies the specific confidence state of each sample and determines the appropriate degree of smoothing in each training step is needed, tailoring the adjustment to the individual sample. We propose FedLAS: Feature-Modulated Bidirectional Label Smoothing, a plug-and-play algorithm for label smoothing-based losses. In FedLAS, we introduce a Feature Norm-based Confidence Indicator (NCI) to control smoothing and a Bidirectional Calibration Gating (BCG) module to detect both over and under-confidence. Our algorithm can be integrated with LS and MbLS based losses when applied to standard DNNs, enhancing performance. Extensive experiments on standard and fine-grained high-resolution vision benchmarks show that FedLAS consistently improves calibration compared to modern baselines, reducing Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Adaptive ECE while maintaining Top-1 accuracy. Code: github.com/nadarasarbahavan/FEDLAS

items.title: Researchers derive closed-form gradient of Wolkowicz-Styan upper bound to guide neural network parameters toward flat minima, proposing Hessian Spectral Range regularization for three-layer networks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Closed-Form Steepest Descent Direction toward Flat Minima: Reducing Upper Bounds on the Loss Hessian Eigenspectrum in Neural Networks
items.summary:
Researchers have derived a closed-form gradient of the Wolkowicz-Styan (WS) upper bound on the maximum eigenvalue of the loss Hessian in three-layer neural networks, enabling analytical characterization of directions toward flat minima. Building on this, they propose Hessian Spectral Range (HSR) Regularization, which updates network parameters along the steepest descent direction of the WS bound to promote convergence to flat minima associated with better generalization.

Experiments show that HSR Regularization effectively narrows the Hessian eigenvalue spectrum, helping avoid sharp minima and saddle points. While currently limited to cross-entropy loss and three-layer architectures, this approach is the first to provide a closed-form gradient that guides neural networks toward flat minima without relying on numerical approximations, offering a theoretical foundation for further advances in neural network optimization.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The flatness hypothesis suggests that flatness of the loss landscape, as measured by the eigenvalues of the loss Hessian, correlates with better neural network generalization. While various algorithms reduce these eigenvalues, most focus on procedural design, leaving it unclear how data distributions and NN parameters structurally determine directions toward flat minima. Characterizing these directions analytically is generally intractable. To overcome this mathematical difficulty, recent studies derived the Wolkowicz-Styan (WS) upper bound on the maximum eigenvalue of the cross-entropy loss Hessian in three-layer NNs. Although this upper bound is differentiable, its gradient was not derived. Therefore, we analytically derive the gradient of the WS upper bound to characterize directions leading to flat minima. Based on this, we propose Hessian Spectral Range (HSR) Regularization, which updates parameters along the steepest descent direction of the WS bound. Experiments demonstrate that HSR Regularization narrows the Hessian eigenvalue spectrum, avoids sharp minima and saddle points, and promotes convergence to flat minima. Although the applicability of this method is currently limited to cross-entropy loss and three-layer architectures, to the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to report a closed-form gradient that promotes convergence to flat minima without numerical approximations. Therefore, the theoretical analysis of this gradient is expected to contribute to the further development of NNs.

items.title: Researchers introduce MACROCAST, a vintage-consistent time series foundation model for real-time macroeconomic forecasting that eliminates data leakage and outperforms benchmarks in out-of-sample tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MACROCAST: A Vintage-Consistent Time Series Foundation Model for Real-Time Macroeconomic Forecasting
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MACROCAST, a novel Time Series Foundation Model designed for real-time macroeconomic forecasting that avoids common data leakage issues. Unlike existing models, MACROCAST is trained exclusively on synthetic and vintage-specific data, ensuring it only uses information available to forecasters at the time of prediction. This approach eliminates temporal contamination and revision bias, which have previously compromised forecasting accuracy.

The model is initially trained on synthetic time series and then fine-tuned using real-time vintage data from various econometric models, all without exposure to future or revised values. In real-time out-of-sample tests on the FRED-MD database, MACROCAST outperformed traditional benchmarks, including AR(1), Bayesian VAR, dynamic factor models, and the leading TSFM, Chronos-2, demonstrating its effectiveness and reliability in macroeconomic forecasting without data leakage.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28670v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce MACROCAST, a lightweight Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) for real-time macroeconomic forecasting. Existing TSFMs suffer from data leakage in two forms: temporal contamination, as the model may have seen the realized values of the series it forecasts, and revision bias, as training on fully revised data diverges from the preliminary, vintage-specific releases available to real-time forecasters. items.originalTitle: Constrained Tabular Diffusion for Finance
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Constrained Tabular Diffusion for Finance (CTDF), a new generative model designed to produce synthetic financial data that meets strict regulatory and economic constraints without violations. CTDF integrates a training-free feasibility operator into the diffusion sampling process, ensuring compliance and realistic data generation for applications like simulation and legal adherence.

Extensive testing on large financial datasets showed that CTDF achieves zero constraint violations and enhances data utility, especially in scenarios with limited data. This approach offers a reliable method for generating trustworthy synthetic financial data, potentially advancing rigorous modeling and analysis in the finance sector.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models in finance face the dual challenge of producing realistic data while satisfying strict regulatory and economic objectives, a requirement that standard tabular diffusion models cannot provide. To address this difficulty, we introduce Constrained Tabular Diffusion for Finance (CTDF), a novel integration of sampling-time feasibility operations with mixed-type tabular diffusion in financial applications. By incorporating a training-free feasibility operator into the reverse-diffusion sampling loop, CTDF enforces hard constraints for applications such as simulation, legal compliance, and extrapolation. Extensive experiments on large-scale financial datasets demonstrate zero constraint violations and improvement in scarce data utility. CTDF establishes a robust method for generating trustworthy and compliant synthetic data, opening new avenues for rigorous generative modeling and analysis in the financial domain.

items.title: Researchers introduce SEATauBench, an agent-focused evaluation framework adapting TauBench to five Southeast Asian languages, revealing limits of English-only AI assessments and challenges in localized task adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SEATauBench: Adapting Tool-Agent-User Evaluation Into Low-Resource Southeast Asian Languages
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SEATauBench, the first agent-focused evaluation framework tailored for Southeast Asian languages, including Mandarin, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, and Filipino. This framework adapts the existing TauBench to assess AI agents in progressively localized settings, varying user-agent interaction languages, tool specifications, and task domains to better understand AI capabilities in the region.

Testing across three recent AI models revealed that while English-based agent capabilities transfer reasonably well when only the conversation language changes, performance and robustness decline significantly as tasks become more localized, especially in full domain adaptation. SEATauBench highlights the limitations of English-only assessments for evaluating AI in Southeast Asian languages and offers a diagnostic benchmark and reusable adaptation pipeline to support the development of reliable multilingual agents in linguistically diverse areas.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While AI development and evaluation for Southeast Asia (SEA) has grown rapidly, agent capabilities in regional languages are still poorly understood despite its importance to sovereign AI. To fill this gap, we introduce SEATauBench, the first agent-focused evaluation framework for SEA sovereign AI. SeaTau adapts TauBench to five languages -- Mandarin, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, and Filipino -- and evaluates agents across progressively localized settings that vary the language of user-agent interaction, tool specifications, and task domains. Across three recent models, we find that English agent capabilities transfer reasonably well when only the conversation language changes, but quality and robustness degrade sharply as more task contexts are localized, with the largest losses in full domain adaptation. We also the limits of English-only agent assessment for measuring agent capabilities in SEA languages. More broadly, SeaTau provides a diagnostic benchmark and reusable adaptation pipeline for building reliable multilingual agents for linguistically diverse regions. Data and code can be accessed at github.com/SEACrowd/SEATauBench.

items.originalTitle: 5ting at SemEval-2026 Task 8: Strong End-to-End Multi-Turn RAG via LLM-Based Reranking and Faithfulness Control
items.summary: The 5ting system, developed for SemEval-2026 Task 8, demonstrates strong performance in multi-turn Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) by integrating BGE-M3 dense retrieval with FAISS indexing, dual-query merged retrieval, and large language model (LLM) based reranking. It addresses challenges such as context drift, under specification, and hallucination risk by employing role-separated generation constrained to retrieved evidence. items.title: Researchers find majority vote annotation in HateXplain masks 42.6% of disagreement at hate/offensive boundary, causing AI models to inherit false certainty and drop accuracy by up to 28 points [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Majority Vote Silences Minority Values: Annotator Disagreement at the Hate/Offensive Boundary in HateXplain
items.summary:
Researchers have found that majority vote annotation in the HateXplain dataset masks 42.6% of annotator disagreement specifically at the boundary between hate speech and offensive language. This disagreement arises because annotators apply different thresholds for what constitutes hate speech. Models trained on these majority vote labels, including hard-label and soft-label BERT models, show a significant drop in accuracy—up to 28 percentage points—when classifying posts with annotator disagreement compared to agreed posts. Furthermore, models tend to express false certainty on these boundary cases, which standard evaluation metrics fail to detect.

The study highlights that this issue is structural, as majority vote aggregation treats contested judgments as ground truth, causing AI models to inherit misleading confidence. Attempts to improve accuracy through downstream interventions were unsuccessful, suggesting that solutions must focus on redesigning annotation processes upstream to better capture and represent annotator disagreement.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hate speech annotation pipelines routinely collapse annotator disagreement into majority vote labels before training. We show that this aggregation is not neutral: 42.6% of all annotator disagreement in HateXplain concentrates specifically at the hate/offensive boundary, a pattern consistent with annotators applying different thresholds for where hate begins (chi-squared = 135.199, df = 2, p < 0.0001). Both a hard-label BERT model (Model A) and a soft-label model (Model B) drop 22 percentage points in accuracy from agreed posts (~80%) to disagreement posts (~58%), confirmed at p < 0.0001. A per-annotator multi-head model (Model C) widens this gap further to 28 points while collapsing offensive disagreement accuracy to 0.245. Critically, Model A expresses significantly higher confidence on boundary case errors than Model C (0.710 vs. 0.495, p < 0.0001), meaning standard evaluation metrics will not detect the failure. Three downstream interventions of increasing sophistication all fail to recover boundary accuracy. We argue the problem is structural. Majority vote presents a contested judgment as ground truth, and models inherit that false certainty. The intervention must be upstream in annotation design.

items.title: Mathswitch uses LLM voting ensembles to categorize and filter noisy mathematical concept data imported from Wikidata and linked sources [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Categorizing Mathematical Concepts with LLM Voting Ensembles in Mathswitch
items.summary:
Mathswitch is an open-source project that aggregates mathematical concept records from various sources including Wikidata, Wikipedia, MathWorld, and others, linking entries that refer to the same concept without altering their original structure. The project currently focuses on importing data from Wikidata and its linked resources, but the data is noisy due to the collaborative nature of Wikidata, containing non-mathematical or ambiguous items. To address this, the study tests a voting ensemble of large language model (LLM) judges to filter out noise and improve classification accuracy.

The evaluation uses Wikidata items with known MathWorld identifiers as a benchmark and examines how classification changes when database identifiers are removed. Disagreements between the LLM judges and MathWorld classifications are analyzed and categorized into degenerate descriptions, narrow scope bias, and editorial-scope mismatches, each suggesting different strategies for improving data quality and concept linking in Mathswitch.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28815v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mathswitch is an open-source project that imports mathematical concept records from sources such as Wikidata, Wikipedia, MathWorld, Encyclopedia of Mathematics, nLab, ProofWiki, and Agda-Unimath, and links records that refer to the same concept. It does not reorganize or redefine the imported content; each source retains its own structure. The current focus is on importing concept data from Wikidata and the resources it links to, with plans to expand to further sources and better concept linking. Because the concept set is approximated through queries over Wikidata's collaboratively edited graph, the imported data is noisy: some items are non-mathematical, while others are ambiguous. In this paper, we test whether a voting ensemble of LLM judges can filter this noise. We evaluate it on Wikidata items with known MathWorld identifiers as a positive control, and examine how classification changes when database identifiers are removed from context. We then inspect the cases where the judges disagree with MathWorld and group these disagreements into three categories (degenerate descriptions, narrow scope bias, and editorial-scope mismatches) that suggest different remediation strategies.

items.originalTitle: HARD-KV: Head-Adaptive Regularization for Decoding-time KV Compression
items.summary:
Researchers have developed HARD-KV, a head-adaptive regularization framework designed to improve decoding-time key-value compression for long-context large language model (LLM) inference. HARD-KV addresses the conflict between dynamic memory allocation methods, which enhance accuracy, and the static memory patterns required by modern inference engines. By introducing a Cascade Cache hierarchy and a Logits Calibration mechanism, the framework manages token lifecycles efficiently and normalizes importance metrics for consistent budgeting across model heads.

The system-level solution also restructures dynamic indices into contiguous layouts compatible with high-performance inference engines, enabling up to a twofold increase in throughput while maintaining accuracy in scenarios involving over 10,000 tokens. Extensive testing on math-reasoning benchmarks such as AIME and U-Math confirms HARD-KV's effectiveness in balancing speed and fidelity during long-context LLM inference.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-context LLM inference faces a fundamental conflict: head-adaptive compression algorithms (e.g., Top-$p$ nucleus sampling) offer superior accuracy by dynamically fluctuating memory budgets, yet modern inference engines (e.g., vLLM) demand rigid, static memory patterns to leverage CUDA Graphs and PagedAttention. We resolve this ``Static-Dynamic'' mismatch with HARD-KV, a unified framework that that bridges dynamic selection with rigid system constraints. HARD-KV introduces a Cascade Cache hierarchy, managing the token lifecycle across dense, sparse, and condensed tiers. Crucially, we propose a Logits Calibration mechanism that normalizes diverse importance metrics into a unified probability space, enabling consistent Top-$p$ budgeting across heterogeneous heads. To bridge the efficiency gap, we offer a system-level solution, which rewrites fragmented, dynamic indices into contiguous physical layouts compatible with high-performance inference engine. Extensive experiments on math-reasoning benchmarks (AIME, U-Math) verify that HARD-KV achieves up to 2$\times$ throughput improvement over static baselines while maintaining high-fidelity generation in 10k+ token scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/SuDIS-ZJU/HARDInfer.

items.title: Researchers propose Fisher-Routed Mixture of Experts framework for federated class-incremental learning to address capacity conflict, data heterogeneity, and class misalignment with proven convergence and benchmark superiority [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Fisher-Routed Mixture of Experts for Federated Class-Incremental Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the Fisher-Routed Mixture of Experts (FedFMX) framework to improve federated class-incremental learning, addressing challenges such as capacity conflict, data heterogeneity, and class misalignment. This approach uses adaptive expert specialization to route data samples to expert subsets that balance knowledge acquisition and retention, enhancing model performance across distributed clients.

The framework incorporates a Fisher-Routed Expert Scoring module to assess expert importance based on stability and plasticity metrics, alongside an Adaptive Expert Selection module that determines expert subsets by evaluating their marginal contributions. Additionally, routing-aware regularization ensures balanced workload distribution and efficient training. The method demonstrates a proven convergence rate and outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in extensive benchmark tests.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) emerged as a promising distributed machine learning paradigm. However, extending FL to the class incremental learning scenarios introduces unique challenges: 1) Capacity conflict and catastrophic forgetting from the shared model overloading, 2) Heterogeneity from Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (Non-IID) data, and 3) Synchronized class misalignment. In this paper, we propose \textbf{F}isher-Routed \textbf{M}i\textbf{X}ture of Experts for \textbf{Fed}erated Class-Incremental Learning (\textsc{FedFMX}), a novel framework to address these challenges via adaptive expert specialization across clients. The crucial insight is to route each sample to an expert subset that jointly optimizes knowledge acquisition and retention. Specifically, we introduce a Fisher-Routed Expert Scoring (FRES) module to estimate expert importance via Fisher-based stability cost and gradient-based plasticity gain. Then, we design an Adaptive Expert Selection (AES) module by quantifying marginal contributions for adaptive expert subset determination. Finally, by the routing-aware regularization (RAR), we achieve load balance and efficient FL training. We theoretically prove the $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$ convergence rate. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks compared with state-of-the-art methods demonstrate the superiority of \textsc{FedFMX}.

items.title: Researchers present LAMP, a Lean 4 multi-agent framework using Model Context Protocol and ontology-based knowledge to synthesize kernel-verified proofs for 96.7% of Combinatorics on Words theorems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LAMP: Lean-based Agentic framework with MCP and Proof Repair
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LAMP, a multi-agent framework built on Lean 4 that synthesizes kernel-verified proofs for the specialized domain of Combinatorics on Words (CoW). By integrating an ontology-based knowledge system and a Model Context Protocol, LAMP coordinates multiple agents to generate verified proofs for 96.7% of tested CoW theorems, significantly outperforming existing provers and unscaffolded baselines. This approach addresses the limitations of current interactive theorem provers, which are constrained by the formalized knowledge available in repositories like Mathlib, especially in underrepresented areas such as CoW.

The team also introduced a comprehensive Lean 4 formalization of CoW, comprising eight modules and 93 core definitions and lemmas. LAMP's architecture separates planning, building, and verification tasks, leveraging explicit domain knowledge at inference time rather than relying on fine-tuning. Ablation studies demonstrate that both the tool-grounded design and the division between planner and builder are critical to its high performance, each contributing roughly a 12 percentage point improvement in proof synthesis success.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28841v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models are increasingly capable of mathematical reasoning, but the proofs they generate are often unreliable and hard to verify. Interactive theorem provers such as Lean 4 address this by accepting only kernel-checked proofs; however, their reach is bounded by the formalized knowledge available. While Mathlib, a repository of formalized Lean 4 theorems that covers diverse mathematical areas, certain specialized areas remain underrepresented; notably, the domain of Combinatorics on Words (CoW). CoW studies sequences, exploring their properties such as periodicity, borders, conjugacy, and morphisms. As a result, specialized provers, trained on Mathlib-centered data, lack the lemmas to operate in CoW. We present two contributions. First, we introduce a Lean 4 formalization of CoW containing eight modules and \textbf{93} declarations of core definitions and foundational lemmas. Second, we present LAMP, a multi-agent framework that synthesizes kernel-verified Lean 4 proofs by providing explicit, structured domain knowledge at inference time through an ontology, rather than by fine-tuning a prover. LAMP coordinates a Planner, Builder, and Verifier with Model Context Protocol based access to a domain-specific CoW ontology. In a suite of 90 CoW theorems that span all eight modules and three difficulty levels, LAMP synthesizes verified proofs for 96.7% of theorems, substantially exceeding both an unscaffolded baseline and existing specialized provers. An ablation shows that removing LAMP's tool-grounded architecture or its Planner/Builder separation each cost roughly 12 percentage points, even with the backbone model held fixed.

items.title: Researchers find multilingual fine-tuning of Llama-3.2, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 models causes heterogeneous safety impacts, with adversarial compliance rates rising up to four-fold across nine languages [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Heterogeneous Safety Impacts of Benign Multilingual Fine-Tuning
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a comprehensive study on the effects of multilingual fine-tuning on large language models, specifically Llama-3.2, Qwen3, and Gemma-3. They found that fine-tuning with benign data translated into nine different languages can significantly impact model safety, with adversarial compliance rates increasing up to four times depending on the fine-tuning and evaluation languages. The study reveals that safety outcomes vary widely across languages and models and are not directly linked to general capability improvements.

The research highlights that fine-tuning in non-English languages often causes smaller internal changes than English fine-tuning, but these changes can lead models to either overly comply with or refuse adversarial prompts. This indicates that evaluating safety impacts solely in English is insufficient for ensuring safe deployment across languages. To support further investigation into these multilingual safety issues, the researchers have released the Multilingual-Benign-Tune dataset and the SORRY-Bench-Multilingual evaluation suite.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning a large language model is a ubiquitous method for enhancing its capability on a specific downstream task. However, prior work has shown that this increase in capability comes with a cost: it can increase a model's tendency to respond to unsafe adversarial prompts, even when fine-tuning with non-adversarial data. We present the first comprehensive empirical study of this phenomenon in multilingual settings by fine-tuning Llama-3.2, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 models using benign data translated across nine languages. We find that safety outcomes are highly sensitive to both the choice of fine-tuning language and the evaluation language, with adversarial compliance rates increasing four-fold in some settings. Multilingual safety drift is decoupled from general capability metrics, and occurs heterogeneously across languages and models. Fine-tuning in non-English languages often induces smaller internal representational drifts than English, but these shifts lead models to default to either exaggerated compliance or refusal. As such, assessing fine-tuning impacts solely in English provides inadequate assurance for deployment. To facilitate further research into these cross-lingual safety blind spots, we release the Multilingual-Benign-Tune dataset and the SORRY-Bench-Multilingual evaluation suite.

items.title: Researchers analyze latent factor indeterminacy in generative models, showing determinacy emerges as feature dimension grows, with implications for psychometrics, statistics, and AI representation learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Perspectives on Latent Factor Indeterminacy and its Implications for Data Representation
items.summary:
Researchers have examined the issue of latent factor indeterminacy in generative models, focusing on the common factor analytic model, which relates to Helmholtz and Boltzmann machines and can be viewed as a linear autoencoder or a single-hidden-layer generative neural network. They highlight that even when the latent vector's intrinsic dimension is known and rotational indeterminacy is resolved, an inherent uncertainty and non-uniqueness in identifying causative latent sources persists, affecting data representation. This problem, rooted in psychometrics, also connects to latent variable collapse in variational autoencoders used in deep generative modeling.

The study explores this indeterminacy from multiple perspectives, demonstrating mathematical and conceptual links and discussing implications for psychometrics, statistics, and artificial intelligence. The researchers show that latent factor determinacy emerges as the feature dimension grows infinitely large, enabling a distribution-free estimation approach for high-dimensional data. They conclude that the factor model is well-suited for representation learning in very-high-dimensional settings due to these emergent properties at scale.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28854v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The common factor analytic model is related to Helmholtz and Boltzmann machines, can be conceived as a linear autoencoder, or can be thought of as a single-hidden-layer generative neural network. We thus consider it a basal generative representation learner that can be used as a minimal model for studying the foundational characteristics of (deep) generative model architectures. We focus on the fundamental problem of indeterminacy in latent factor projections. This indeterminacy implies that, even when the intrinsic dimension of the latent vector is known, regularity conditions are met, and rotational indeterminacy is resolved, an inherent indefiniteness in the retrieval of causative latent sources remains: they will be uncertain, distributionally deviant, and non-unique. This can have major implications for data representation but remains an elusive issue, even to practitioners and theorists well-versed in the factor model. Moreover, this classic psychometric problem is intricately related to the modern issue of latent variable collapse in the variational autoencoder framework for deep generative modeling. Here, we assess this indeterminacy from various perspectives and show how these are mathematically and conceptually related and we discuss subsequent implications for the Psychometrics, Statistics, and Artificial Intelligence communities. We show that one has latent factor determinacy across all its facets when the feature-dimension grows to infinity. This feeds into an essentially distribution-free estimation approach in the sample case when the number of features grows very large. We conclude, as these are emergent properties at scale, that the factor model is suited for representation learning of very-high-dimensional data.

items.title: Research proposes UBP-CAP, an integrated machine learning pipeline combining LightGBM, calibration metrics, and GLMM to predict student performance and analyze metacognitive calibration on multi-signal telemetry [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: An Integrated Machine Learning and Hierarchical Variance Decomposition Pipeline for Student Performance Prediction and Metacognitive Calibration on Multi-Signal Telemetry
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Unified Behavioral Prediction and Calibration Analysis Pipeline (UBP-CAP), an integrated machine learning framework designed to predict student performance and analyze metacognitive calibration using multi-signal behavioral telemetry. The pipeline combines a LightGBM classifier with SHAP for predicting correctness, formal calibration metrics to assess metacognitive alignment, and a crossed Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Model (GLMM) to decompose calibration deviations. The study introduces the Predictive-Explanatory Divergence Index (PEDI) to measure structural differences between predictive and explanatory features.

Evaluated on data from 27 students across 45 tasks, the approach showed that Logistic Regression slightly outperformed LightGBM in prediction accuracy. items.originalTitle: A Task-Driven and Quality-Assured Agent Framework for SAR Data Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SAGA, a schema-grounded agent framework designed to enhance synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data generation and augmentation for task-driven applications. SAGA addresses challenges in SAR data augmentation such as heterogeneous dataset formats, task-specific metadata needs, diverse generation methods, and insufficient validation of generated samples. The framework processes natural-language requests and varied SAR inputs to extract dataset facts, validate schemas, plan augmentation strategies, and produce auditable workflows, ensuring quality and reliability in the augmented data.

SAGA further evaluates generated data using multiple criteria including quality, distribution, artifact detection, duplication, leakage, and downstream task performance to support evidence-based augmentation claims. By separating semantic proposal from deterministic validation and execution, SAGA improves the reproducibility and reliability of augmentation decisions. Experimental results demonstrate that SAGA outperforms existing rule-based, large language model-only, and fixed-augmentation methods in schema grounding, planning, invalid sample rejection, and downstream utility in SAR interpretation tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce GRAB pipeline for multi-table question answering, combining graph encoding with frozen LLMs to improve relational QA performance efficiently [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Latent Bridges for Multi-Table Question Answering
items.summary:
Researchers have developed GRAB, a new pipeline for multi-table question answering that integrates relational data into a heterogeneous graph, encodes it through message passing, and conveys the information to a large language model (LLM) using a set of query-conditioned latent tokens. This approach provides the LLM with a concise, task-specific structural representation alongside the flattened text, while keeping the LLM itself frozen to maintain its general reasoning abilities. Only the lightweight graph encoder and latent bridge are trained, enabling efficient training of the entire system.

GRAB significantly enhances performance on relational question answering tasks, especially in complex multi-table scenarios. By combining relational deep learning techniques with frozen LLMs, this method offers an effective and principled solution for improving relational question answering without compromising the LLM's pre-trained capabilities.

items.title: Researchers introduce WildChat benchmark with 3,000 prompts and 12-agent catalog for multi-agent routing as set-valued prediction, evaluating accuracy-cost trade-offs with supervised and zero-shot methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-Agent Routing as Set-Valued Prediction: A WildChat Benchmark and Cost-Aware Evaluation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the WildChat benchmark, featuring 3,000 prompts and a fixed catalog of 12 agents, to address multi-agent routing as a set-valued prediction problem. This benchmark evaluates the trade-offs between accuracy and execution cost when routing natural-language prompts to multiple agents, using AI-assisted heuristic labels and a controlled evaluation protocol that includes set-level metrics, latency, and cost-aware routing scenarios.

The study compares various methods such as nearest-neighbor matching, linear multilabel classification, dependency-aware baselines, a fine-tuned encoder, and a zero-shot large language model baseline. Results indicate that supervised routing methods outperform nearest-neighbor and zero-shot approaches, with the fine-tuned encoder achieving the highest unconstrained accuracy and the linear multilabel model serving as a strong practical baseline. Additionally, applying a weighted routing layer improves performance in cost-constrained settings, particularly when combined with the fine-tuned encoder.

Overall, the WildChat benchmark and its evaluation framework provide a reproducible platform for studying accuracy-cost trade-offs in multi-agent routing tasks, supporting further research and development in efficient and effective agent selection from fixed catalogs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool and agent routing from natural-language prompts is naturally a set-valued prediction problem: a single query may require multiple agents, while over-selection increases execution cost. The benchmark introduced here is derived from WildChat and contains 3,000 prompts over a fixed 12-agent catalog, with AI-assisted heuristic labels under a fixed schema and controlled rebalancing for multi-label evaluation. The evaluation protocol combines set-level metrics (Precision, Recall, F1, Jaccard, and Exact Match), latency, an execution-oriented capability-coverage simulation, and a constrained weighted-routing setting based on ordinal agent-cost tiers. Compared methods include nearest-neighbor matching, linear multilabel classification, dependency-aware baselines, a fine-tuned encoder, deterministic weighted post-scoring via Weighted Agent Routing (WAR), and a zero-shot LLM baseline. Results show that supervised routers substantially outperform nearest-neighbor and zero-shot LLM routing. The fine-tuned encoder achieves the strongest unconstrained set accuracy, while the linear multilabel model provides the strongest practical baseline. In the constrained setting, the weighted routing layer improves utility when applied on top of strong supervised scorers, with the largest gain observed for Encoder+WAR. Overall, the benchmark and evaluation protocol support reproducible study of accuracy-cost trade-offs in fixed-catalog multi-agent routing.

items.title: Researchers propose DLR, a zero-parameter, foldable plug-in to improve low-rank pre-training efficiency and quality in LLaMA models from 60M to 7B parameters [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DLR: Zero-Inference-Cost Latent Residuals for Low-Rank Pre-Training
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Duplicated Latent Residual (DLR), a zero-parameter, foldable plug-in designed to enhance low-rank pre-training efficiency and quality in LLaMA language models ranging from 60 million to 7 billion parameters. DLR improves the standard low-rank output by adding a fixed structured residual that replicates latent coordinates, requiring no additional learnable parameters during training and maintaining the same deployment cost as the original low-rank model.

DLR integrates seamlessly into the training process and can be absorbed into the model's up-projection after training, ensuring no increase in parameter count, FLOPs, or memory usage during deployment. Experiments show that DLR consistently improves validation perplexity on the C4 dataset, particularly for models with 130 million parameters and above, and the enhanced models transfer effectively to supervised fine-tuning on standard benchmarks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have driven recent progress in language and multimodal AI, yet pre-training them at scale is prohibitively expensive. Low-rank pre-training, which factorizes each weight matrix into a rank-r product to reduce both parameters and FLOPs, is a promising response but typically lags full-rank training in quality. We propose Duplicated Latent Residual (DLR), a training-only, parameter-free, foldable plug-in for low-rank pre-training. DLR augments the standard low-rank output Bz with a fixed structured residual alpha/sqrt(K) * Expand_K(z) that replicates each latent coordinate K = ceil(d_out/r) times across the output. With alpha fixed, DLR adds zero learnable parameters per layer; after training, it is absorbed into the up-projection in closed form, B* = B + alpha/sqrt(K) R^T, so deployment parameter count, FLOPs and memory match the underlying low-rank backbone exactly. Across LLaMA models from 60M to 7B parameters, DLR strengthens low-rank pre-training on C4 validation perplexity in most settings, with the clearest gains at 130M and above; folded checkpoints transfer cleanly to supervised fine-tuning on standard benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers define machine-learnable discrete sets using bounded-complexity Boolean autoencoders and demonstrate learnability on Rorschach patterns and evolving wild sets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Machine-learnable Sets
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a formal definition of large discrete sets characterized by elements that are easily recognized, generated, and learned from examples. They focus on sets of binary strings and define "machine-learnability" through the existence of bounded-complexity Boolean autoencoders that can fix the elements of these sets. Experiments demonstrate this concept using Boolean threshold function networks to implement the autoencoders.

The study showcases machine-learnability on Rorschach patterns, including those with reversed contrast in mirrored halves, as well as on more complex "wild" sets whose elements are only approximately fixed by admissible autoencoders. For these wild sets, the researchers present an iterative method that evolves them into properly machine-learnable sets, highlighting a novel approach to learning complex discrete structures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this study we present a formal definition of large discrete sets having, informally, three properties: their elements are easily recognized, easily generated, and the latter tasks are easily learned from examples. The formalism is specialized to sets of binary strings and a definition of "machine-learnability" based on the existence of a bounded-complexity Boolean autoencoder that fixes the elements of the set. We present experiments where the autoencoders are implemented by nets of Boolean threshold functions. items.title: Researchers propose unsupervised clustering defense reducing poisoning attack success on speech command classifiers from 99.75% to 0.25% with 10% poisoned data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Clustering Unsupervised Representations as Defense against Poisoning Attacks on Speech Commands Classification System
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a defense method against dirty-label poisoning attacks on speech command classification systems, where attackers alter training data by adding triggers to audio samples and changing their labels. Their approach uses unsupervised learning with DIstillation with NO labels (DINO) to generate representations of training data, followed by clustering with K-means and LDA to filter out poisoned samples. This method significantly reduces the attack success rate from 99.75% to 0.25% when 10% of the source class data is poisoned.

The defense was tested across various threat models, including different source and target classes and trigger variations, demonstrating its robustness. By retaining only the most consistently labeled samples within clusters for training, the approach effectively mitigates the impact of poisoned data on the classifier's performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28953v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Poisoning attacks entail attackers intentionally tampering with training data. In this paper, we consider a dirty-label poisoning attack scenario on a speech commands classification system. The threat model assumes that certain utterances from one of the classes (source class) are poisoned by superimposing a trigger on it, and its label is changed to another class selected by the attacker (target class). We propose a filtering defense against such an attack. First, we use DIstillation with NO labels (DINO) to learn unsupervised representations for all the training examples. Next, we use K-means and LDA to cluster these representations. Finally, we keep the utterances with the most repeated label in their cluster for training and discard the rest. For a 10% poisoned source class, we demonstrate a drop in attack success rate from 99.75% to 0.25%. We test our defense against a variety of threat models, including different target and source classes, as well as trigger variations.

items.title: Researchers propose Modification-Considering Value Learning to mitigate reward hacking in reinforcement learning, demonstrating safety and improvement across gridworld and MuJoCo tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Modification-Considering Value Learning for Reward Hacking Mitigation in RL
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Modification-Considering Value Learning (MCVL), a new approach to reduce reward hacking in reinforcement learning (RL). Reward hacking occurs when RL agents exploit flawed reward signals to achieve high scores without fulfilling the intended goals. MCVL addresses this by evaluating each potential policy update through forecasting training outcomes with and without the update, only accepting changes that do not reduce a safety score derived from a learned reward model and value function.

MCVL integrates with existing off-policy learners like DDQN and TD3 and has been tested across various safety-critical gridworld environments and modified MuJoCo continuous-control tasks. The method effectively mitigates reward hacking while allowing the agent to continue improving on the intended objectives, balancing safety and performance in RL training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning agents can exploit misspecified reward signals to achieve high apparent returns while failing on the intended objective, a failure mode known as reward hacking. Existing practical defenses typically constrain policy updates to stay near a known safe reference, creating a tension between suppressing hacking and permitting legitimate improvement. We propose Modification-Considering Value Learning (MCVL), which operationalizes the theoretical idea of current utility optimization for standard value-based RL. MCVL wraps an off-policy learner and treats each incoming transition as a candidate modification: it forecasts two training paths, one that includes the transition and one that does not, and scores both with a frozen bootstrapped-return estimator derived from a learned reward model and value function. The transition is admitted only if inclusion does not decrease the score. We formalize conditions under which this filtering is both safe and permissive, and instantiate MCVL with DDQN and TD3. Across four safety-relevant gridworlds and three modified MuJoCo continuous-control tasks with diverse hacking mechanisms, MCVL mitigates reward hacking while continuing to improve the intended objective. Project website: ktolnos.github.io/mcvl/.

items.title: Researchers propose RGLD, a randomized global-local density estimator for efficient unsupervised tabular anomaly detection, outperforming 23 baselines on 47 datasets with significant speedups [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RGLD: Randomized Global-Local Density Estimation for Tabular Anomaly Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced RGLD, a randomized global-local density estimator designed for efficient unsupervised anomaly detection in tabular data. RGLD integrates a global density branch that identifies broadly low-density samples with a local neighbor branch that detects samples weakly supported by nearby data points. Both branches use feature-bagged randomized views to uncover anomalies that might be missed by single representations.

The method was tested on 47 tabular datasets against 23 statistical and deep learning baselines, achieving the highest dataset-level AUROC performance and ranking first in dataset wins. RGLD also demonstrated significant speed advantages, running 50 to 580 times faster than deep detectors while maintaining competitive runtime with statistical methods, offering a strong balance between accuracy and efficiency.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unsupervised tabular anomaly detection requires methods that are accurate, robust across heterogeneous datasets, and computationally efficient. Classical statistical detectors are often efficient, but they usually rely on a fixed data view and a single notion of abnormality. Deep anomaly detectors can learn more flexible scoring functions, but they are substantially slower and difficult to tune in unsupervised settings due to the lack of a reliable supervisory signal. We propose RGLD, a randomized global-local density estimator for efficient unsupervised tabular anomaly detection. RGLD combines a global random-feature density branch, which identifies samples in broadly low-density regions, with a local neighbor branch, which detects samples that are weakly supported by nearby observations. Both branches operate over feature-bagged randomized views, allowing RGLD to expose anomaly evidence that may be hidden in any single representation. We conduct experiments on 47 tabular datasets against 23 statistical and deep anomaly detection baselines under fully unsupervised setting. RGLD achieves the strongest dataset-level AUROC performance, ranking 1st in dataset wins, and ranks 2nd in AUPRC wins. RGLD is also faster than all evaluated deep detectors, achieving 50x-580x speedups, and remains competitive with statistical methods in runtime, yielding a favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoff.

items.title: Researchers propose OvESyn, a text-conditioned 3D CT synthesis framework for ovarian cancer using CT-derived descriptors and clinical metadata without radiology reports, tested on 493 patients [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evidence-Based Text-Conditioned 3D CT Synthesis for Ovarian Cancer
items.summary:
Researchers have developed OvESyn, a novel framework for synthesizing 3D contrast-enhanced CT images of ovarian cancer conditioned on text generated from CT-derived imaging descriptors and clinical metadata, without relying on original radiology reports. Tested on data from 493 patients with high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, OvESyn is the first text-conditioned 3D CT synthesis model tailored to the abdomino-pelvic oncologic setting, addressing the challenge of limited annotated imaging data and privacy constraints in this domain.

The framework uses a latent diffusion model adapted through generator fine-tuning and vision-language encoder alignment to bridge the domain gap from thoracic pretraining to abdomino-pelvic anatomy. Generator adaptation proved essential for accurate synthesis, while encoder alignment enhanced image detail and intensity. OvESyn achieves a balance between fidelity and coverage, supporting transferability to settings lacking radiology reports and enabling synthetic cohort generation for oncologic imaging research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ovarian cancer is frequently diagnosed at an advanced stage, making preoperative contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) central to staging and surgical planning; yet the scarcity of annotated imaging data, compounded by privacy regulations, limits the development of generalizable computational models in this domain. Text-conditioned 3D CT synthesis has shown promise, but existing pipelines depend on paired radiology reports and have been evaluated only on chest CT. We propose OvESyn (Ovarian Evidence-based Synthesis), a framework that constructs standardized Findings and Impression sections directly from CT-derived imaging descriptors and routine clinical metadata, without any original radiology report, and uses them to condition a latent diffusion model adapted to 493 high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma patients. This is the first text-conditioned 3D CT synthesis framework adapted to an abdomino-pelvic oncologic setting. A systematic ablation over two adaptation axes, vision-language encoder alignment and generator fine-tuning, identifies generator domain adaptation as the operative mechanism for crossing the domain gap and establishing the target anatomy: without it, synthesis remains anchored to the thoracic pretraining domain, with Precision and Recall collapsing to zero and FID2.5D exceeding 140, regardless of encoder alignment. Encoder alignment instead refines intensity and fine detail. The full OvESyn attains the best distributional and intensity fidelity (FID2.5D 29.35, Precision 0.671, Wasserstein-1 0.044), while the generator-only variant maximizes coverage (Recall 0.645), reflecting a fidelity/coverage trade-off governed by encoder adaptation. Requiring only automatic segmentations and routine preoperative metadata, OvESyn supports transferability to report-scarce settings and provides a foundation for synthetic cohort generation in abdomino-pelvic oncologic imaging.

items.originalTitle: Fine-Tuning General-Purpose Large Language Models for Agricultural Applications:A Reproducible Framework and Evaluation Protocol Based on Qwen3-8B
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced AgriTune-R, a reproducible and auditable framework designed to fine-tune the general-purpose Qwen3-8B large language model for agricultural applications. This framework addresses the unique challenges of agriculture, such as domain specificity, regional variation, time sensitivity, and safety concerns, by incorporating data governance, expert evaluation, and safety controls to ensure reliable and evidence-based advice.

AgriTune-R integrates techniques like LoRA/QLoRA parameter-efficient fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation, alongside a structured workflow and an evaluation protocol covering agricultural knowledge, pest and disease consultation, cultivation management, and policy explanation. The framework also includes an expert-review rubric that assesses factuality, safety, evidence consistency, and uncertainty expression, providing a clear separation between protocol design and empirical conclusions to support future research and application development in agricultural AI.

Instead, we propose AgriTune-R, a reproducible and auditable frameworkfor adapting general-purpose LLMs to agricultural tasks. The framework selects the publiclyverifiable Qwen3-8B model as the recommended base model and integrates agricultural datagovernance, instruction construction, LoRA/QLoRA parameter-efficient fine-tuning, retrievalaugmented generation, expert evaluation, and safety control for high-risk questions. The contributions are: (1) a structured workflow for agricultural LLM adaptation; (2) an evaluationprotocol for agricultural knowledge QA, pest and disease consultation, cultivation management,and policy explanation; (3) an expert-review rubric combining factuality, safety, evidence consistency, and uncertainty expression; and (4) a clear separation between protocol design andempirical conclusions, providing an executable baseline for future empirical studies.

items.summary:
Researchers have developed BERTomelo, a new Portuguese monolingual encoder built on the ModernBERT architecture and trained from scratch on a large corpus of 106 million Portuguese documents. This model offers Base and Large versions with enhanced context windows and hardware optimizations, outperforming previous Portuguese encoders like BERTimbau and Albertina in natural language processing tasks such as semantic textual similarity and named entity recognition.

BERTomelo addresses the limitations of earlier models by incorporating recent architectural advances and aligning closely with contemporary Portuguese usage. Its design includes features like FlashAttention and alternating attention mechanisms, which contribute to improved scalability and efficiency compared to both prior monolingual models and large multilingual alternatives.

The introduction of BERTomelo represents a significant step forward in Portuguese language processing, providing a more robust and efficient tool for various NLP applications. Its superior performance suggests potential for broader adoption in tasks requiring deep contextual understanding of Portuguese text.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Encoders have become the state of the art for multiple NLP tasks, especially those requiring deep contextual understanding. While multilingual models offer broad coverage, dedicated monolingual encoders are essential for capturing the unique lexical and syntactic nuances of specific languages. For Portuguese, however, existing monolingual options like BERTimbau and Albertina have not kept pace with recent architectural breakthroughs, often lagging behind English benchmarks in scalability and efficiency. This work introduces BERTomelo, a next-generation monolingual encoder pre-trained from scratch and specifically optimized for the Portuguese language. By leveraging the ModernBERT architecture, BERTomelo overcomes the limitations of previous models, offering Base and Large versions with a 1,024-token context window and hardware-level optimizations like FlashAttention and alternating attention mechanisms. The model was trained on ClassiCC-PT, a massive, high-quality Portuguese corpus of 106 million documents, ensuring superior alignment with the language's contemporary usage. The results demonstrate that BERTomelo not only outperforms previous Portuguese encoders but also provides a more robust and efficient alternative to massive multilingual models in downstream tasks such as STS and NER.

items.title: Researchers analyze distributional gap between synthetic and real speech in LLM-based ASR systems and propose RIR augmentation with layer selection to match real-data performance using 25% real speech [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: How to Leverage Synthetic Speech for LLM-Based ASR Systems?
items.summary: Researchers have investigated the distributional differences between synthetic and real speech in large language model (LLM)-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems, particularly in privacy-sensitive domains like banking and healthcare where real speech data is limited. They identified that the early-to-middle layers of the LLM backbone are key in distinguishing synthetic from real speech, with temporal and prosodic variations playing a significant role. By applying room impulse response (RIR) augmentation to synthetic audio and incorporating a layer-selection module during training, they achieved ASR performance comparable to models trained on fully real data using only 25% of real speech, and surpassed it with higher proportions of real data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In regulated domains such as banking and healthcare, where privacy constraints make real speech costly to collect and retain, synthetic speech from modern text-to-speech (TTS) is an appealing alternative for training automatic speech recognition (ASR) without exposing sensitive customer recordings. Yet a persistent distributional gap between synthetic and real data limits how far it can replace genuine recordings. Prior work largely treats this gap as a black box to be engineered around, but in our work, we instead examine its origin directly by probing a SLAM-ASR architecture. Then, we localise where its LLM backbone separates real from synthetic speech and find the discriminative signal concentrated in the early-to-middle layers, where temporal and prosodic perturbations disrupt it most. We further show that representation-level separability, help, but does not directly predict downstream ASR gains. On the other hand, convolving synthetic audio with room impulse responses (RIRs) narrows the gap not by making synthetic speech sound cleaner or more natural, but by reproducing the acoustic irregularities of real recordings. Translating these findings into the training procedure, by adding a layer-selection module combined with RIR augmentation matches a fully real-data baseline using only 25% of the real speech (13.6h) and surpasses it at all higher proportions.

items.title: Researchers present AB-RAG, an adaptive, training-free retrieval-augmented generation framework that estimates answer confidence and adjusts retrieval budget for reliable question answering across multiple language model backbones [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AB-RAG: Adaptive Budgeted Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Reliable Question Answering
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced AB-RAG, an adaptive, training-free framework for retrieval-augmented generation that enhances question answering by estimating answer confidence and dynamically adjusting the retrieval budget. Unlike traditional systems that retrieve a fixed number of passages regardless of question difficulty, AB-RAG uses a combination of signals—including model certainty, answer-evidence agreement, and retrieval score variance—to decide when to stop or continue retrieving information, improving reliability without retraining the underlying language model.

The framework is backbone-agnostic and works with both open models that expose token probabilities and closed APIs by approximating confidence through self-consistency. Evaluations across three language model backbones and two datasets demonstrated that AB-RAG effectively distinguishes correct from incorrect answers, significantly improving accuracy on capable models. The study also transparently reports limitations and adjustments made during development, all conducted efficiently on a consumer laptop with minimal API costs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the standard way to ground large language models in external knowledge, yet most systems retrieve a fixed number of passages for every question regardless of its difficulty. This wastes computation on easy questions, starves hard ones, and gives no signal for when a generated answer can be trusted. With a growing share of question answering systems built on top of commercial language model APIs, a method that can decide how much to retrieve, and how far to trust its own answers, without retraining the underlying model, is of clear practical value. This paper presents AB-RAG (Adaptive Budgeted Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a training-free and backbone-agnostic framework that generates an answer, estimates its confidence from a combination of three signals, and then decides whether to stop or to retrieve more evidence, subject to a fixed retrieval budget. The estimator combines the model's own certainty, the agreement between the answer and the evidence, and the variance of the retrieval scores. For models that expose token probabilities the certainty signal is read directly; for closed APIs it is approximated by self-consistency, so the method works without access to model internals. Across three backbones and two datasets, the central result is that the confidence estimate reliably separates correct from incorrect answers on every backbone, reaching a clean split of 57.6% against 0% Exact Match between high- and low-confidence answers on a factoid dataset. The adaptive policy improves accuracy on capable backbones, and the study reports its negative and nuanced findings honestly, including a confidence signal that proved unsuitable for short answers and a retrieval signal whose sign was found and corrected through measurement. The entire study was carried out on a single consumer laptop with only a few dollars of API spend.

items.title: Researchers establish a formal barrier for tabular foundation models showing they cannot distinguish rule-violating from legal database states without operational grounding, despite access to schema and data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Statistically Indistinguishable, Operationally Distinct: A Formal Barrier for Tabular Foundation Models
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated a formal limitation for tabular foundation models, showing that these models cannot reliably distinguish between rule-compliant and rule-violating database states without access to the operational rules governing the data. Using the Operational Turing Test (OTT), they created pairs of database states with nearly identical statistical properties, proving that classifiers relying solely on data values perform no better than random guessing. Only models incorporating executable rule-based audits achieved perfect classification accuracy.

The study tested various baseline models, including XGBoost and large language models like GPT-5.5, which failed to correctly identify legal states even when provided with schema, triggers, and rule tables. This limitation was consistent across different database schemas and rule types, indicating that the barrier arises from identifiability issues rather than model capacity or data scale.

These findings imply that without operational grounding—explicit knowledge of the rules that generate data—tabular foundation models cannot effectively reason about dynamic, rule-governed systems. This highlights the necessity of integrating rule-based information to improve model reliability in applications involving complex database states.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tabular foundation models cannot reason about data produced by running systems without access to the rules that govern them. We make this statement falsifiable. The \emph{Operational Turing Test} (OTT) constructs pairs of legal and rule-violating database states whose $1$- and $2$-way column-value marginals match to a total variation of $<0.02$; Le~Cam's lemma then bounds any values-only classifier at $\geq0.49$ Bayes error. Three values-only baselines (XGBoost, TabICL, TabPFN) hit the bound exactly (accuracy $0.50$, pre-registered two one-sided tests (TOST) $p<0.002$), raw row-level access does not help, exposing relational value consistency closes most of the gap, and only a classifier fed by seven executable rule-derived audits reaches $1.00$ classification accuracy. In three matched $100$-state frontier large-language-model (LLM) runs, models given the schema, trigger source, rule tables, and state files classify at most $2/50$ legal states as LEGAL; GPT-5.5 accepts $0/50$ legal states even with higher reasoning effort and a Structured Query Language (SQL) executor. The access-ladder pattern also appears on a second schema with structurally distinct rule families (banking ledger: cross-row balance, cumulative aggregate). The barrier is identifiability, not capacity: scale, data, and richer features cannot cross it without operational grounding.

items.title: Researchers develop normal-fan geometry for finite-horizon adversarial MDPs to analyze dynamic regret and non-stationarity costs through priced face-crossing motion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Priced Motion Through Optimal Faces: A Normal-Fan Geometry for Non-Stationary Adversarial MDPs
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new geometric framework called normal-fan geometry to analyze dynamic regret and non-stationarity costs in finite-horizon adversarial Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with fixed transitions. This approach models occupancy measures as a polytope where each loss vector corresponds to an optimal face, allowing the study of how changes in rewards affect the optimal policy through movements within and across these faces. The concept of a face-crossing price quantifies the minimum regret incurred when the optimal policy changes due to shifts in the loss function.

This framework distinguishes between harmless and consequential non-stationarity by showing that large variations in loss can occur without increasing regret if the optimal face remains the same, while even small changes crossing a face boundary can lead to significant regret. The theory decomposes dynamic regret into intrinsic costs associated with moving between optimal faces and errors within a face, providing a more precise understanding of the impact of non-stationarity on learning performance in adversarial MDPs.
