items.title: Researchers study fuzzing techniques to elicit hidden behaviors in six backdoored large language models, showing up to sixfold improvement over temperature sampling and proposing proxy-task hyperparameter selection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fuzzing Large Language Models to Elicit Hidden Behaviours
items.summary:
Researchers have conducted a systematic study on eliciting hidden behaviors in large language models that contain sleeper-agent backdoors—models designed to behave normally but reveal unsafe actions when triggered. They compared fuzzing techniques, which involve injecting Gaussian noise into model weights or activations, against traditional temperature sampling across six backdoored models ranging from 7B to 13B parameters. Fuzzing outperformed temperature sampling on four models, achieving up to six times better elicitation, though effectiveness varied by task and hyperparameter settings.

The study found that hyperparameter selection is critical, as uniform parameter sweeps yielded low elicitation rates, while optimized settings improved results significantly. To address the challenge of selecting hyperparameters without direct access to ground truth, the researchers introduced a proxy task involving secret elicitation using base64-encoded prompts and applied Thompson sampling to identify promising hyperparameters. This approach enhanced elicitation rates by up to fourfold for activation fuzzing and 1.3 to 1.8 times for weight fuzzing compared to uniform sweeps.

This work represents the first systematic evaluation of fuzzing on sleeper-agent backdoors and demonstrates that proxy-task hyperparameter tuning can effectively transfer to real backdoor elicitation. The authors recommend reporting results as a triple—uniform baseline, proxy-selected, and oracle performance—to clarify distinct claims and improve comparability in future research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sleeper agents are the canonical model organism of deception: models trained to behave normally but to emit an unsafe behaviour on a specific trigger. Eliciting that behaviour without knowing the trigger has not been studied systematically. We study fuzzing: injecting Gaussian noise into a model's weights or residual-stream activations and checking whether the perturbed outputs reveal the behaviour. On 6 backdoored models (7B-13B) we compare both forms of fuzzing head-to-head against temperature-sampling baselines. Fuzzing elicits the hidden behaviour more often than temperature sampling on 4 of 6 models (up to ~6x on OpenHermes-13B), and which form wins depends on the task, so both are worth running. Elicitation is uneven across each method's hyperparameter grid: a uniform sweep gives only a few percent on most models, while the best cell is 2-10x higher, so the bottleneck is hyperparameter selection, not the technique. To select hyperparameters without ground-truth access, we use a cheap proxy task (in-context secret elicitation, where a base64-encoded secret is placed in the system prompt for the model to hide) and run Thompson sampling on it to pick candidate cells, which we evaluate on the real backdoor. On the four models that can decode the secret, proxy-selected cells raise activation-fuzzing elicitation ~4x over the uniform-sweep mean (recovering ~70% of the best-cell rate on the best performing model) and weight-fuzzing by 1.3-1.8x. To our knowledge this is the first systematic study of fuzzing on sleeper-agent backdoors and the first to show proxy-task hyperparameter selection transferring to real-task elicitation. We also propose reporting such results as a (uniform-baseline, proxy-selected, oracle) triple, since these are three distinct claims that prior work has often blurred.

items.title: Researchers use Claude Fable 5 and Lean 4 to produce a machine-verified proof of the Farhi-Goldstone-Gutmann quantum optimization conjecture after a decade [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Machine-Verified Proof of a Quantum-Optimization Conjecture
items.summary:
Researchers have achieved a machine-verified proof of the Farhi-Goldstone-Gutmann (FGG) conjecture in quantum optimization, which had remained unresolved for over a decade. The conjecture states that the depth-$p$ Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) on the ring of disagrees attains an exact approximation ratio of $(2p+1)/(2p+2)$. This proof was generated using the large language model Claude Fable 5 and fully verified by the Lean 4 proof assistant, marking a significant advancement in automated theorem proving within quantum information science.

The team formalized the QAOA components and existing knowledge into a Lean library, reducing the conjecture to a single open mathematical statement. Claude Fable 5 then constructed the proof through an iterative process combining natural-language reasoning and mechanical verification by Lean. The model discovered a hidden dynamical symmetry and applied techniques from related fields to transform a challenging existence problem into an explicit construction. This approach required human oversight only to ensure the formal statement accurately represented the original claim, while the proof itself was machine-generated and certified.

This breakthrough demonstrates the potential of integrating advanced language models with formal proof systems to resolve longstanding open problems in quantum information and beyond. It opens new avenues for leveraging AI-assisted methods to tackle complex mathematical conjectures with rigorous verification.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29687v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We report a machine-verified resolution of a problem open for over a decade in quantum optimization: the Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann (FGG) conjecture that depth-$p$ Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) on the ring of disagrees attains approximation ratio $(2p+1)/(2p+2)$ exactly. We found the proof using a large language model, Claude Fable 5, and verified its correctness end-to-end by the Lean 4 proof assistant. Our methodology includes several ingredients: building on a substantial Lean library of quantum information, we formalized the QAOA components and the known parts of the problem, and reduced the conjecture to a single open mathematical statement. The model was then handed the library and our agentic toolkit, and tasked with closing that gap by constructing a proof in Lean. The resulting process is a feedback loop between the model's natural-language reasoning and Lean's mechanical verification, which converged to a machine-verified proof. Human verification is required only for the structural scaffolding - that the formal statement faithfully encodes the intended claim - while the proof itself is supplied by the model and certified mechanically by Lean. The proof is nevertheless striking - the model uncovered a hidden dynamical symmetry of the problem and exploited it, borrowing tools and machinery from an adjacent field to turn a hard existence problem into an explicit construction. This work paves the way for resolving open conjectures in quantum information science and beyond.

items.title: Researchers use an autonomous LLM coding agent to optimize crystal graph networks for band-gap prediction, achieving highest accuracy on MatBench benchmark without external pretraining [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Optimizing Expert-Designed Crystal Graph Networks for Band-Gap Prediction with an Autonomous LLM Research Loop
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an autonomous large language model (LLM) coding agent that optimized crystal graph networks to predict material band gaps with the highest accuracy on the MatBench benchmark, surpassing all seventeen expert-designed models without relying on external pretraining. This achievement highlights the potential of autonomous AI-driven research in computational materials science.

The agent improved performance by implementing established techniques such as element-pair features on message-passing edges and crystal space-group embeddings, which are either standard in crystal neural networks or adapted from other machine learning domains. The study also explores the limitations of autonomous research agents in optimizing expert-designed models for material property prediction.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29717v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predicting a material's properties from its structure is a central, fast-advancing problem in computational materials science. A decade of work has produced standard public benchmarks and many published machine-learning models for the task (Dunn et al., 2020). The task's fixed metric and these baselines make it a natural setting for autonomous agent research (Karpathy, 2026). On the MatBench band-gap benchmark ($>$100k crystals), a general-purpose coding agent autonomously built the most accurate model trained without external pretraining, ahead of all seventeen expert-designed models reported for the task. A closer analysis shows it reached this by implementing known methods: either already standard in crystal neural-network models, or borrowed from other areas of machine learning. The contributing implementations include element-pair features on each message-passing edge and a crystal space-group embedding. The work not only demonstrates that LLM-agent autonomous research can optimize an expert-designed machine learning model for material property prediction, but also investigates the limitations of such autonomous research.

Researchers have developed an autonomous large language model (LLM) coding agent that optimized crystal graph networks to predict material band gaps with the highest accuracy on the MatBench benchmark, surpassing all seventeen expert-designed models without relying on external pretraining. This achievement highlights the potential of autonomous AI-driven research in computational materials science.

The agent improved performance by implementing established techniques such as element-pair features on message-passing edges and crystal space-group embeddings, which are either standard in crystal neural networks or adapted from other machine learning domains. The study also explores the limitations of autonomous research agents in optimizing expert-designed models for material property prediction.

items.title: Researchers diagnose context rot in large language models during long-horizon search tasks and propose mitigation strategies including context management and rot-aware rejection sampling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Diagnosing and Mitigating Context Rot in Long-horizon Search
items.summary:
Researchers have identified and analyzed a phenomenon called context rot in large language models (LLMs), where increasing the length of input context during long-horizon search tasks leads to degraded model performance. Their study, involving four major open-source models across three benchmarks, found that extensive context causes models to either give up or produce uncertain answers prematurely, with the issue worsening as context length grows. They demonstrated the link between accumulated context and context rot through pruning experiments and explored mitigation strategies including context management and rot-aware rejection sampling.

The team systematically evaluated seven context management methods based on performance, cost, and impact on context rot, offering guidance for selecting appropriate strategies. Additionally, they developed a rot-aware filtering approach for rejection sampling, which proved effective across multiple aggregation methods. Combining these two approaches further improved model performance, providing practical solutions to address context rot in deep search scenarios involving LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29718v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Extensive context has become the norm as Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in long-horizon tasks. The concern that increasing context length degrades model capabilities, known as context rot, has become a central issue for these applications. In this paper, we focus on deep search scenarios, aiming to investigate the rot phenomenon and its mitigation strategies. By evaluating four flagship open-source models across three benchmarks, we reveal a prevalent but unnoticed rot phenomenon: extensive context causes models to directly give up or prematurely provide uncertain answers, and this issue is exacerbated as the context grows. Through pruning experiments, we demonstrate the relationship between the accumulated context and the rot phenomenon. Furthermore, we investigate mitigating this issue through context management and post-hoc rejection sampling. For context management, we systematically evaluate seven different methods across three categories, based on performance, cost, and impact on context rot, providing clear guidance for strategy selection and usage. For rejection sampling, we develop a rot-aware filtering strategy and demonstrate its effectiveness across three aggregation methods. Finally, we show that these two approaches can be combined for further performance improvements.

items.title: Researchers propose equation-grounded taxonomy and LLM-guided pipeline for maritime anomaly detection using AIS data, enabling synthetic anomaly labeling and benchmark evaluation across anomaly types [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Redefining Maritime Anomaly Detection via Equation-Grounded Synthetic Anomalies
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new approach to maritime anomaly detection using Automatic Identification System (AIS) data, addressing the lack of predefined anomaly labels in existing datasets. They propose an equation-based taxonomy categorizing anomalies into unexpected AIS activity, route deviation, and close approach, covering both individual and interaction-driven vessel anomalies. This framework is supported by a pipeline that uses large language model-guided plausibility scores to synthesize anomalies and assign precise labels, enabling more systematic evaluation of detection methods across different anomaly types.

The team also designed benchmark evaluation settings that consider variations in temporal window lengths and anomaly compositions, testing a wide range of time-series and anomaly detection models. This work aims to overcome limitations of previous methods that relied on statistical rarity or expert labeling, which often miss critical events or are difficult to scale. The researchers have made their code publicly available to facilitate further development and benchmarking in maritime safety and traffic management.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Maritime anomaly detection is essential for ensuring maritime safety, security, and efficient traffic management at sea, with Automatic Identification System (AIS) data serving as a primary data source. Despite its importance, most publicly available AIS datasets lack predefined anomaly labels, forcing prior studies to rely on either distribution-based rarity or domain rule/expert-assisted labeling. These approaches, however, face fundamental limitations: statistical rarity often fails to reflect practically critical events, while expert-based labeling is costly, subjective, and difficult to scale. Moreover, both paradigms tend to overlook interaction-driven hazards such as near-miss approaches between vessels. To address these challenges, we propose an equation-grounded anomaly taxonomy that is implementable under a limited AIS observation schema and extensible to other AIS datasets. Specifically, the taxonomy defines three anomaly types: unexpected AIS activity (A1), route deviation (A2), and close approach (A3), covering both single-vessel and inter-vessel anomalies. Building on this taxonomy, we introduce a unified score-synthesize-label pipeline that produces LLM-guided plausibility scores, uses them to synthesize anomalies, and assigns timestamp-level labels. To rigorously assess detection performance, we further design benchmark evaluation settings that account for variations in temporal-window length and anomaly-type composition, and evaluate a broad range of time-series models and anomaly detection models. Together, these contributions provide a systematic basis for evaluating maritime anomaly detection methods across different anomaly types. Our code is available at https://github.com/snudial/open-maritime-anomaly-detection.

items.title: Researchers propose PS-PPO, a compute-efficient critic-free RLHF method using prefix sampling to reduce training compute and GPU memory while maintaining accuracy on reasoning benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PS-PPO: Prefix-Sampling PPO for Critic-Free RLHF
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Prefix-Sampling Proximal Policy Optimization (PS-PPO), a new critic-free reinforcement learning method designed to improve the efficiency of training large language models using human feedback. PS-PPO reduces computational demands by sampling and backpropagating through only a prefix of each trajectory during training, rather than the full sequence, while maintaining unbiased gradient estimates. This approach addresses the high optimization costs associated with long reasoning traces in existing methods.

The method incorporates a prompt-conditioned cutoff distribution to determine the prefix length for each trajectory and applies importance-weighting corrections to ensure accuracy. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and reinforcement learning from human feedback benchmarks demonstrate that PS-PPO significantly lowers training compute and peak GPU memory usage without sacrificing performance compared to strong critic-free baselines.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) for Large Language Models increasingly relies on critic-free methods as a practical alternative to actor--critic training. Despite their simplicity, existing critic-free approaches propagate a trajectory-level learning signal uniformly across all tokens in a trajectory. This requires full-trajectory policy updates for every rollout, leading to substantial optimization cost for long reasoning traces, even though intermediate prefixes often contain enough information to largely determine the final outcome. We propose Prefix-Sampling Proximal Policy Optimization (PS-PPO), a compute-efficient critic-free method for RLHF that exploits this temporal redundancy. PS-PPO introduces a prompt-conditioned cutoff distribution and samples a cutoff timestep for each trajectory. During the update pass, PS-PPO backpropagates only through the sampled prefix of each trajectory and applies an importance-weighting correction so that the resulting truncated gradient estimator remains unbiased with respect to the full-trajectory objective. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and RLHF benchmarks show that PS-PPO achieves large reductions in training compute and peak GPU memory, while maintaining accuracy comparable to strong critic-free baselines.

items.title: Researchers present NMRAgent, a large language model-powered AI that improves molecular structure elucidation from NMR spectra by 46.5% accuracy and offers interpretable, evidence-based reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Generalizable and Evidential Nuclear Magnetic Resonance-Based Molecular Structure Elucidation via Large Language Model Agent
items.summary:
Researchers have developed NMRAgent, an AI system powered by large language models that significantly enhances molecular structure elucidation from Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectra. NMRAgent improves accuracy by 46.5% compared to existing methods and offers interpretable, evidence-based reasoning by mimicking the deductive process of human experts. It integrates spectral analysis tools with chemical knowledge graphs to propose and verify candidate molecular structures, refining them through formula-aware optimization.

Unlike previous AI approaches that either rely on database retrieval or operate as black boxes, NMRAgent provides atom-level interpretability, enabling rigorous scientific validation. The system demonstrated its practical utility by elucidating structures of two previously unknown natural products and correcting structural misassignments in established literature. This advancement establishes a new paradigm for transparent and high-accuracy AI applications in analytical chemistry.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is the gold standard for molecular structure elucidation, yet interpreting complex spectra for unknown molecules remains a bottleneck reliant on human expertise. While artificial intelligence has advanced this field, current methods face a critical trade-off: database retrieval cannot identify novel scaffolds, while de novo molecular structure elucidation models operate as black boxes, lacking the atom-level interpretability required for rigorous scientific validation. Here, we present NMRAgent, an evidential reasoning agent powered by large language models (LLMs) that bridges this gap by integrating specialized spectral analysis tools with chemical knowledge graphs. Unlike previous approaches, NMRAgent mimics the deductive reasoning of human experts: it takes experimental NMR spectra and molecular formula as input, plans the elucidation process, proposes candidate structures, verifies peak-atom consistency, and refines misaligned substructure through formula-aware fragment optimization. Enabled by its evidential reasoning, NMRAgent outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improving top-1 accuracy by 46.5% and Tanimoto similarity by 0.502 on a scaffold-split benchmark with novel scaffolds in the test set. Besides, we demonstrate the agent's practical utility by elucidating the structures of two previously unknown natural products isolated from Hydrangea davidii and Vitex trifolia, and by correcting structural misassignments in established literature. By combining high-accuracy prediction with transparent and evidence-based reasoning, NMRAgent establishes a new paradigm for interpretable AI in analytical chemistry.

items.title: Researchers propose Mandol, an agglomerative agent memory system unifying vector and graph data for long-term conversations, achieving 5.4x retrieval speedup and improved accuracy on benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Mandol: An Agglomerative Agent Memory System for Long-Term Conversations
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Mandol, an agglomerative memory system designed to enhance long-term conversational agents by unifying vector and graph data into a single memory-native architecture. Mandol organizes memory hierarchically into raw and abstract layers represented as semantic graphs, and employs a hybrid data structure that integrates key-value, vector, and graph formats to eliminate cross-database input/output latency. This system also features a quantitative query mechanism that improves retrieval accuracy and efficiency without involving large language models during the retrieval process.

Tests on established benchmarks for long-term conversations, LoCoMo and LongMemEval, demonstrate that Mandol outperforms existing agent memory systems in accuracy. Additionally, it achieves a 5.4 times speedup in retrieval and a 4.8 times speedup in insertion under concurrent load, while maintaining low latency on consumer-grade hardware, indicating its potential for practical deployment in conversational AI applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29778v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-term conversational agents need to remember and query cross-session, multi-typed information with complex correlations. Existing agent memory systems rely on heterogeneous vector and graph databases, which fragment memory information and cause high cross-database I/O latency. For retrieval, common RAG-style methods tend to introduce noise, miss correlated clues, and lack token budget control, degrading LLM accuracy and efficiency. We propose Mandol, an agglomerative memory system that consolidates fragmented memory representations and storage into a unified memory-native architecture. Its core components include: (1) a hierarchical memory model that organizes memory into a basic layer representing raw memory information and a high-level abstract layer that agglomerates basic memories into traceable abstract memories, both uniformly represented as structured semantic graphs; (2) an agglomerative semantic data structure combining SemanticMap and SemanticGraph, which natively fuses key-value, vector, and graph structures and provides unified hybrid retrieval operators to eliminate cross-database I/O; and (3) a quantitative query mechanism with query-adaptive routing, quantitative denoising and conflict resolution, and token-constrained context generation, all without involving LLMs during retrieval. Experiments on two widely used long-term conversation benchmarks, LoCoMo and LongMemEval, show that Mandol achieves the best overall accuracy among representative agent memory systems. For performance comparison, Mandol also obtains a 5.4x retrieval speedup and a 4.8x insertion speedup under 10 QPS concurrent load, while still maintaining low latency on consumer-grade hardware.

items.originalTitle: What Drives the Inlier-Memorization Effect? A Theory of Outlier Detection via Early Training Dynamics
items.summary:
Researchers have conducted a theoretical study on the inlier-memorization (IM) effect in outlier detection, focusing on the early training dynamics of autoencoders. They demonstrate that under certain conditions, models memorize normal data (inliers) earlier than anomalies (outliers), which helps distinguish outliers effectively. Their analysis characterizes the emergence, strength, and persistence of the IM effect and how it depends on data distribution and parameter initialization.

Building on these insights, the researchers propose practical guidelines such as data preprocessing and parameter initialization strategies to enhance the IM effect. These methods achieve state-of-the-art results on the ADBench datasets, providing a theoretical foundation and actionable improvements for IM-based outlier detection techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Outlier detection (OD) aims to identify anomalous instances by learning the underlying structure of normal data (inliers), and is particularly challenging in fully unsupervised settings where no information about anomalies is available during training. Recent advances have leveraged the inlier-memorization (IM) effect, a phenomenon in which deep models memorize inlier patterns earlier than those of outliers, as a powerful signal for distinguishing outliers. However, despite its empirical success, the theoretical understanding of the IM effect remains limited. In this work, we present a theoretical study of the IM effect. Focusing on a simple autoencoder, we show that, under mild assumptions, the model can successfully memorize inliers while failing to memorize outliers during certain stages of early training. In particular, we characterize not only the emergence of the IM effect, but also its strength and persistence, and analyze how these properties depend on the data distribution and parameter initialization. In addition, building on these insights, we derive simple yet practical guidelines for enhancing the IM effect, including data preprocessing and parameter initialization schemes, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the ADBench datasets. Our findings provide a theoretical foundation for the IM effect and offer actionable directions for improving IM-based outlier detection methods.

items.title: Researchers propose Multi-Level Distributional Entropy framework for explainable network intrusion detection using flow-level statistics without raw packet data, achieving competitive performance across four benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-Level Distributional Entropy for Explainable Network Intrusion Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a Multi-Level Distributional Entropy (MDE) framework for network intrusion detection that uses interpretable entropy features derived directly from flow-level summary statistics, eliminating the need for raw packet data or training sets. This approach evaluates entropy at three levels—within-flow Gaussian differential entropy, cross-directional Jensen-Shannon divergence, and TCP flag-pattern Shannon entropy—and achieves competitive performance across four benchmark datasets, matching traditional feature-based methods without loss of accuracy.

The study highlights that while aggregate F1 scores appear strong, they can mask significant detection failures, such as low detection rates on certain attack families and under temporal shifts in network traffic. A large-scale pseudo-live replay experiment revealed that fixed detection thresholds may fail over time despite preserved score rankings, and recalibration does not fully restore performance. Additionally, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis confirmed that the entropy-based features are stable and consistent across diverse environments, supporting their interpretability and robustness for practical intrusion detection applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29797v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning network intrusion detection systems (IDS) rely on aggregate flow statistics that discard distributional structure, while established entropy measures require raw packet sequences unavailable in pre-aggregated flow datasets. We propose Multi-Level Distributional Entropy (MDE), an analytical framework that derives interpretable entropy features directly from flow-level summary statistics at three levels: within-flow Gaussian differential entropy, cross-directional Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), and Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) flag-pattern Shannon entropy, without raw packet access or training data. Across four benchmarks (NSL-KDD, CICIDS-2017, CICIDS-2018, UNSW-NB15) under a leakage-free fold-local pipeline, entropy-only features achieve weighted F1 of 0.708-0.989, matching conventional features without degrading performance. Full operational metric reporting then exposes failure modes that aggregate F1 conceals. On CICIDS-2018, F1=0.74 hides a detection rate (DR) of 0.48, and on held-out attack families F1 exceeds 0.998 while DR falls to zero. Under temporal shift, a pseudo-live replay of 703K flows reveals a threshold-ranking divergence in which score ranking is preserved (AUC=0.87) but fixed thresholds collapse (DR=0.082) and recalibration offers no recovery. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) fold-stability analysis (Spearman rho=0.80-0.95) confirms that entropy attributions are reproducible and domain-coherent across heterogeneous environments.

items.title: Researchers introduce mean-expansion layer to accelerate Q-learning by sharing action-values within states, improving performance across 57 Atari games and reducing value overestimation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Accelerating Q-learning through Efficient Value-Sharing across Actions
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a mean-expansion layer to enhance Q-learning by sharing action-values across different actions within the same state. This approach accelerates the learning process by shifting from directly estimating large action-values to learning a more compact representation, improving efficiency without altering the underlying algorithm. When integrated into deep Q-networks and implicit quantile networks, this method demonstrated improved performance across 57 Atari games, increased action gaps, and significantly reduced value overestimation.

The mean-expansion layer functions as a parameter-free addition to existing Q-network architectures, enabling faster convergence of action-values that typically start near zero and require many updates to reach their true values. By leveraging shared value structures within states, the technique addresses inefficiencies in traditional Q-learning, where each state-action pair is updated independently.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Action-values are foundational to many control algorithms such as Q-learning. Therefore learning action-values efficiently is central to reinforcement learning (RL). However, learning them can be slow, requiring many updates to move values from their initialization, typically near zero, to their true values, which may be far from zero. Moreover, action-value learning algorithms typically update each state-action pair independently, without learning shared value structure across actions within a state. In this paper, we address these inefficiencies by introducing the mean-expansion layer, which accelerates action-value learning by sharing values across actions within a state and by changing the problem from directly learning potentially large action-values to learning a lower-norm representation of them. In deep RL, this layer can be applied as a parameter-free addition to Q-network architectures without altering the underlying algorithm. Applied to deep Q-networks and implicit quantile networks, it improves aggregate performance across 57 Atari games while increasing action gaps and dramatically reducing value overestimation.

items.title: Researchers benchmark five lightweight, CPU-based hallucination detection methods across question answering, dialogue, and summarisation, finding task-dependent performance and poor results on summarisation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Far Can You Get Without a GPU? A Systematic Benchmark of Lightweight Hallucination Detection Across Question Answering, Dialogue, and Summarisation
items.summary:
Researchers have benchmarked five lightweight, CPU-based methods for detecting hallucinations in AI-generated text across question answering, dialogue, and summarisation tasks. These methods, which include ROUGE-L, semantic similarity, BERTScore, a Natural Language Inference detector, and an ensemble approach, were evaluated on the HaluEval benchmark using publicly available models and standard laptop CPUs. The study found that no single method consistently outperformed others, with performance varying significantly by task and notably poor results on summarisation.

The ensemble method achieved the best results in question answering, while the NLI detector was most effective for dialogue. However, all methods performed near chance levels on summarisation, highlighting the challenges of hallucination detection without GPU resources. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting hallucination detection techniques under computational constraints and map the current limits of GPU-free approaches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hallucination detection has become a pressing requirement for trustworthy AI deployment at scale. The most accurate detection methods depend on GPU-intensive inference, proprietary API calls, or white-box access to the generating model. This puts them out of reach for resource-constrained researchers and practitioners. In this paper, we explore a practical alternative: how well can hallucination detection perform using only lightweight, CPU-feasible methods built on publicly available models? We systematically benchmark five such methods: ROUGE-L, semantic similarity, BERTScore, a Natural Language Inference (NLI) detector based on a FEVER-trained DeBERTa model, and a score-level ensemble of similarity and NLI. We evaluate them across all three tasks of the HaluEval benchmark: question answering (QA), dialogue, and summarisation. We calibrate each method on a held-out validation split and evaluate it on 2,000 test instances per task. We find that no single method dominates and performance is highly task-dependent. The ensemble performs best on QA (F1 = 0.792, AUC-ROC = 0.873), the NLI detector leads on dialogue (AUC-ROC = 0.713), and all five methods degrade to near-random performance on summarisation (AUC-ROC between 0.469 and 0.574). This task-dependence and the systematic failure on summarisation map the practical frontier of GPU-free hallucination detection. They give practical guidance for method selection under computational constraints. All experiments run on a standard laptop CPU using public models.

items.title: Researchers propose Dual-Flow RL, a unified actor-critic framework with state-aware exploration regulator, achieving state-of-the-art results on DeepMind Control Suite and Humanoid-Bench tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Dual-Flow Reinforcement Learning with State-Aware Exploration
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Dual-Flow RL, a unified actor-critic framework designed to improve continuous-control reinforcement learning by jointly modeling a continuous return distribution and a multimodal policy distribution using conditional flow matching. This approach addresses challenges in value estimation and exploration caused by multimodal optimal actions and uncertain return distributions. The framework also incorporates an Entropy-Covariance Exploration Regulator (ECER) to enable state-aware exploration by leveraging policy entropy and action-uncertainty covariance.

Experiments conducted on the DeepMind Control Suite and Humanoid-Bench demonstrate that Dual-Flow RL achieves state-of-the-art performance on most tasks, significantly outperforming previous diffusion-based and flow-based methods. This advancement offers a more reliable and expressive method for value estimation and sustained multimodal exploration in complex reinforcement learning environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In complex continuous-control reinforcement learning tasks, multimodal optimal actions often coincide with uncertain, multimodal return distributions, making reliable value estimation and multimodal exploration challenging. Existing value estimation methods using unimodal Gaussians restrict expressiveness and yield biased estimates. Recent generative policies can represent multimodal actions but often collapse to a few modes and under-explore high-value areas of the action space. Motivated by these challenges, we propose Dual-Flow RL, a unified actor-critic framework that jointly models a continuous return distribution and a multimodal policy distribution using conditional flow matching (CFM). This design supports reliable value estimation and sustained multimodal exploration. To further enhance exploration, we introduce an Entropy-Covariance Exploration Regulator (ECER) that enables state-aware exploration regulation leveraging policy entropy and action-uncertainty covariance. Experiments on DeepMind Control Suite and Humanoid-Bench show that Dual-Flow RL achieves state-of-the-art performance on most tasks, significantly outperforming prior diffusion-based and flow-based methods.

items.title: Researchers introduce Neural Procedural Memory, a training-free framework using implicit activation steering to enhance LLM agents' procedural memory and task execution across four benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Neural Procedural Memory: Empowering LLM Agents with Implicit Activation Steering
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Neural Procedural Memory (NPM), a training-free framework that enhances large language model (LLM) agents by using implicit activation steering to improve procedural memory and task execution. Unlike traditional methods that rely on explicit textual instructions, NPM distills procedural skills into steering vectors that directly activate relevant neural mechanisms, enabling more effective task performance. Evaluations across four benchmarks demonstrate that NPM matches the performance of explicit instruction-based approaches and that combining both methods yields even more robust results.

NPM addresses the limitations of current LLM agents, which struggle with persistent procedural memory during continuous environmental interaction. By leveraging historical contrastive experiences, NPM encodes consistent task logic within the activation space, forming organized structures that guide task execution. This approach reduces the disconnect between symbolic instructions and neural activation, offering a promising direction for managing agent memory and improving autonomous agent capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29824v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel as static solvers, transforming them into autonomous agents remains challenging. This transition requires continuous environmental interaction, yet current agents lack the necessary persistent procedural memory. Existing approaches predominantly employ Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to inject explicit textual guidelines into model contexts. Furthermore, the results show that combining implicit steering with explicit workflows provides complementary advantages, leading to more robust task execution. Representational analyses indicate that these steering vectors encode consistent task logic, forming organized structures within the activation space. These findings suggest that implicit activation steering provides a promising approach for managing agent memory.

items.title: Study uses deep learning to classify motivations for algorithm mentions in NLP papers, finding increased use over description and evolving trends across algorithm types [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Exploring Motivations for Algorithm Mention in the Domain of Natural Language Processing: A Deep Learning Approach
items.summary:
A recent study applies deep learning techniques to classify the motivations behind algorithm mentions in natural language processing (NLP) research papers. By analyzing full-text papers, the researchers identified algorithm-related sentences and categorized the reasons for mentioning algorithms, such as describing, using, comparing, or improving them. The study found that deep learning models with data augmentation outperform traditional methods in this classification task, revealing that direct use is the most common motivation, while improvement is least frequent. Over time, the diversity of motivations has increased, with use motivations gradually replacing description motivations across various algorithm types.

The research also highlights differences among algorithm categories: grammar-based algorithms are more often mentioned for description, whereas machine learning algorithms are primarily cited for use. Additionally, the number of motivation types associated with individual algorithms has decreased significantly. This work sheds light on how algorithms are referenced in academic writing and provides a foundation for future studies on algorithm relationships and impact assessment in scientific research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rise of data-intensive science, algorithms have become central to scientific research. In academic papers, algorithms are mentioned for different purposes, such as describing, using, comparing, or improving methods for specific research tasks. Identifying these purposes can reveal relationships among algorithms and help assess their roles and value. Taking natural language processing (NLP) as an example, this study proposes a sentence-level framework for identifying, analyzing, and tracing the evolution of motivations for mentioning algorithms. We first identify algorithm entities and algorithm-related sentences from full-text papers through manual annotation and machine learning. We then classify mention motivations using pretrained models and data augmentation, and analyze their distribution and temporal evolution. The results show that deep learning models trained with augmented data outperform traditional machine learning models in motivation classification. In NLP papers, more than half of algorithm-related sentences express direct use, whereas improvement is the least frequent motivation. The diversity of motivations has increased over time. For specific algorithm categories, grammar-based algorithms are more often mentioned for description, while machine learning algorithms are more often mentioned for use. Over time, use motivations have gradually replaced description motivations across different algorithms, and the number of motivation types associated with individual algorithms has declined significantly. This study reveals how authors mention algorithm entities in academic writing and provides a basis for future research on algorithm relationship identification and algorithm impact evaluation.

items.title: Researchers release RoAd-RL, an open-source unified library and benchmark for robust adversarial reinforcement learning with 192 attack-defense evaluations on DQN, PPO, and SAC agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RoAd-RL: A Unified Library and Benchmark for Robust Adversarial Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced RoAd-RL, an open-source library and benchmark designed to unify and standardize robust adversarial reinforcement learning (RL) research. The framework integrates policies, attacks, defenses, and robustness metrics with reproducible evaluation pipelines, supporting popular RL algorithms like DQN, PPO, and SAC. It has been tested across 192 attack-defense scenarios in environments such as LunarLander and Highway-v0, revealing significant differences in agent robustness and highlighting that some defenses may inadvertently harm performance more than the attacks themselves.

RoAd-RL addresses challenges in the field caused by fragmented implementations and inconsistent evaluation methods by providing a cohesive platform compatible with Stable-Baselines3 and Gymnasium. The benchmark's results emphasize the effectiveness of temporal smoothing as a defense strategy and establish a foundation for more reliable and comparable adversarial RL research. The library is publicly available for use and further development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has achieved significant success in robotics and autonomous systems, yet remains vulnerable to adversarial perturbations that can severely degrade performance. Research in adversarial reinforcement learning is often limited by fragmented implementations, inconsistent evaluation protocols, and poor reproducibility. To address these challenges, we present \textbf{RoAd-RL}, an open-source benchmarking framework that provides unified abstractions for policies, attacks, defenses, and robustness metrics, together with reproducible evaluation pipelines and seamless integration with Stable-Baselines3 and Gymnasium. We evaluate DQN, PPO, and SAC agents in LunarLander and Highway-v0 under 192 attack-defense configurations. Results reveal substantial variations in robustness across environments and show that some commonly used defenses can be more detrimental than the attacks they aim to mitigate, while temporal smoothing consistently achieves strong performance. RoAd-RL establishes a standardized benchmark for adversarial reinforcement learning research and is publicly available at https://pypi.org/project/road-rl.

items.title: Researchers propose ARKD, a reinforcement learning-based adaptive bidirectional KL divergence distillation method for text generation that improves LLM compression and generation quality on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ARKD: Adaptive Reinforcement Learning-Guided Bidirectional KL Divergence Distillation for Text Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ARKD, a novel reinforcement learning-based method for knowledge distillation that improves the compression and generation quality of Large Language Models (LLMs). This approach dynamically balances forward and reverse KL divergence during training to better align the student model with the teacher's distribution, addressing limitations of previous methods that relied on a single KL objective. Experiments show that ARKD consistently enhances performance on multiple benchmarks, outperforming existing techniques in key metrics like Rouge-L and BertScore.

The method uses a policy network to adaptively assign weights to forward and reverse KL divergence based on the characteristics of the teacher and student distributions, guided by immediate reward signals. This dual alignment strategy effectively captures both primary and long-tail distribution modes, leading to improved generalization and generation quality. The results demonstrate that ARKD surpasses greedy heuristics by 0.4 to 0.6 points and outperforms other baseline distillation methods across diverse datasets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a key technique for compressing Large Language Models (LLMs), yet methods relying on a single KL objective often fail to balance primary distribution fitting with long-tail probability modeling, limiting both generation quality and generalization. To address this, we analyze the complementary roles of forward and reverse KL divergence (FKL/RKL) in distribution alignment from theoretical and empirical perspectives. We then propose a reinforcement-learning-based adaptive KL-weighted distillation framework, in which a policy network dynamically assigns weights to FKL and RKL based on teacher-student distributional characteristics, guided by immediate reward signals to achieve dual alignment on principal and long-tail modes. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across Rouge-L and BertScore metrics, surpassing greedy heuristics by 0.4-0.6 points and outperforming other baseline methods on diverse benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers introduce clinical reasoning graphs to evaluate LLM diagnostic reasoning, finding competence without consistent schema-scale reasoning across 750 traces from five models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Clinical Reasoning Graphs: Structured Evaluation of LLM Diagnostic Reasoning Reveals Competence Without Consistency
items.summary:
Researchers have developed clinical reasoning graphs to evaluate the diagnostic reasoning of large language models (LLMs) in clinical settings. By analyzing 750 diagnostic traces from five LLMs across 50 complex medical cases, they found that while these models achieve 60-70% diagnostic accuracy, their reasoning lacks consistent schema-scale patterns across similar cases. This suggests that LLMs demonstrate diagnostic competence but do not consistently apply stable, clinically grounded reasoning schemas.

The study used a structured graph representation based on a domain-specific ontology to compare reasoning patterns, revealing that graph similarity did not significantly differ between clinically similar and dissimilar cases or between correct and incorrect diagnoses. Although prompting techniques increased detailed feature analysis within individual traces, they did not improve reasoning consistency across cases. The researchers emphasize that evaluating LLMs should go beyond final-answer accuracy to include process-level assessments and have made their ontology, extraction tools, and data publicly available to support further structured evaluation of clinical reasoning in LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) reach 60-70% diagnostic accuracy on complex clinical case benchmarks, but accuracy alone cannot distinguish stable clinically-grounded reasoning from pattern matching. We introduce clinical reasoning graphs, structured graph representations extracted from free-text LLM diagnostic traces using a domain-grounded ontology with 5 node types and 7 edge types. We apply this pipeline to 750 traces from five LLMs across 50 New England Journal of Medicine Clinicopathological Conference cases and three prompt conditions, and test whether diagnostic traces show stable structured reasoning patterns, or diagnostic schemas, for clinically similar cases. We operationalize this as higher graph similarity among clinically similar cases than among clinically dissimilar ones. Across 15 model-condition comparisons, within-cluster and between-cluster composite similarity are nearly equal, and no comparison survives multiple-testing correction; a component-level analysis finds any residual content signal far below schema scale. Graph similarity is also nearly identical for pairs of models that are both correct (0.488) and both incorrect (0.484), suggesting that graph structure captures a dimension not reflected in diagnostic accuracy. Structured reflection prompting increases explicit discriminating-feature analysis within traces (+33%) but does not increase cross-case consistency. These results show diagnostic competence without schema-scale reasoning consistency, and indicate that final-answer accuracy should be complemented by process-level evaluation. We release the ontology, extraction pipeline, validation protocol, and the extracted reasoning graphs and similarity artifacts as resources for structured evaluation of LLM clinical reasoning.

items.title: Researchers propose CW-B, a class-weighted XGBoost framework for five-class cardiac discharge phenotyping addressing real-world class imbalance and missing data with improved accuracy and interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CW-B: Class Weighted Boosting Framework for Imbalance Resilient Multi Class Cardiac Phenotyping
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CW-B, a class-weighted XGBoost framework designed to improve five-class cardiac discharge phenotyping in clinical settings where data is often incomplete and imbalanced. This approach addresses the challenge of accurately identifying high-risk cardiac phenotypes by integrating class-balanced instance weighting, missing data indicators, and classwise error auditing to enhance both accuracy and interpretability.

In tests using five-fold stratified cross-validation, CW-B outperformed other tree-based, ensemble, and neural network models in key metrics such as Accuracy, Macro-F1, Balanced Accuracy, and Prioritized F1. The framework offers a practical solution for more reliable cardiac phenotyping, supporting better-informed post-discharge treatment and follow-up decisions in real-world healthcare environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cardiac discharge phenotyping informs post-discharge treatment and follow-up, but real-world records are often incomplete and class-imbalanced, increasing the risk of missed high-risk phenotypes. We propose CW-B, a clinical risk-aligned class-weighted XGBoost pipeline for five-class cardiac discharge phenotyping under real-world class imbalance and missingness. CW-B combines fold-specific class-balanced instance weighting, missingness-indicator augmentation, and classwise error auditing to improve recognition of clinically prioritized phenotypes while preserving interpretable and auditable decision logic. In five-fold stratified cross-validation, CW-B achieves the best Accuracy, Macro-F1, Balanced Accuracy, and Prioritized F1 among tree-based, ensemble, and neural baselines. Overall, CW-B provides a practical and deployment-oriented approach for more reliable cardiac discharge phenotyping in real-world clinical settings.

items.title: Researchers introduce EVAF, a test-retest protocol for selective parametric consolidation in language models, showing improved behavioral persistence in GPT-2 and TinyLlama [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EVAF: A Test-Retest Protocol for Selective Parametric Consolidation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed EVAF, an Echo-Valence Attractor Field mechanism combined with a test-retest protocol, to improve selective parametric consolidation in language models like GPT-2 and TinyLlama. This approach enables models to selectively internalize high-valence, high-surprise experiences while maintaining access to factual memory through a separate retrieval path. EVAF demonstrates stronger behavioral persistence after interference compared to existing methods, with minimal parameter drift and reduced cross-persona contamination.

The study highlights a distinction between memory access and memory depth, suggesting that retrieving information and internalizing experiences are separate computational processes. By selectively consolidating experiences, EVAF offers a promising method for enhancing the long-term behavioral consistency of language agents beyond simple retrieval-based memory systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-running language agents need mechanisms for deciding which experiences should persist after the working context is gone. Retrieval systems can reinsert past text, but they do not by themselves show that an experience has been selectively consolidated into the model's own behavior. We introduce EVAF, an Echo-Valence Attractor Field mechanism for gated LoRA consolidation, and a test-retest protocol for measuring selective parametric consolidation under controlled interference. Across GPT-2 and TinyLlama, EVAF preferentially consolidates high-valence, high-surprise experiences while preserving retrieval-accessible factual memory through a complementary routed memory path. Test-retest measurements show stronger post-interference behavioral persistence than frozen, retrieval-only, and ungated continual-update baselines, while keeping parameter drift and cross-persona contamination low. The results support a separation between memory access and memory depth: retrieving a fact and internalizing an experience are distinct computational operations.

items.title: Researchers propose Fold, a lightweight flatness-modulated out-of-distribution detector leveraging feature Hessian and AutoFold self-supervised tuning, improving AUROC by 1.63% and reducing FPR95 by 2.30% on benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Exploiting Local Flatness for Efficient Out-of-Distribution Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Fold, a lightweight out-of-distribution (OOD) detection method that leverages feature Hessian curvature and partial feature normalization to distinguish OOD data from in-distribution (ID) data more effectively. Fold improves detection performance by increasing the average AUROC by 1.63% and reducing the false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95) by 2.30% on standard benchmarks, while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to a standard forward pass.

The study systematically investigates the curvature differences between ID and OOD inputs, finding that OOD data exhibit larger Hessian curvature, especially under stronger distributional shifts. To adapt Fold across diverse datasets without external data, the researchers also propose AutoFold, a self-supervised tuning scheme that generates pseudo-OOD samples for automatic calibration. Supported by theoretical analysis and extensive experiments, Fold offers a practical and principled approach for robust OOD detection in real-world machine learning deployments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) data is crucial for reliable machine learning deployment. Among detection strategies, post-hoc methods are particularly attractive due to their efficiency, as they operate directly on pre-trained networks without requiring retraining. Within this paradigm, one promising direction exploits loss-landscape curvature to estimate model uncertainty; however, such methods incur substantial computational cost and rely on implicit assumptions about how landscape flatness differs between in-distribution (ID) and OOD data. In this work, we provide the first systematic investigation of this curvature discrepancy and show that OOD inputs exhibit larger Hessian curvature than ID data, with the gap widening under stronger distributional shifts. Motivated by these observations, we propose Fold, a lightweight flatness-modulated OOD detector that leverages the feature Hessian and partial feature normalization to improve ID-OOD separability while avoiding costly parameter-space curvature approximations. To optimally adapt this normalization across diverse datasets, we further introduce AutoFold, a self-supervised tuning scheme that synthesizes pseudo-OOD samples via ID logit masking for automatic calibration without requiring external data. Experiments on OOD benchmarks show that Fold outperforms prior methods, improving the average AUROC by 1.63% and reducing FPR95 by 2.30%, while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to a standard forward pass. Supported by theoretical analysis and extensive ablations, Fold provides a principled and practical solution for robust real-world deployment.

items.title: Researchers introduce DuoMem, a dual-space distillation framework that boosts on-device memory agent performance from 4.3% to 77.9% task success on ALFWorld using a 4B-parameter model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DuoMem: Towards Capable On-Device Memory Agents via Dual-Space Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DuoMem, a dual-space distillation framework designed to enhance the performance of on-device memory agents by transferring procedural problem-solving skills from large teacher models to smaller student models. Tested on the ALFWorld benchmark, DuoMem significantly improved the task success rate of a 4-billion-parameter model from 4.3% to 77.9%, nearing the 87.1% success rate of a much larger 72-billion-parameter teacher model. This improvement was achieved with minimal additional parameters and pre-computed memories, enabling faster task completion suitable for real-time deployment on resource-constrained devices.

DuoMem operates through two complementary distillation methods: context-space distillation, which replaces student-generated memories with higher-quality teacher-generated ones, and parameter-space distillation, which fine-tunes lightweight adapters based on successful teacher trajectories. The approach not only boosts performance but also reduces inference time, making advanced memory-augmented agents more practical for edge computing environments. Extensive testing across models ranging from 2 billion to 72 billion parameters confirmed the complementary benefits of both distillation techniques.

items.title: Researchers propose learned stochastic stopping to stabilize extrapolation and reduce out-of-distribution variance in looped transformers for variable-length algorithmic tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Stabilizing Extrapolation in Looped Transformers via Learned Stochastic Stopping
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a method called learned stochastic stopping to improve the stability and reduce out-of-distribution variance in looped transformers, which are designed for variable-length algorithmic tasks. Looped transformers apply a shared transformer block repeatedly and can generalize to longer sequences than those seen during training, but this generalization is often unstable due to a spurious correlation between sequence length and the number of loops. Introducing stochasticity in the number of loops during training significantly reduces this variance and stabilizes predictions across different loop counts during inference.

The study further explores RL-Halting as a learned stochastic schedule, which generally enhances the trade-off between accuracy and stability compared to heuristic randomization methods. Experiments on tasks such as binary addition, Dyck-1, Unique Set, and Copy demonstrate that learned stochastic stopping can improve this trade-off, although it may sometimes stabilize suboptimal computations. The findings suggest that deciding when to stop looping should be considered a training-time design choice rather than solely an inference-time computation rule.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped Transformers, which repeatedly apply a shared transformer block, are an architecturally natural fit for variable-length algorithmic tasks. Although they can exhibit strong length generalization beyond the length of training sequences, this behavior is brittle, yielding high out-of-distribution (OOD) variance, even across well-performing in-distribution solutions. We trace this variance to the spurious correlation in simple algorithmic tasks between sequence length and number of loops. Introducing stochasticity into the number of loops during training sharply reduces OOD variance and stabilizes predictions across inference-time loop counts. To improve upon heuristic randomization schemes, we further analyze RL-Halting as a learned stochastic schedule and find that it generally improves the accuracy-stability trade-off. Across binary addition, Dyck-1, Unique Set, and Copy, learned stochastic stopping often improves this trade-off but can also stabilize a suboptimal computation. Our work suggests that "when to stop" should be treated as a training-time design choice, not merely an inference-time computation-allocation rule.

items.title: Researchers propose T3R method for deeper test-time adaptation of Graph Neural Networks using gradient rotation, improving performance on regression and cross-domain classification benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: T3R: Deeper Test-Time Adaptation for Graph Neural Networks via Gradient Rotation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced T3R, a novel method for deeper test-time adaptation of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that uses gradient rotation to enhance model performance under distribution shifts. Unlike traditional fine-tuning, which requires labeled data and is often impractical, T3R adapts nearly the entire network architecture using unlabeled test data by leveraging multiple Rotograd matrices to align auxiliary and target tasks. This approach enables more effective test-time training and improves results on regression and cross-domain classification benchmarks.

Empirical evaluations show that T3R reduces mean absolute error by 0.172 points in regression tasks and achieves at least a 9.37% relative improvement on cross-domain Open Graph Benchmark classification tasks compared to models without adaptation. These findings suggest that T3R offers a promising adaptation pipeline for graph-based systems, especially in scenarios where conventional fine-tuning or retraining is not feasible.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) deployed in real-world systems typically have fixed weights, often leading to degraded performance under distribution shifts. This issue can be mitigated by conventional fine-tuning, but in many real-world cases, collecting labeled data is expensive or infeasible. A potential approach is Test-Time Training (TTT), which adapts models' weights using unlabeled test data, yet it is typically limited to shallow updates that affect only a subset of model parameters. We propose T3R, leveraging multiple Rotograd matrices to improve task affinity between the target and auxiliary tasks, essential for effective test-time training. T3R further introduces a rotation technique that reorients self-supervised signals using these matrices to create surrogate gradients for the target task, allowing deeper adaptation across nearly the entire architecture. Empirically, T3R reduces MAE by 0.172 points over standard inference in regression datasets and achieves at least 9.37% relative improvement on cross-domain OGB classification benchmarks compared to models without adaptation. These results highlight the potential to develop an adaptation pipeline for graph-based systems, particularly in settings where conventional fine-tuning or retraining is infeasible.

items.originalTitle: Little Brains, Big Feats: Exploring Compact Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that small language models can effectively operate within Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems directly on-device without the need for GPU hardware. items.title: Researchers introduce Neural Subspace Reallocation for continual learning using compressible, retrievable LoRA memory units, achieving 10x faster recovery and improved accuracy on benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Neural Subspace Reallocation: Continual Learning as Retrieval-Based Subspace Memory Management
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Neural Subspace Reallocation (NSR), a novel approach to continual learning that treats Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules as compressible, retrievable memory units rather than disposable adapters. NSR operates by compressing learned LoRAs, storing them in a TaskKnowledgeBank, recalling related past LoRAs through embedding similarity, and reallocating active subspaces while protecting prior tasks via distillation. This method significantly accelerates recovery time and improves accuracy on benchmarks such as Split-CIFAR-100 and a heterogeneous 5-Datasets benchmark, outperforming memoryless allocation policies and achieving minimal forgetting.

The study demonstrates that the key driver of continual learning performance under fixed capacity is the memory mechanism—specifically compression and similarity-based retrieval—rather than a learned allocation policy. Empirical results show a 10-fold reduction in recovery time and a substantial decrease in backward transfer errors. Additionally, the compressed TaskKnowledgeBank remains compact, requiring only 0.29 MB of parameter memory per task, enabling efficient memory management with a capped total footprint while maintaining fast task recovery.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Neural Subspace Reallocation (NSR), which reframes continual learning as memory management over parameter subspaces. Instead of treating Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules as disposable per-task adapters, NSR manages them as compressible, retrievable memory units on a frozen backbone through a recurring cycle: (1) compress learned LoRAs via SVD, (2) reserve them in a TaskKnowledgeBank, (3) recall related past LoRAs by embedding similarity to warm-start new or returning tasks, and (4) reallocate the active subspace accordingly, with distillation protecting prior tasks. We prove that in cyclic environments any memoryless allocation policy incurs cumulative regret Omega(T(M-1)Delta_switch) relative to a history-aware policy backed by the Bank (Theorem 1). Empirically, on Split-CIFAR-100 the Bank reduces cyclic recovery time by 10x, exactly as predicted, and on the heterogeneous 5-Datasets benchmark NSR achieves the highest accuracy and the least forgetting, about 9x closer to zero backward transfer than the memoryless heuristics. Crucially, we run a controlled study that isolates which component matters: holding the Bank fixed and varying only the allocation rule, we find that a simple similarity-based retrieval rule matches or beats a learned reinforcement-learning controller (recovering recurring tasks in 0 vs 1.8 steps and reaching equal accuracy). Our central, honest finding is therefore that the memory mechanism -- compression and similarity retrieval -- rather than a learned allocation policy, drives continual-learning performance under fixed capacity. A memory-budget analysis confirms the compressed Bank stays small -- 0.29 MB of parameter memory per task -- so a top-K retention cap bounds the total footprint while preserving fast recovery for retained tasks.

items.title: Researchers propose GAIA framework using Gaussian Processes for global online data selection in instruction tuning, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines on three datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Online Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Gaussian Processes
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced GAIA, a new framework that uses Gaussian Process regression for global online data selection in instruction tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs). GAIA addresses limitations of existing batch-constrained methods by modeling data utility across the semantic space and dynamically prioritizing high-quality samples. This approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines on three datasets, demonstrating improved efficiency and robustness in instruction tuning.

GAIA incorporates an adaptive strategy fusion mechanism and leverages the fixed-share Hedge framework to maintain performance despite changing data quality during training. This global estimation process enables more effective data valuation compared to local batch optimization, marking a scalable advancement in LLM fine-tuning techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training and fine-tuning shifting its focus from data volume to data quality, quality data selection has emerged as a critical research topic. Existing online data selection methods for LLM training are typically "batch-constrained", limiting optimization to local utility within random batches. To overcome this, we propose GAIA (Global Adaptive Instruction tuning via GAussian processes), a framework that formulates data valuation as a global estimation process. GAIA employs Gaussian Process regression to model continuous utility manifolds across the semantic space, utilizing an adaptive strategy fusion mechanism to dynamically prioritize high-utility samples. By casting the strategy-posterior update as an instance of the classical fixed-share Hedge framework for tracking the best expert, we inherit a dynamic-regret guarantee that characterizes GAIA's robustness under non-stationary quality scores during training. Empirical evaluations on three datasets demonstrate that GAIA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines like \greats, establishing our method as a scalable and robust solution for efficient instruction tuning.

items.title: Researchers introduce AgentCanvas and KDLoop to automate architecture search for embodied agents, showing success-rate gains and revealing challenges in simulator-based evaluations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Automating the Design of Embodied AgentArchitectures
items.summary:
Researchers have developed AgentCanvas and KDLoop to automate the design of embodied agent architectures, which traditionally rely on manual composition of perception, memory, planning, and action modules. Their approach enables systematic architecture search through simulator rollouts, demonstrating improved success rates across tasks like vision-language navigation, embodied question answering, and language-conditioned manipulation. This work highlights both the potential benefits and current challenges of automated architecture search in embodied agents.

AgentCanvas provides a typed-graph runtime for editable node-and-wire programs with simulator-aware execution and detailed logging, while KDLoop is a search procedure that iteratively proposes, critiques, experiments, and distills architectures. Evaluations across multiple agents and search variants revealed that architecture-level search can yield deployable improvements, though issues such as rollout noise, local search traps, and partial credit assignment remain significant obstacles. These findings offer insights into the complexities of transferring automated architecture search methods from text-based to perceptual embodied domains.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30111v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embodied agents are typically built as hand-designed compositions of perception, memory, planning, and action modules. This modularity exposes a large architectural design space, but current systems still rely on researcher intuition to choose where information is stored, how observations are processed, and how model calls are connected. Agent Architecture Search (AAS) automates such design for text-domain agents, but has not been systematically evaluated on perceptual embodied agents through simulator rollouts. We study this transfer. We introduce AgentCanvas, a typed-graph runtime that hosts embodied executors as editable node-and-wire programs with simulator-aware execution and episode-level logs, and KDLoop, a coding-agent search procedure that cycles through proposal, critique, experiment, and distillation, with triggered reflection after stalls. We evaluate three AAS variants across four embodied executors spanning vision-language navigation, embodied question answering, and language-conditioned manipulation. The resulting 3x4 matrix shows that architecture-level search can produce deployable and directional success-rate gains on embodied tasks, while one apparent high-scoring candidate is rejected as leak-bearing. At the same time, the experiments expose constraints that are muted in text-domain AAS: optimization signals can be masked by rollout noise, search can become trapped in local edit basins, and episode-level credit assignment only partially emerges even when detailed logs are available. These results characterize both the promise and the current limits of automated architecture search for embodied agents.

items.title: Researchers extend Physics-Informed Neural Networks to reconstruct holographic duals with large hierarchies and false vacua in strongly coupled quantum field theories [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Gravitational Duals from Equations of State II: Large Hierarchies and False Vacua
items.summary:
Researchers have advanced the use of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to reconstruct holographic duals of strongly coupled quantum field theories, particularly in complex regimes featuring large hierarchies and false vacua. These conditions correspond to intricate thermodynamic behaviors and unusual renormalization group flows within the gauge/gravity duality framework. The team developed new methodological improvements to overcome challenges such as near-degenerate states and unprobed regions of the scalar potential, enabling accurate reconstruction of bulk scalar potentials from boundary thermodynamic data even in numerically stiff scenarios.

This work extends previous PINNs-based approaches by addressing conceptual and computational difficulties associated with large energy scale hierarchies and exotic vacuum structures. The researchers demonstrated robust agreement between the reconstructed potentials and the underlying thermodynamics, highlighting the potential of data-driven techniques to deepen understanding of strongly coupled systems. Their findings strengthen the connection between holography and machine learning, suggesting new avenues for exploring the structure of quantum field theories through inverse problems.
